sources.title: Nvidia's board launches investigation into CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy - Yahoo Finance
passages: Nvidia's ( NVDA ) board is launching an independent investigation into reports that a woman CEO Jensen Huang was having an affair with was allegedly spying on him for the Chinese government.

Last month, the New York Times reported the US intelligence service believed a Chinese national named Alice Huang, a former leader at Megaspeed, an Nvidia chip customer, and someone with a well-documented relationship with Huang himself, may have acted as an intelligence asset , sharing information with the ruling party in Beijing.
"There is clearly risk that Jensen could be removed as CEO depending on the Board investigation, and this will add risk to the stock as he is so important to the Nvidia story and strategy globally.
This will also increase major scrutiny regarding selling chips to China, which remains a key battleground issue in DC," he added.
"The key question investors will be asking is: Will Jensen remain CEO of Nvidia?….
The investigation will be key, and we would expect Jensen to continue in his role as CEO with no interruption in the near-term," Ives wrote.

"To my colleagues at Nvidia, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me.
My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust.
I am fully committed to Nvidia and will work to earn back your confidence," the CEO added.
"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," the board said in a statement.
Nvidia stock fell 5% before the bell on Monday.

Yorkville Ives partner and senior managing director Dan Ives wrote in a note to investors on Sunday that the investigation is a "black eye" for Huang and will likely spark multiple congressional investigations. This will also increase major scrutiny regarding selling chips to China, which remains a key battleground issue in DC," he added. The US government banned the sale of Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China, though the company has lobbied to continue offering the hardware, arguing that it is better for the world to use processors from a US company. sources.title: Jensen Huang’s affair with alleged Chinese spy puts Nvidia’s China ambitions under scrutiny
passages: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has never been quiet about his belief that the U.S. should continue selling AI chips to China, rather than shutting the country off from the technology.
The revelation that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy threatens to complicate that argument.
The Financial Times reported Friday on Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer.
Jensen Huang admitted to the affair and apologized in a memo to the company on Sunday.
U.S. intelligence officials believe Alice Huang was recruited by Chinese intelligence to gather information about the CEO and influence the company’s efforts to loosen chip export restrictions.
Once made, rumors of questionable allegiances can be hard to shake.

Even if Nvidia’s investigation finds that Huang didn’t share secrets with his paramour, the question is whether he’ll be able to convince Washington that Nvidia can still responsibly do business with China.

Huang met repeatedly with President Donald Trump and administration officials last year; afterward, the government reversed restrictions on Nvidia’s H20 chips and allowed exports of its more powerful H200 processors.

The idea that Huang needed any encouragement in the form of an attractive woman to push for greater access to China seems like a stretch, particularly because his lobbying efforts predate their reported meeting at an Nvidia event in early 2024.
At the end of the day, Huang is a salesman trying to dominate one of the world’s biggest AI markets.
The controversy comes at a sensitive moment for Nvidia.
Historically, China has been a big market for the company.
It has shrunk in recent years due to strict U.S. export controls and an aggressive push by Beijing for domestic alternatives.
In the three months ended July 26, Nvidia recorded $7.9 billion in revenue from customers headquartered in China, roughly 8% of total revenue.
Reuters reported last week that about 600,000 H200 chips are being held in Hong Kong, awaiting shipment to mainland China.
Beijing is pushing AI companies to prioritize buying chips from Chinese companies instead.
Nvidia’s independent directors, working with outside legal counsel, are investigating the matter, and Congress is already demanding answers .
Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment.

The company has been linked to investigations into the alleged diversion of Nvidia chips to China, which faces US restrictions on acquiring some of the most advanced processors.Here is what we know about the people, companies and allegations involved.Who is Jensen Huang?Born in Taipei in 1963, Jensen Huang, originally named Jen-Hsun, is one of the most recognisable figures in the global technology industry.Little known to the wider public until a few years ago, the 63-year-old has become a prominent face of the artificial intelligence boom.

While Nvidia has maintained a largely drama-free image around its chief, a former employee described Huang as a "very paradoxical" individual who was fiercely protective of his employees but could also, within the executive circle, be capable of "ripping people to shreds" over major mistakes or poor decisions..As the world debates the risks of AI, China closes the technology gap with US.Who is Alice Huang?Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, is the Chinese national identified in media reports as the woman allegedly recruited by Beijing to gather intelligence on Jensen Huang.Despite sharing the same surname, the two are not related.Public information about Alice Huang remains limited.

extraction.body: Jensen Huang, the billionaire chief executive of US chipmaker Nvidia, has built a reputation as one of the most influential figures in the global artificial intelligence industry. But the man behind the technology powering AI tools such as ChatGPT is now at the centre of a controversy involving an alleged Chinese spy, an extramarital affair and questions over the movement of advanced computer chips to China.Media reports last week said US intelligence officials believe Huang grew close to a Chinese executive who was funneling information to Beijing. The woman, identified as Alice Huang, is alleged to have been recruited by China to gather intelligence on the Nvidia chief.Nvidia's board said on Sunday it had opened a probe into its CEO and co-founder. Huang, 63, acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife and told employees he was "deeply sorry".The allegations have drawn attention to the intersection of personal relationships, corporate espionage and the increasingly sensitive technology rivalry between the United States and China.While the alleged relationship has put Huang's personal life under scrutiny, questions have also emerged over Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based data centre company where Alice Huang reportedly held a senior position. The company has been linked to investigations into the alleged diversion of Nvidia chips to China, which faces US restrictions on acquiring some of the most advanced processors.Here is what we know about the people, companies and allegations involved.Who is Jensen Huang?Born in Taipei in 1963, Jensen Huang, originally named Jen-Hsun, is one of the most recognisable figures in the global technology industry.Little known to the wider public until a few years ago, the 63-year-old has become a prominent face of the artificial intelligence boom. He regularly draws stadium-sized crowds at technology events, where he presents Nvidia's latest products and computing systems.His company makes Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), specialised processors that were initially developed to handle complex graphics but have since become essential to training and running advanced AI systems.Nvidia's rapid rise has pushed its market valuation to around $4.5 trillion, making it one of the world's most valuable companies. Huang, who owns roughly four per cent of the company, has an estimated fortune of $160 billion, according to Forbes.He founded Nvidia in 1993 with two friends after meeting them at a Silicon Valley diner. The company created the first GPU in 1999 and went on to benefit from the growth of video games, data centres, cloud computing and, more recently, generative AI.Huang has also developed a close informal relationship with US President Donald Trump, advising him on artificial intelligence. He travelled with Trump aboard Air Force One during the president's visit to Beijing earlier this year. His influence over an industry increasingly viewed as critical to national security has made the latest allegations particularly sensitive..China dismisses spy plot claim involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang as smear campaign.How did Jensen Huang rise to prominence?Huang's journey to the top of the technology industry began with an unconventional childhood. At the age of nine, he was sent with his brother to a boarding school in Kentucky after his uncle recommended the institution to their Taiwanese parents, believing it to be a prestigious school. It was, in fact, a school for troubled youth.Too young to enrol as a student, Huang boarded there but attended a nearby public school alongside the children of tobacco farmers. Struggling with English, he was bullied and made to clean toilets during what he later described as a difficult two-year period."We worked really hard, we studied really hard, and the kids were really tough," he recounted in an interview with US broadcaster NPR.But "the ending of the story is I loved the time I was there," Huang said.His parents later brought him home after settling in Oregon in the northwestern United States. sources.title: Nvidia shares drop nearly 6% in pre-market as alleged China spy links put Jensen Huang under board scrutiny
passages: Shares of US-based technology giant Nvidia witnessed renewed selling pressure in Monday's trade, falling 6% in pre-market trading to $176 apiece after the company's board launched an investigation into Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang, following his admission of an affair with a woman identified in a series of reports as a suspected Chinese spy.The shares had already faced significant volatility last week as concerns mounted over Big Tech's spending on AI infrastructure following the Democrats' sweeping victory in the US midterm elections.This latest controversy has added another layer of uncertainty to the stock, which has been under pressure since hitting its peak and has declined 22% from that level.

Jensen Huang is a huge figure in the artificial intelligence revolution and a close informal adviser to US President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly spoken out against regulating the industry so as not to let China gain the upper hand in the AI race.

The post said Huang “did something incredibly dumb” that was “bad for America” but added that “Jensen is irreplaceable for America's AI leadership.”China rejects allegationsChina swiftly rejected allegations of Beijing's involvement in the controversy“The so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated,” China's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said at a regular press briefing in Beijing, Bloomberg reported.
Nvidia is likely to face a barrage of questions about the controversy at its upcoming earnings report on November 17.

Billionaire investor Bill Ackman, founder of Pershing Square Capital Management, said on X that the Nvidia CEO was an “incredible human,” but added that if “indeed this is more than an affair, then it is obviously a real problem.” “I am hoping for a simple affair, not a risk to our national security,” he added.

coreStoryFacts.text: Nvidia's ( NVDA ) board is launching an independent investigation into reports that a woman CEO Jensen Huang was having an affair with was allegedly spying on him for the Chinese government.

Last month, the New York Times reported the US intelligence service believed a Chinese national named Alice Huang, a former leader at Megaspeed, an Nvidia chip customer, and someone with a well-documented relationship with Huang himself, may have acted as an intelligence asset , sharing information with the ruling party in Beijing.
"There is clearly risk that Jensen could be removed as CEO depending on the Board investigation, and this will add risk to the stock as he is so important to the Nvidia story and strategy globally.
This will also increase major scrutiny regarding selling chips to China, which remains a key battleground issue in DC," he added.
"The key question investors will be asking is: Will Jensen remain CEO of Nvidia?….
The investigation will be key, and we would expect Jensen to continue in his role as CEO with no interruption in the near-term," Ives wrote.

"To my colleagues at Nvidia, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me.
My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust.
I am fully committed to Nvidia and will work to earn back your confidence," the CEO added.
"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," the board said in a statement.
Nvidia stock fell 5% before the bell on Monday.
In an email to employees Sunday, Huang admitted to having an extramarital affair.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has never been quiet about his belief that the U.S. should continue selling AI chips to China, rather than shutting the country off from the technology.
The revelation that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy threatens to complicate that argument.
The Financial Times reported Friday on Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer.
Jensen Huang admitted to the affair and apologized in a memo to the company on Sunday.
U.S. intelligence officials believe Alice Huang was recruited by Chinese intelligence to gather information about the CEO and influence the company’s efforts to loosen chip export restrictions.
Once made, rumors of questionable allegiances can be hard to shake.

Even if Nvidia’s investigation finds that Huang didn’t share secrets with his paramour, the question is whether he’ll be able to convince Washington that Nvidia can still responsibly do business with China.

Huang met repeatedly with President Donald Trump and administration officials last year; afterward, the government reversed restrictions on Nvidia’s H20 chips and allowed exports of its more powerful H200 processors.

The idea that Huang needed any encouragement in the form of an attractive woman to push for greater access to China seems like a stretch, particularly because his lobbying efforts predate their reported meeting at an Nvidia event in early 2024.
At the end of the day, Huang is a salesman trying to dominate one of the world’s biggest AI markets.
The controversy comes at a sensitive moment for Nvidia.

sources.title: Jensen Huang’s affair with alleged Chinese spy puts Nvidia’s China ambitions under scrutiny
passages: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has never been quiet about his belief that the U.S. should continue selling AI chips to China, rather than shutting the country off from the technology.
The revelation that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy threatens to complicate that argument.
The Financial Times reported Friday on Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer.
Jensen Huang admitted to the affair and apologized in a memo to the company on Sunday.
U.S. intelligence officials believe Alice Huang was recruited by Chinese intelligence to gather information about the CEO and influence the company’s efforts to loosen chip export restrictions.
Once made, rumors of questionable allegiances can be hard to shake.

Even if Nvidia’s investigation finds that Huang didn’t share secrets with his paramour, the question is whether he’ll be able to convince Washington that Nvidia can still responsibly do business with China.

Huang met repeatedly with President Donald Trump and administration officials last year; afterward, the government reversed restrictions on Nvidia’s H20 chips and allowed exports of its more powerful H200 processors.

The idea that Huang needed any encouragement in the form of an attractive woman to push for greater access to China seems like a stretch, particularly because his lobbying efforts predate their reported meeting at an Nvidia event in early 2024.
At the end of the day, Huang is a salesman trying to dominate one of the world’s biggest AI markets.
The controversy comes at a sensitive moment for Nvidia.
Historically, China has been a big market for the company.
It has shrunk in recent years due to strict U.S. export controls and an aggressive push by Beijing for domestic alternatives.
In the three months ended July 26, Nvidia recorded $7.9 billion in revenue from customers headquartered in China, roughly 8% of total revenue.
Reuters reported last week that about 600,000 H200 chips are being held in Hong Kong, awaiting shipment to mainland China.
Beijing is pushing AI companies to prioritize buying chips from Chinese companies instead.
Nvidia’s independent directors, working with outside legal counsel, are investigating the matter, and Congress is already demanding answers .
Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment.

extraction.body: Jensen Huang, the billionaire chief executive of US chipmaker Nvidia, has built a reputation as one of the most influential figures in the global artificial intelligence industry. But the man behind the technology powering AI tools such as ChatGPT is now at the centre of a controversy involving an alleged Chinese spy, an extramarital affair and questions over the movement of advanced computer chips to China.Media reports last week said US intelligence officials believe Huang grew close to a Chinese executive who was funneling information to Beijing. The woman, identified as Alice Huang, is alleged to have been recruited by China to gather intelligence on the Nvidia chief.Nvidia's board said on Sunday it had opened a probe into its CEO and co-founder. Huang, 63, acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife and told employees he was "deeply sorry".The allegations have drawn attention to the intersection of personal relationships, corporate espionage and the increasingly sensitive technology rivalry between the United States and China.While the alleged relationship has put Huang's personal life under scrutiny, questions have also emerged over Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based data centre company where Alice Huang reportedly held a senior position. The company has been linked to investigations into the alleged diversion of Nvidia chips to China, which faces US restrictions on acquiring some of the most advanced processors.Here is what we know about the people, companies and allegations involved.Who is Jensen Huang?Born in Taipei in 1963, Jensen Huang, originally named Jen-Hsun, is one of the most recognisable figures in the global technology industry.Little known to the wider public until a few years ago, the 63-year-old has become a prominent face of the artificial intelligence boom. He regularly draws stadium-sized crowds at technology events, where he presents Nvidia's latest products and computing systems.His company makes Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), specialised processors that were initially developed to handle complex graphics but have since become essential to training and running advanced AI systems.Nvidia's rapid rise has pushed its market valuation to around $4.5 trillion, making it one of the world's most valuable companies. Huang, who owns roughly four per cent of the company, has an estimated fortune of $160 billion, according to Forbes.He founded Nvidia in 1993 with two friends after meeting them at a Silicon Valley diner. The company created the first GPU in 1999 and went on to benefit from the growth of video games, data centres, cloud computing and, more recently, generative AI.Huang has also developed a close informal relationship with US President Donald Trump, advising him on artificial intelligence. He travelled with Trump aboard Air Force One during the president's visit to Beijing earlier this year. His influence over an industry increasingly viewed as critical to national security has made the latest allegations particularly sensitive..China dismisses spy plot claim involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang as smear campaign.How did Jensen Huang rise to prominence?Huang's journey to the top of the technology industry began with an unconventional childhood. At the age of nine, he was sent with his brother to a boarding school in Kentucky after his uncle recommended the institution to their Taiwanese parents, believing it to be a prestigious school. It was, in fact, a school for troubled youth.Too young to enrol as a student, Huang boarded there but attended a nearby public school alongside the children of tobacco farmers. Struggling with English, he was bullied and made to clean toilets during what he later described as a difficult two-year period."We worked really hard, we studied really hard, and the kids were really tough," he recounted in an interview with US broadcaster NPR.But "the ending of the story is I loved the time I was there," Huang said.His parents later brought him home after settling in Oregon in the northwestern United States. He graduated from university at the age of 20 and went on to work at chipmakers AMD and LSI Logic.Huang eventually decided to establish his own company, with a focus on developing processors capable of handling computing tasks beyond the capabilities of conventional computers.Nvidia was founded in 1993 to "solve problems that normal computers can't," he said during an interview on the "No Priors" podcast.Shaping Nvidia's AI ambitionsHuang is known for his distinctive public image, almost always appearing in a black T-shirt and leather jacket. He also has a Nvidia logo tattoo and a fondness for sports cars.One former senior Nvidia employee described him to AFP as "the most driven person" he had ever met.His approach to artificial intelligence has also attracted attention. While some technology insiders have warned that unchecked AI development could pose an existential threat to humanity within a decade, Huang has rejected calls to deliberately slow the industry down."That kind of narrative is dramatic, it gets a lot of attention," but "it's not grounded on facts," he told CBS News in September."We should go as fast as we can" on AI, but labs should not release products that are not safe, he said.In Taiwan, where he was born, Huang is treated almost like a celebrity. Fans regularly crowd around him for photographs and autographs, while journalists have followed him to his barber shop and favourite night market."He has created the phenomena because of his personal charm," noted Wayne Lin of Witology Market Trend Research Institute."A person like him must be very busy and his schedule should be full every day meeting big bosses. But he remembers to eat street food when he comes to Taiwan," he said, calling Huang "unusually friendly."However, his public image has not always reflected the atmosphere inside the company. While Nvidia has maintained a largely drama-free image around its chief, a former employee described Huang as a "very paradoxical" individual who was fiercely protective of his employees but could also, within the executive circle, be capable of "ripping people to shreds" over major mistakes or poor decisions..As the world debates the risks of AI, China closes the technology gap with US.Who is Alice Huang?Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, is the Chinese national identified in media reports as the woman allegedly recruited by Beijing to gather intelligence on Jensen Huang.Despite sharing the same surname, the two are not related.Public information about Alice Huang remains limited. According to the New York Times, she was a senior executive at Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based company that rents out computing power to businesses seeking to train and operate AI systems.The newspaper, citing people briefed on the surveillance operation, reported that she was well connected at the highest levels of the global AI chip industry and spoke good English.An online search also brought up a short profile of Alice Huang, accompanied by a photograph, on a Chinese fund database. It listed previous employment at HSBC bank and as a reporter for Chinese media outlets CCTV and Hunan TV.US intelligence officials reportedly concluded last year that Alice Huang was targeting the Nvidia chief. The alleged relationship has since become a focus of media reports.What is known about their alleged relationship?Reports about the pair's relationship emerged last week, with Huang acknowledging to Nvidia employees on Sunday that he had been unfaithful to his wife. Photographs and videos from industry gatherings have also drawn attention to their association.One photograph from an industry party in 2024, posted on LinkedIn, appears to show Huang sitting next to a long-haired woman wearing elaborate jewellery, believed to be Alice Huang.The following year, both attended a dinner hosted by the Nvidia chief at a Chinese restaurant in Taipei during Computex, Taiwan's leading technology exhibition.Journalists filmed through the restaurant's glass windows and doors as Huang and a woman identified as Alice Huang, wearing a pink dress, mingled with other guests.At one point, Huang is seen putting his arm around her as she kisses him on the right cheek, according to press livestreams.She is also seen following the Nvidia chief as he re-enters the restaurant after speaking to journalists outside, running her fingers down his lower back. The two later leave in the same car.The reports have brought renewed scrutiny to Huang's personal life, although the alleged espionage operation has potentially wider implications for the global technology industry..China's spy chief warns 'hostile forces' using AI to threaten national security.What is Megaspeed and why is it under scrutiny?Megaspeed International is a Singapore-based data centre company that rents out computing power to other businesses for training and running AI systems. These chips are also considered strategically important because of their potential military applications.The United States has imposed restrictions on exports of Nvidia's most advanced chips to China, citing national security concerns. The restrictions are also part of Washington's broader effort to maintain its technological advantage over Beijing in artificial intelligence.The measures have made access to advanced computing hardware a sensitive issue for companies operating across international markets.The New York Times reported that the US government had been investigating Megaspeed since 2024 over concerns that it may have helped direct Nvidia chips to China. The newspaper also reported that Singapore authorities had investigated the company and questioned Alice Huang in 2025.Last year, Bloomberg News separately reported on the Singapore investigation into Megaspeed over the alleged smuggling of Nvidia chips to China. The claims have not been independently established, while the investigations into Megaspeed and the Nvidia chief's conduct could have significant implications for one of the most powerful companies in the technology industry.(With inputs from AFP and AP).Washington accuses Chinese AI firms of 'systematic' theft from US rivals.As the US and China form AI blocs, countries are increasingly torn between them.Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

He graduated from university at the age of 20 and went on to work at chipmakers AMD and LSI Logic.Huang eventually decided to establish his own company, with a focus on developing processors capable of handling computing tasks beyond the capabilities of conventional computers.Nvidia was founded in 1993 to "solve problems that normal computers can't," he said during an interview on the "No Priors" podcast.Shaping Nvidia's AI ambitionsHuang is known for his distinctive public image, almost always appearing in a black T-shirt and leather jacket.

He also has a Nvidia logo tattoo and a fondness for sports cars.One former senior Nvidia employee described him to AFP as "the most driven person" he had ever met.His approach to artificial intelligence has also attracted attention.

While some technology insiders have warned that unchecked AI development could pose an existential threat to humanity within a decade, Huang has rejected calls to deliberately slow the industry down."That kind of narrative is dramatic, it gets a lot of attention," but "it's not grounded on facts," he told CBS News in September."We should go as fast as we can" on AI, but labs should not release products that are not safe, he said.In Taiwan, where he was born, Huang is treated almost like a celebrity.

Fans regularly crowd around him for photographs and autographs, while journalists have followed him to his barber shop and favourite night market."He has created the phenomena because of his personal charm," noted Wayne Lin of Witology Market Trend Research Institute."A person like him must be very busy and his schedule should be full every day meeting big bosses.
But he remembers to eat street food when he comes to Taiwan," he said, calling Huang "unusually friendly."However, his public image has not always reflected the atmosphere inside the company.

While Nvidia has maintained a largely drama-free image around its chief, a former employee described Huang as a "very paradoxical" individual who was fiercely protective of his employees but could also, within the executive circle, be capable of "ripping people to shreds" over major mistakes or poor decisions..As the world debates the risks of AI, China closes the technology gap with US.Who is Alice Huang?Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, is the Chinese national identified in media reports as the woman allegedly recruited by Beijing to gather intelligence on Jensen Huang.Despite sharing the same surname, the two are not related.Public information about Alice Huang remains limited.

According to the New York Times, she was a senior executive at Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based company that rents out computing power to businesses seeking to train and operate AI systems.The newspaper, citing people briefed on the surveillance operation, reported that she was well connected at the highest levels of the global AI chip industry and spoke good English.An online search also brought up a short profile of Alice Huang, accompanied by a photograph, on a Chinese fund database.

It listed previous employment at HSBC bank and as a reporter for Chinese media outlets CCTV and Hunan TV.US intelligence officials reportedly concluded last year that Alice Huang was targeting the Nvidia chief.

The alleged relationship has since become a focus of media reports.What is known about their alleged relationship?Reports about the pair's relationship emerged last week, with Huang acknowledging to Nvidia employees on Sunday that he had been unfaithful to his wife.

Photographs and videos from industry gatherings have also drawn attention to their association.One photograph from an industry party in 2024, posted on LinkedIn, appears to show Huang sitting next to a long-haired woman wearing elaborate jewellery, believed to be Alice Huang.The following year, both attended a dinner hosted by the Nvidia chief at a Chinese restaurant in Taipei during Computex, Taiwan's leading technology exhibition.Journalists filmed through the restaurant's glass windows and doors as Huang and a woman identified as Alice Huang, wearing a pink dress, mingled with other guests.At one point, Huang is seen putting his arm around her as she kisses him on the right cheek, according to press livestreams.She is also seen following the Nvidia chief as he re-enters the restaurant after speaking to journalists outside, running her fingers down his lower back.

The two later leave in the same car.The reports have brought renewed scrutiny to Huang's personal life, although the alleged espionage operation has potentially wider implications for the global technology industry..China's spy chief warns 'hostile forces' using AI to threaten national security.What is Megaspeed and why is it under scrutiny?Megaspeed International is a Singapore-based data centre company that rents out computing power to other businesses for training and running AI systems.

These chips are also considered strategically important because of their potential military applications.The United States has imposed restrictions on exports of Nvidia's most advanced chips to China, citing national security concerns.

The restrictions are also part of Washington's broader effort to maintain its technological advantage over Beijing in artificial intelligence.The measures have made access to advanced computing hardware a sensitive issue for companies operating across international markets.The New York Times reported that the US government had been investigating Megaspeed since 2024 over concerns that it may have helped direct Nvidia chips to China.

The newspaper also reported that Singapore authorities had investigated the company and questioned Alice Huang in 2025.Last year, Bloomberg News separately reported on the Singapore investigation into Megaspeed over the alleged smuggling of Nvidia chips to China.

The claims have not been independently established, while the investigations into Megaspeed and the Nvidia chief's conduct could have significant implications for one of the most powerful companies in the technology industry.(With inputs from AFP and AP).Washington accuses Chinese AI firms of 'systematic' theft from US rivals.As the US and China form AI blocs, countries are increasingly torn between them.Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

sources.title: Nvidia shares drop nearly 6% in pre-market as alleged China spy links put Jensen Huang under board scrutiny
passages: Shares of US-based technology giant Nvidia witnessed renewed selling pressure in Monday's trade, falling 6% in pre-market trading to $176 apiece after the company's board launched an investigation into Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang, following his admission of an affair with a woman identified in a series of reports as a suspected Chinese spy.The shares had already faced significant volatility last week as concerns mounted over Big Tech's spending on AI infrastructure following the Democrats' sweeping victory in the US midterm elections.This latest controversy has added another layer of uncertainty to the stock, which has been under pressure since hitting its peak and has declined 22% from that level.

Jensen Huang is a huge figure in the artificial intelligence revolution and a close informal adviser to US President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly spoken out against regulating the industry so as not to let China gain the upper hand in the AI race.

The post said Huang “did something incredibly dumb” that was “bad for America” but added that “Jensen is irreplaceable for America's AI leadership.”China rejects allegationsChina swiftly rejected allegations of Beijing's involvement in the controversy“The so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated,” China's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said at a regular press briefing in Beijing, Bloomberg reported.
Nvidia is likely to face a barrage of questions about the controversy at its upcoming earnings report on November 17.

Billionaire investor Bill Ackman, founder of Pershing Square Capital Management, said on X that the Nvidia CEO was an “incredible human,” but added that if “indeed this is more than an affair, then it is obviously a real problem.” “I am hoping for a simple affair, not a risk to our national security,” he added.

passages: On its conference call, traders on prediction markets platform Kalshi think the company might talk about President Donald Trump after CEO Jensen Huang joined him on his trip to China .
Trump has 50-50 odds of being mentioned on the call, with the chances rising recently.
Huang joined Trump for his summit in Beijing with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
After the U.S.-China summit, neither country revealed if Trump or Xi discussed Taiwan , which is home to critical chip manufacturers.
Traders now only place 15% odds that the company discusses Taiwan Semiconductor Company , down from previously a 78% chance.
And there's a 55% chance the company will discuss humanoid robots.
In his keynote address at the CES Trade Show in January, Huang said he expects to see robots with some human-level capabilities this year.
This would be a new feature of the Nvidia calls as that topic didn't come up in the company's February earnings call.
In January, Trump cleared the way for Chinese purchases of the chip model.
That came with a 25% tariff on imports for chips that will be sent to China.
Huang's presence on the trip came as the status of Nvidia's H200 chip sales in China remains uncertain.
China, though, hasn't allowed firms to purchase the chip, Trump claimed to reporters.
All eyes are on Nvidia , the world's most valuable company and artificial intelligence trade darling, as it is set to report fiscal first-quarter earnings on Wednesday after the closing bell.
Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes a CNBC minority investment.

passages: "You’re not talking to someone who woke up a loser” - Jensen HuangJensen nearly lost his composure during a heated debate about selling chips to China, despite showing tremendous patience in response to the pushback. pic.twitter.com/A6F7RAXAgh April 16, 2026
During part of the conversation, which you can see by expanding the tweet embedded below, Patel said he doesn’t know whether it’s actually good to give Chinese access to AI chips.
“We have to keep innovating and, as you probably know, our share is growing, not decreasing.
While these two products are still leaders in their markets, many Chinese companies are now building products that can compete with them on price, features, and quality.
This could also happen in the AI chip industry.
Jensen says China already has access to a lot of compute power.
Although Nvidia still makes the most advanced, most efficient chips, he argues that China can still create advanced AI models through sheer brute force, like Huawei’s AI CloudMatrix cluster .
So, keeping the chipmaker out of the country would not stop its development of frontier AI models and would only result in Chinese AI being trained outside of the American tech stack.
Tom's Hardware is part of Future US Inc, an international media group and leading digital publisher.
Huang had a fairly nuanced response to this, but he also first pointed out that Mythos was trained on “fairly mundane capacity, and a fairly mundane amount of it."

The Nvidia boss says that keeping Chinese AI researchers using the American tech stack is a good thing for the U.S. When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works . Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang got into a heated debate during a recent podcast, during which he talked with Dwarkesh Patel about whether the U.S. should be selling chips to China. During part of the conversation, which you can see by expanding the tweet embedded below, Patel said he doesn’t know whether it’s actually good to give Chinese access to AI chips. Still, since he likes to play devil’s advocate during his interviews, where he takes an opposing stance to his guest, he asked the leather-clad chief of the world's largest AI chipmaker if doing so is a threat to American companies and national security . Patel gave Anthropic’s Claude Mythos as an example for his argument, which apparently revealed “thousands of zero-day vulnerabilities” in “every major operating system and every major web browser.” He said that if China had access to the massive amounts of compute that Nvidia delivers, it could probably have used it to develop cyber-offensive capabilities that threaten the United States' security. Huang had a fairly nuanced response to this, but he also first pointed out that Mythos was trained on “fairly mundane capacity, and a fairly mundane amount of it." "You’re not talking to someone who woke up a loser” - Jensen HuangJensen nearly lost his composure during a heated debate about selling chips to China, despite showing tremendous patience in response to the pushback. pic.twitter.com/A6F7RAXAgh April 16, 2026 You can expand the tweet above to see the meat of the tense exchange, which is about three minutes long. Jensen says China already has access to a lot of compute power. Although Nvidia still makes the most advanced, most efficient chips, he argues that China can still create advanced AI models through sheer brute force, like Huawei’s AI CloudMatrix cluster . So, keeping the chipmaker out of the country would not stop its development of frontier AI models and would only result in Chinese AI being trained outside of the American tech stack. “We want to make sure that all the AI developers in the world are developing on the American tech stack, and making the contributions, the advancements of AI — especially when it’s open source — available to the American ecosystem,” Huang said. “It would be extremely foolish to create two ecosystem: the open-source ecosystem, and it only runs on a foreign tech stack, and a closed ecosystem that runs on the American tech stack. I think that would be a horrible outcome for the United States.” Another argument against selling advanced AI chips to China is that it will do the same thing the country did with iPhones and Tesla. While these two products are still leaders in their markets, many Chinese companies are now building products that can compete with them on price, features, and quality. This could also happen in the AI chip industry. If and when Chinese-made AI chips get the same capabilities as Nvidia’s latest offerings, couldn’t Chinese AI companies just easily switch over to a Chinese AI chip in the future, should it become available, or if Beijing forces them to? “We have to keep innovating and, as you probably know, our share is growing, not decreasing. The premise that even if we competed in China, that we’re going to lose that market anyways… You’re not talking to somebody who woke up a loser,” Huang said. “That loser attitude, that loser premise makes no sense to me.” Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox. He then went on to say that AI chips aren’t as simple as vehicles, where users can easily swap one brand for another daily. “Computing is not like that. There’s a reason why the x86 deal exists. There’s a reason why ARM is so sticky. These ecosystems are hard to replace; it costs an enormous amount of time and energy, and most people don’t want to do it. So, it’s our job to continue to nurture that ecosystem, to keep advancing the technology so that we can compete in the marketplace,” the Nvidia chief added. “Conceding a marketplace based on the premise you described, I simply can’t acknowledge that. It makes no sense. Because I don’t think that the United States is a loser. Our industry is not a loser. That losing proposition, that losing mindset, makes no sense to me.” The biggest point Jensen makes is that AI technology has five layers — energy, chips, infrastructure, models, and applications — and that none should be ignored just for the sake of one. He says, “Why are you causing one layer of the AI industry to lose an entire market so that you could benefit from another layer of the AI industry? There are five layers, and every single layer has to succeed. The layer that has to succeed most is actually the AI applications. Why are you so fixated on that AI model? That one company? For what reason?” You can watch the complete podcast episode below. Follow Tom's Hardware on Google News , or add us as a preferred source , to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds. He then went on to say that AI chips aren’t as simple as vehicles, where users can easily swap one brand for another daily. “Computing is not like that. There’s a reason why the x86 deal exists. There’s a reason why ARM is so sticky. These ecosystems are hard to replace; it costs an enormous amount of time and energy, and most people don’t want to do it. So, it’s our job to continue to nurture that ecosystem, to keep advancing the technology so that we can compete in the marketplace,” the Nvidia chief added.

“Conceding a marketplace based on the premise you described, I simply can’t acknowledge that. It makes no sense. Because I don’t think that the United States is a loser. Our industry is not a loser. That losing proposition, that losing mindset, makes no sense to me.”

The biggest point Jensen makes is that AI technology has five layers — energy, chips, infrastructure, models, and applications — and that none should be ignored just for the sake of one. He says, “Why are you causing one layer of the AI industry to lose an entire market so that you could benefit from another layer of the AI industry? sources.title: Jensen Huang’s affair with alleged Chinese spy puts Nvidia’s China ambitions under scrutiny - TechCrunch
passages: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has never been quiet about his belief that the U.S. should continue selling AI chips to China, rather than shutting the country off from the technology.
The revelation that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy threatens to complicate that argument.
The Financial Times reported Friday on Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer.
Jensen Huang admitted to the affair and apologized in a memo to the company on Sunday.
U.S. intelligence officials believe Alice Huang was recruited by Chinese intelligence to gather information about the CEO and influence the company’s efforts to loosen chip export restrictions.
Once made, rumors of questionable allegiances can be hard to shake.

Even if Nvidia’s investigation finds that Huang didn’t share secrets with his paramour, the question is whether he’ll be able to convince Washington that Nvidia can still responsibly do business with China.

Huang met repeatedly with President Donald Trump and administration officials last year; afterward, the government reversed restrictions on Nvidia’s H20 chips and allowed exports of its more powerful H200 processors.

The idea that Huang needed any encouragement in the form of an attractive woman to push for greater access to China seems like a stretch, particularly because his lobbying efforts predate their reported meeting at an Nvidia event in early 2024.
At the end of the day, Huang is a salesman trying to dominate one of the world’s biggest AI markets.
The controversy comes at a sensitive moment for Nvidia.
Historically, China has been a big market for the company.
It has shrunk in recent years due to strict U.S. export controls and an aggressive push by Beijing for domestic alternatives.
In the three months ended July 26, Nvidia recorded $7.9 billion in revenue from customers headquartered in China, roughly 8% of total revenue.
Reuters reported last week that about 600,000 H200 chips are being held in Hong Kong, awaiting shipment to mainland China.
Beijing is pushing AI companies to prioritize buying chips from Chinese companies instead.
Nvidia’s independent directors, working with outside legal counsel, are investigating the matter, and Congress is already demanding answers .
Rebecca Bellan is a senior reporter at TechCrunch where she covers the business, policy, and emerging trends shaping artificial intelligence.
Her work has also appeared in Forbes, Bloomberg, The Atlantic, The Daily Beast, and other publications.
Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment.

coreStoryFacts.text: On its conference call, traders on prediction markets platform Kalshi think the company might talk about President Donald Trump after CEO Jensen Huang joined him on his trip to China .
Trump has 50-50 odds of being mentioned on the call, with the chances rising recently.
Huang joined Trump for his summit in Beijing with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
After the U.S.-China summit, neither country revealed if Trump or Xi discussed Taiwan , which is home to critical chip manufacturers.
Traders now only place 15% odds that the company discusses Taiwan Semiconductor Company , down from previously a 78% chance.
And there's a 55% chance the company will discuss humanoid robots.
In his keynote address at the CES Trade Show in January, Huang said he expects to see robots with some human-level capabilities this year.
This would be a new feature of the Nvidia calls as that topic didn't come up in the company's February earnings call.
In January, Trump cleared the way for Chinese purchases of the chip model.
That came with a 25% tariff on imports for chips that will be sent to China.
Huang's presence on the trip came as the status of Nvidia's H200 chip sales in China remains uncertain.
China, though, hasn't allowed firms to purchase the chip, Trump claimed to reporters.
All eyes are on Nvidia , the world's most valuable company and artificial intelligence trade darling, as it is set to report fiscal first-quarter earnings on Wednesday after the closing bell.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has never been quiet about his belief that the U.S. should continue selling AI chips to China, rather than shutting the country off from the technology.
The revelation that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy threatens to complicate that argument.
The Financial Times reported Friday on Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer.
Jensen Huang admitted to the affair and apologized in a memo to the company on Sunday.
U.S. intelligence officials believe Alice Huang was recruited by Chinese intelligence to gather information about the CEO and influence the company’s efforts to loosen chip export restrictions.
Once made, rumors of questionable allegiances can be hard to shake.

Even if Nvidia’s investigation finds that Huang didn’t share secrets with his paramour, the question is whether he’ll be able to convince Washington that Nvidia can still responsibly do business with China.

Huang met repeatedly with President Donald Trump and administration officials last year; afterward, the government reversed restrictions on Nvidia’s H20 chips and allowed exports of its more powerful H200 processors.

The idea that Huang needed any encouragement in the form of an attractive woman to push for greater access to China seems like a stretch, particularly because his lobbying efforts predate their reported meeting at an Nvidia event in early 2024.
At the end of the day, Huang is a salesman trying to dominate one of the world’s biggest AI markets.
The controversy comes at a sensitive moment for Nvidia.
Historically, China has been a big market for the company.
It has shrunk in recent years due to strict U.S. export controls and an aggressive push by Beijing for domestic alternatives.
In the three months ended July 26, Nvidia recorded $7.9 billion in revenue from customers headquartered in China, roughly 8% of total revenue.
Reuters reported last week that about 600,000 H200 chips are being held in Hong Kong, awaiting shipment to mainland China.
Beijing is pushing AI companies to prioritize buying chips from Chinese companies instead.
Nvidia’s independent directors, working with outside legal counsel, are investigating the matter, and Congress is already demanding answers .
Rebecca Bellan is a senior reporter at TechCrunch where she covers the business, policy, and emerging trends shaping artificial intelligence.
Her work has also appeared in Forbes, Bloomberg, The Atlantic, The Daily Beast, and other publications.
The revelation could have far-reaching ramifications for Nvidia and Huang, one of the most prominent advocates for the global AI infrastructure rollout and for relaxing US chip restrictions on China.
The allegations also raise national security questions given the strategic importance of Nvidia’s technology to the US.

8, Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang admitted he had been unfaithful in his marriage, effectively confirming a series of reports linking him romantically with a woman who has been identified as a suspected Chinese spy and whose company bought chips from Nvidia.

The Nvidia boss says that keeping Chinese AI researchers using the American tech stack is a good thing for the U.S. When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works . Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang got into a heated debate during a recent podcast, during which he talked with Dwarkesh Patel about whether the U.S. should be selling chips to China. During part of the conversation, which you can see by expanding the tweet embedded below, Patel said he doesn’t know whether it’s actually good to give Chinese access to AI chips. Still, since he likes to play devil’s advocate during his interviews, where he takes an opposing stance to his guest, he asked the leather-clad chief of the world's largest AI chipmaker if doing so is a threat to American companies and national security . Patel gave Anthropic’s Claude Mythos as an example for his argument, which apparently revealed “thousands of zero-day vulnerabilities” in “every major operating system and every major web browser.” He said that if China had access to the massive amounts of compute that Nvidia delivers, it could probably have used it to develop cyber-offensive capabilities that threaten the United States' security. Huang had a fairly nuanced response to this, but he also first pointed out that Mythos was trained on “fairly mundane capacity, and a fairly mundane amount of it." "You’re not talking to someone who woke up a loser” - Jensen HuangJensen nearly lost his composure during a heated debate about selling chips to China, despite showing tremendous patience in response to the pushback. pic.twitter.com/A6F7RAXAgh April 16, 2026 You can expand the tweet above to see the meat of the tense exchange, which is about three minutes long. Jensen says China already has access to a lot of compute power. Although Nvidia still makes the most advanced, most efficient chips, he argues that China can still create advanced AI models through sheer brute force, like Huawei’s AI CloudMatrix cluster . So, keeping the chipmaker out of the country would not stop its development of frontier AI models and would only result in Chinese AI being trained outside of the American tech stack. “We want to make sure that all the AI developers in the world are developing on the American tech stack, and making the contributions, the advancements of AI — especially when it’s open source — available to the American ecosystem,” Huang said. “It would be extremely foolish to create two ecosystem: the open-source ecosystem, and it only runs on a foreign tech stack, and a closed ecosystem that runs on the American tech stack. I think that would be a horrible outcome for the United States.” Another argument against selling advanced AI chips to China is that it will do the same thing the country did with iPhones and Tesla. The Nvidia boss says that keeping Chinese AI researchers using the American tech stack is a good thing for the U.S.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang got into a heated debate during a recent podcast, during which he talked with Dwarkesh Patel about whether the U.S. should be selling chips to China. During part of the conversation, which you can see by expanding the tweet embedded below, Patel said he doesn’t know whether it’s actually good to give Chinese access to AI chips. Still, since he likes to play devil’s advocate during his interviews, where he takes an opposing stance to his guest, he asked the leather-clad chief of the world's largest AI chipmaker if doing so is a threat to American companies and national security .

Patel gave Anthropic’s Claude Mythos as an example for his argument, which apparently revealed “thousands of zero-day vulnerabilities” in “every major operating system and every major web browser.” He said that if China had access to the massive amounts of compute that Nvidia delivers, it could probably have used it to develop cyber-offensive capabilities that threaten the United States' security. Huang had a fairly nuanced response to this, but he also first pointed out that Mythos was trained on “fairly mundane capacity, and a fairly mundane amount of it."

"You’re not talking to someone who woke up a loser” - Jensen HuangJensen nearly lost his composure during a heated debate about selling chips to China, despite showing tremendous patience in response to the pushback. pic.twitter.com/A6F7RAXAgh April 16, 2026
You can expand the tweet above to see the meat of the tense exchange, which is about three minutes long.

Jensen says China already has access to a lot of compute power. Although Nvidia still makes the most advanced, most efficient chips, he argues that China can still create advanced AI models through sheer brute force, like Huawei’s AI CloudMatrix cluster . So, keeping the chipmaker out of the country would not stop its development of frontier AI models and would only result in Chinese AI being trained outside of the American tech stack.

“We want to make sure that all the AI developers in the world are developing on the American tech stack, and making the contributions, the advancements of AI — especially when it’s open source — available to the American ecosystem,” Huang said. “It would be extremely foolish to create two ecosystem: the open-source ecosystem, and it only runs on a foreign tech stack, and a closed ecosystem that runs on the American tech stack. I think that would be a horrible outcome for the United States.”

Another argument against selling advanced AI chips to China is that it will do the same thing the country did with iPhones and Tesla. While these two products are still leaders in their markets, many Chinese companies are now building products that can compete with them on price, features, and quality. This could also happen in the AI chip industry. If and when Chinese-made AI chips get the same capabilities as Nvidia’s latest offerings, couldn’t Chinese AI companies just easily switch over to a Chinese AI chip in the future, should it become available, or if Beijing forces them to?

“We have to keep innovating and, as you probably know, our share is growing, not decreasing. The premise that even if we competed in China, that we’re going to lose that market anyways… You’re not talking to somebody who woke up a loser,” Huang said. “That loser attitude, that loser premise makes no sense to me.”
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

He then went on to say that AI chips aren’t as simple as vehicles, where users can easily swap one brand for another daily. “Computing is not like that. There’s a reason why the x86 deal exists. There’s a reason why ARM is so sticky. These ecosystems are hard to replace; it costs an enormous amount of time and energy, and most people don’t want to do it. So, it’s our job to continue to nurture that ecosystem, to keep advancing the technology so that we can compete in the marketplace,” the Nvidia chief added.

“Conceding a marketplace based on the premise you described, I simply can’t acknowledge that. It makes no sense. Because I don’t think that the United States is a loser. Our industry is not a loser. That losing proposition, that losing mindset, makes no sense to me.”

The biggest point Jensen makes is that AI technology has five layers — energy, chips, infrastructure, models, and applications — and that none should be ignored just for the sake of one. He says, “Why are you causing one layer of the AI industry to lose an entire market so that you could benefit from another layer of the AI industry? There are five layers, and every single layer has to succeed. The layer that has to succeed most is actually the AI applications. Why are you so fixated on that AI model? That one company? For what reason?”

sources.title: Jensen Huang’s affair with alleged Chinese spy puts Nvidia’s China ambitions under scrutiny - TechCrunch
passages: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has never been quiet about his belief that the U.S. should continue selling AI chips to China, rather than shutting the country off from the technology.
The revelation that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy threatens to complicate that argument.
The Financial Times reported Friday on Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer.
Jensen Huang admitted to the affair and apologized in a memo to the company on Sunday.
U.S. intelligence officials believe Alice Huang was recruited by Chinese intelligence to gather information about the CEO and influence the company’s efforts to loosen chip export restrictions.
Once made, rumors of questionable allegiances can be hard to shake.

Even if Nvidia’s investigation finds that Huang didn’t share secrets with his paramour, the question is whether he’ll be able to convince Washington that Nvidia can still responsibly do business with China.

Huang met repeatedly with President Donald Trump and administration officials last year; afterward, the government reversed restrictions on Nvidia’s H20 chips and allowed exports of its more powerful H200 processors.

The idea that Huang needed any encouragement in the form of an attractive woman to push for greater access to China seems like a stretch, particularly because his lobbying efforts predate their reported meeting at an Nvidia event in early 2024.
At the end of the day, Huang is a salesman trying to dominate one of the world’s biggest AI markets.
The controversy comes at a sensitive moment for Nvidia.
Historically, China has been a big market for the company.
It has shrunk in recent years due to strict U.S. export controls and an aggressive push by Beijing for domestic alternatives.
In the three months ended July 26, Nvidia recorded $7.9 billion in revenue from customers headquartered in China, roughly 8% of total revenue.
Reuters reported last week that about 600,000 H200 chips are being held in Hong Kong, awaiting shipment to mainland China.
Beijing is pushing AI companies to prioritize buying chips from Chinese companies instead.
Nvidia’s independent directors, working with outside legal counsel, are investigating the matter, and Congress is already demanding answers .
Rebecca Bellan is a senior reporter at TechCrunch where she covers the business, policy, and emerging trends shaping artificial intelligence.
Her work has also appeared in Forbes, Bloomberg, The Atlantic, The Daily Beast, and other publications.
Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment.

extraction.body: Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation? One of the Artificial Intelligence (AI) industry's most important figures has been accused of having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, prompting an investigation. US intelligence officials believed that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who had a close relationship with Nvidia CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang, was a spy for Beijing , according to a New York Times report. On Sunday, Huang admitted , external to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. US tech giant Nvidia, one of the most valuable companies in the world, has opened an independent investigation into the reports. The firm said it does not believe US national security had been compromised - and added that Huang was committed to continuing to lead the company. President Donald Trump said on Monday that the FBI is also investigating the affair . The FBI declined to comment further when contacted by the BBC. Trump said he spoke with Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign. "I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters. Here is what we know about the affair and why it matters. Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond Jensen Huang (left) and Alice Huang - also known as Huang Le - pictured at an event US officials believed that Alice Huang had been recruited to spy by China's top intelligence agency, the New York Times reported , external . Her current whereabouts are unknown. Alice Huang, who is of no relation to Jensen Huang, was a top executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed between March and November 2023. The firm had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia maintains was investigated and debunked. However, the BBC understands Megaspeed is under investigation by the Singapore government regarding previous allegations that the company was circumventing US sanctions on the export of Nvidia's high-end chips. The BBC has contacted Megaspeed for comment. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters on Monday at a regular daily press briefing: "We have already responded to this. The allegations about Chinese spies are entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China." The New York Times reported in late October that Trump had been briefed last year on intelligence alleging Alice Huang was spying on China's behalf. Asked by reporters on Sunday whether he wished he had "acted on the intelligence", Trump responded: "No, I don't think so. I think he's an honourable guy." US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, refused to comment when asked about Huang. Last spring, the secretary of state reportedly oversaw the drafting of a memo that warned the Trump administration about Huang's relationship with the Chinese businesswoman, according to the New York Times. Nvidia shares slide as US tech giant investigates CEO's affair with suspected Chinese spy Why Trump is all-in on AI despite the warnings Trump has said "whoever wins AI wins", and the fear is that if China gains the upper hand in AI, it will supercharge the country's military and surveillance capabilities. The US advantage is in large part because of US companies like Nvidia, working with producers like the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which makes more than 90% of the world's most advanced chips. Since 2022, the US has used various export controls to keep the top tech out of China, which it says helps retain America's competitive edge and protects its national security. This means companies like Nvidia have been largely locked out of the world's most lucrative market, with Huang once saying that Nvidia's share of the Chinese market had gone from around 95% to effectively zero. Huang has engaged in shuttle diplomacy between Washington and Beijing, hoping to find a US-approved way back in, and shaping US policy on China along the way. Sunday's revelations may explain why Huang has failed to bring home the biggest prize of all to Nvidia: the Trump administration's blessing to sell all but its most advanced chips to China . Huang has soared to international importance with his company Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang was nine years old when his family moved to the West Coast of the US. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a master's degree in the same field from Stanford University. Huang then worked at US chip firm AMD before co-founding Nvidia. Known as "Daddy Huang" in Taiwan and once lauded as the "Taylor Swift of tech" , he has a reputation as a workaholic and perfectionist with incredibly high standards for his staff. He has an estimated fortune of $155bn (£115bn), according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. "Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on Huang, told the BBC, adding that he was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today. Huang has a famously close relationship with Trump. At the recent AI summit at the White House, where 42 tech executives were present, the president was flanked by Elon Musk and Huang. extraction.body: Jensen Huang, the leather-jacket-wearing and autograph-signing co-founder and CEO of Nvidia, has made himself a seemingly inseparable part of the AI chipmaker. But now that an investigation is underway into whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, that tight control at the company's helm is creating worries about whether he could actually be replaced, if such a move were deemed necessary. The investigation comes after the New York Times reported late last week that Huang had a close romantic relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese tech executive who was spying on behalf of China. It's unclear when he met the executive of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, but the two were photographed together in 2024 . Nvidia's board said Sunday it had no reason to believe that state or company secrets were compromised, but was undertaking an independent investigation in light of the reports. U.S. House Republican committee leaders have also called on Huang to sit for a briefing on his relationship with the woman. Nvidia's shares slide as chip giant probes CEO Jensen Huang over spy claims In a message to his staff, Huang admitted to having an affair and apologized to his family and colleagues for breaking their trust. "I am fully committed to Nvidia and will work to earn back your confidence," he wrote. Huang will stay on as CEO while the investigation takes place. But if the board were to oust him, or if he changed course and stepped down, tech analysts like Dan Ives say finding someone to take his place would be nearly impossible. "In my opinion, Jensen is a one of one," said Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., a New York-based modern merchant bank. "Nvidia is here because of Jensen." Nvidia began as a graphics card maker in 1993 until company leaders — Huang in particular — realized that its graphics processor units could power more than just games. The company pivoted to making chips for supercomputers in the early 2010s, betting on an artificial intelligence boom that wouldn't come for many years. An early partnership with OpenAI led to a long-term relationship with the ChatGPT creator, which still relies on Nvidia's chips to power its technology today. Amazon , Meta , Google and virtually every other company building AI tools rely on the chipmaker's hardware to power their systems. Worth about $4.5 trillion US today, Nvidia is the second most valuable company in the world , and invaluable to the AI ecosystem as a whole, according to Ives. Nvidia probes whether CEO Jensen Huang targeted by foreign intelligence as he admits affair Can AI be regulated? Why experts say government intervention is needed — but could be tricky From his place atop the massive company, Huang became something of a rock star, routinely signing fan autographs at public appearances. One of his signature leather jackets sold for more than $1 million at an auction earlier this year. "He's gotten to the point where he's sort of like the king of tech. Everybody listens to what Jensen has to say," said Bob O'Donnell, president and chief analyst at Technalysis Research. Outside of his own company, Huang has also championed the AI buildout, financially backing companies like cloud computing company CoreWeave and Anthropic, maker of the Claude chatbot. He has also dismissed fears about an AI bubble and challenged apocalyptic warnings about the technology's existential threat to humanity, and has forged a close relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump . Nvidia shares tumble as company investigates CEO Jensen Huang Ives says the loss of Huang's advocacy would be a major hit to the industry if he had to step away. Meanwhile, within the company, Huang created an unusually flat chain of command, with many employees reporting directly to him rather than to high-level executives. On a podcast earlier this year, Huang said as many as 60 people reported to him directly. The company's site lists only a handful of high-ranking executives aside from Huang. Two of Huang's children are also on staff at the company — his son Spencer is director of product for robotics, while his daughter Madison is senior director of product marketing. With Huang having held control at Nvidia for so long, analysts say there is no clear successor. "There's no one person or two people or three people that could replace Jensen. And that's a scary thing for investors, given this … black-eye moment that we're seeing," Ives said. If Huang were forced to step down, Ives worries Nvidia would never fully recover from the loss of his leadership, given his integral role in the company's growth. But others say with a firm as big as Nvidia, there are others who could take on the top job. The falling star of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang | About That "You don't create a company that large by yourself, right? It's just not possible. There's a huge team of very strong, smart, capable people," O'Donnell said. While he agrees that Huang's loss would be massive, he says the company's technology roadmap — used to plan the next few years — is already laid out, making any potential successor's job easier. O'Donnell expects Nvidia is on track to keep its leadership position among chipmakers for now, and doesn't expect a shakeup at the top would change that. Furthermore, with the board saying it has confidence in Huang , O'Donnell says he doesn't expect those members would try to oust him. Still, if Huang does stay on as CEO, his grip on the company likely won't be so tight going forward, O'Donnell says, as other high-ranking executives are likely to take centre stage as spokespeople and dealmakers at least some of the time. "It's hard to replace an iconic figure who just lights up a room," he said. But "if the board is smart, and I'm sure they are, they recognize they're going to have to address this so people can regain confidence in the company."

Jensen Huang is the president and CEO of Nvidia and co-founded the multi-national technology company in 1993 with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem. The 63-year-old was born in Taiwan then moved to Thailand with his family as a child before being sent by his parents to live in the U.S. at age nine. He graduated from Oregon State University as an electrical engineer and received a master’s degree in the same field from Stanford University. Ranked the eighth richest man in the world by Forbes and sometimes known as “Daddy Huang,” he’s been also recognized for his trademark leather jackets and high-profile launches. Huang also has a close relationship with President Donald Trump, having travelled to China in May as part of a state visit. He’s also pushed Trump to ease export restrictions on Nvidia chips. He’s been married to his wife Lori Huang since 1985 and has two children. Their daughter Madison is a senior director of product and technical marketing for physical AI platforms at Nvidia, while son Spencer manages robotics software products. The Nvidia CEO apologized to both his wife and children in a letter the company posted Sunday, admitting he was unfaithful. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” Huang wrote. “My family bears no responsibility for my choices. I do. Please give them privacy. But Beijing has been interested in AI microchips from Nvidia for several years. Its most advanced chips are barred from sale in China, but the Trump administration gave permission for Nvidia to sell its H200 chips to 10 approved Chinese firms last year. China has imposed its own restrictions over concerns of dependence on U.S. technology, with Reuters reporting about 600,000 of the company’s chips are stored in Hong Kong awaiting shipment. “We know for a fact that China has engaged in espionage particularly in those areas it has identified as strategic and one of those areas right now is going to be frontier AI,” said Stephanie Carvin, a former national security analyst and associate professor at Carleton University. “It absolutely needs and wants the chips that are produced by Nvidia and other companies to further its ambitions in this kind of geopolitical race.” Alice Huang is a Chinese citizen and former executive of Megaspeed, an AI company that calls itself a specialized Cloud provider and a partner of Nvidia in the Asia-Pacific region. The company has been under investigation by the U.S. government over suspicions it helped Beijing gain access to the U.S. tech giant’s advanced AI chips that are currently barred. In December 2025, Megaspeed posted a message that its company had undergone multiple inspections by U.S. government departments, as well as Nvidia. “These thorough investigations have confirmed that there has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities, and this demonstrates that we are a compliant and legitimate company,” the statement reads. The board said it has confidence in Huang and his leadership team. They’ve asked him to appear on Nov. 18 or to provide an alternative date by Nov. 11. Trump said Monday that the FBI was investigating the affair between Huang and an alleged Chinese spy, adding he didn’t think the CEO would have anything to worry about. “I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he’ll be in good shape,” Trump told reporters.
