extraction.body: Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation? One of the Artificial Intelligence (AI) industry's most important figures has been accused of having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, prompting an investigation. US intelligence officials believed that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who had a close relationship with Nvidia CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang, was a spy for Beijing , according to a New York Times report. On Sunday, Huang admitted , external to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. US tech giant Nvidia, one of the most valuable companies in the world, has opened an independent investigation into the reports. The firm said it does not believe US national security had been compromised - and added that Huang was committed to continuing to lead the company. President Donald Trump said on Monday that the FBI is also investigating the affair . The FBI declined to comment further when contacted by the BBC. Trump said he spoke with Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign. "I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters. Here is what we know about the affair and why it matters. Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond Jensen Huang (left) and Alice Huang - also known as Huang Le - pictured at an event US officials believed that Alice Huang had been recruited to spy by China's top intelligence agency, the New York Times reported , external . Her current whereabouts are unknown. Alice Huang, who is of no relation to Jensen Huang, was a top executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed between March and November 2023. The firm had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia maintains was investigated and debunked. However, the BBC understands Megaspeed is under investigation by the Singapore government regarding previous allegations that the company was circumventing US sanctions on the export of Nvidia's high-end chips. The BBC has contacted Megaspeed for comment. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters on Monday at a regular daily press briefing: "We have already responded to this. The allegations about Chinese spies are entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China." The New York Times reported in late October that Trump had been briefed last year on intelligence alleging Alice Huang was spying on China's behalf. Asked by reporters on Sunday whether he wished he had "acted on the intelligence", Trump responded: "No, I don't think so. I think he's an honourable guy." US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, refused to comment when asked about Huang. Last spring, the secretary of state reportedly oversaw the drafting of a memo that warned the Trump administration about Huang's relationship with the Chinese businesswoman, according to the New York Times. Nvidia shares slide as US tech giant investigates CEO's affair with suspected Chinese spy Why Trump is all-in on AI despite the warnings Trump has said "whoever wins AI wins", and the fear is that if China gains the upper hand in AI, it will supercharge the country's military and surveillance capabilities. The US advantage is in large part because of US companies like Nvidia, working with producers like the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which makes more than 90% of the world's most advanced chips. Since 2022, the US has used various export controls to keep the top tech out of China, which it says helps retain America's competitive edge and protects its national security. This means companies like Nvidia have been largely locked out of the world's most lucrative market, with Huang once saying that Nvidia's share of the Chinese market had gone from around 95% to effectively zero. Huang has engaged in shuttle diplomacy between Washington and Beijing, hoping to find a US-approved way back in, and shaping US policy on China along the way. Sunday's revelations may explain why Huang has failed to bring home the biggest prize of all to Nvidia: the Trump administration's blessing to sell all but its most advanced chips to China . Huang has soared to international importance with his company Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang was nine years old when his family moved to the West Coast of the US. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a master's degree in the same field from Stanford University. Huang then worked at US chip firm AMD before co-founding Nvidia. Known as "Daddy Huang" in Taiwan and once lauded as the "Taylor Swift of tech" , he has a reputation as a workaholic and perfectionist with incredibly high standards for his staff. He has an estimated fortune of $155bn (£115bn), according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. "Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on Huang, told the BBC, adding that he was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today. Huang has a famously close relationship with Trump. At the recent AI summit at the White House, where 42 tech executives were present, the president was flanked by Elon Musk and Huang. extraction.body: Jensen Huang, the leather-jacket-wearing and autograph-signing co-founder and CEO of Nvidia, has made himself a seemingly inseparable part of the AI chipmaker. But now that an investigation is underway into whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, that tight control at the company's helm is creating worries about whether he could actually be replaced, if such a move were deemed necessary. The investigation comes after the New York Times reported late last week that Huang had a close romantic relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese tech executive who was spying on behalf of China. It's unclear when he met the executive of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, but the two were photographed together in 2024 . Nvidia's board said Sunday it had no reason to believe that state or company secrets were compromised, but was undertaking an independent investigation in light of the reports. U.S. House Republican committee leaders have also called on Huang to sit for a briefing on his relationship with the woman. Nvidia's shares slide as chip giant probes CEO Jensen Huang over spy claims In a message to his staff, Huang admitted to having an affair and apologized to his family and colleagues for breaking their trust. "I am fully committed to Nvidia and will work to earn back your confidence," he wrote. Huang will stay on as CEO while the investigation takes place. But if the board were to oust him, or if he changed course and stepped down, tech analysts like Dan Ives say finding someone to take his place would be nearly impossible. "In my opinion, Jensen is a one of one," said Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., a New York-based modern merchant bank. "Nvidia is here because of Jensen." Nvidia began as a graphics card maker in 1993 until company leaders — Huang in particular — realized that its graphics processor units could power more than just games. The company pivoted to making chips for supercomputers in the early 2010s, betting on an artificial intelligence boom that wouldn't come for many years. An early partnership with OpenAI led to a long-term relationship with the ChatGPT creator, which still relies on Nvidia's chips to power its technology today. Amazon , Meta , Google and virtually every other company building AI tools rely on the chipmaker's hardware to power their systems. Worth about $4.5 trillion US today, Nvidia is the second most valuable company in the world , and invaluable to the AI ecosystem as a whole, according to Ives. Nvidia probes whether CEO Jensen Huang targeted by foreign intelligence as he admits affair Can AI be regulated? Why experts say government intervention is needed — but could be tricky From his place atop the massive company, Huang became something of a rock star, routinely signing fan autographs at public appearances. One of his signature leather jackets sold for more than $1 million at an auction earlier this year. "He's gotten to the point where he's sort of like the king of tech. Everybody listens to what Jensen has to say," said Bob O'Donnell, president and chief analyst at Technalysis Research. Outside of his own company, Huang has also championed the AI buildout, financially backing companies like cloud computing company CoreWeave and Anthropic, maker of the Claude chatbot. He has also dismissed fears about an AI bubble and challenged apocalyptic warnings about the technology's existential threat to humanity, and has forged a close relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump . Nvidia shares tumble as company investigates CEO Jensen Huang Ives says the loss of Huang's advocacy would be a major hit to the industry if he had to step away. Meanwhile, within the company, Huang created an unusually flat chain of command, with many employees reporting directly to him rather than to high-level executives. On a podcast earlier this year, Huang said as many as 60 people reported to him directly. The company's site lists only a handful of high-ranking executives aside from Huang. Two of Huang's children are also on staff at the company — his son Spencer is director of product for robotics, while his daughter Madison is senior director of product marketing. With Huang having held control at Nvidia for so long, analysts say there is no clear successor. "There's no one person or two people or three people that could replace Jensen. And that's a scary thing for investors, given this … black-eye moment that we're seeing," Ives said. If Huang were forced to step down, Ives worries Nvidia would never fully recover from the loss of his leadership, given his integral role in the company's growth. But others say with a firm as big as Nvidia, there are others who could take on the top job. The falling star of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang | About That "You don't create a company that large by yourself, right? It's just not possible. There's a huge team of very strong, smart, capable people," O'Donnell said. While he agrees that Huang's loss would be massive, he says the company's technology roadmap — used to plan the next few years — is already laid out, making any potential successor's job easier. O'Donnell expects Nvidia is on track to keep its leadership position among chipmakers for now, and doesn't expect a shakeup at the top would change that. Furthermore, with the board saying it has confidence in Huang , O'Donnell says he doesn't expect those members would try to oust him. Still, if Huang does stay on as CEO, his grip on the company likely won't be so tight going forward, O'Donnell says, as other high-ranking executives are likely to take centre stage as spokespeople and dealmakers at least some of the time. "It's hard to replace an iconic figure who just lights up a room," he said. But "if the board is smart, and I'm sure they are, they recognize they're going to have to address this so people can regain confidence in the company."

extraction.body: When you go poking neighbours garden and picking fruits nothing good comes out of it The CEO of tech giant Nvidia is under scrutiny by both his own company and politicians amid reports he was the target of an alleged Chinese spy. As a result of the allegations and investigation, Nvidia’s stock fell four per cent on Monday. The New York Times reported on Oct. 29 that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had been involved in a relationship with Alice Huang , a former executive of Nvidia Cloud partner Megaspeed. Eight days later on Nov. 6, the New York Times reported U.S. intelligence had alleged she was a spy for Beijing. Huang acknowledged his affair in a letter to his family and the company this weekend. Here’s what is known so far about Huang, his relationship with the Megaspeed former executive and what this means for the Nvidia going forward. Jensen Huang is the president and CEO of Nvidia and co-founded the multi-national technology company in 1993 with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem. The 63-year-old was born in Taiwan then moved to Thailand with his family as a child before being sent by his parents to live in the U.S. at age nine. He graduated from Oregon State University as an electrical engineer and received a master’s degree in the same field from Stanford University. Ranked the eighth richest man in the world by Forbes and sometimes known as “Daddy Huang,” he’s been also recognized for his trademark leather jackets and high-profile launches. Huang also has a close relationship with President Donald Trump, having travelled to China in May as part of a state visit. He’s also pushed Trump to ease export restrictions on Nvidia chips. He’s been married to his wife Lori Huang since 1985 and has two children. Their daughter Madison is a senior director of product and technical marketing for physical AI platforms at Nvidia, while son Spencer manages robotics software products. The Nvidia CEO apologized to both his wife and children in a letter the company posted Sunday, admitting he was unfaithful. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” Huang wrote. “My family bears no responsibility for my choices. I do. Please give them privacy. But Beijing has been interested in AI microchips from Nvidia for several years. Its most advanced chips are barred from sale in China, but the Trump administration gave permission for Nvidia to sell its H200 chips to 10 approved Chinese firms last year. China has imposed its own restrictions over concerns of dependence on U.S. technology, with Reuters reporting about 600,000 of the company’s chips are stored in Hong Kong awaiting shipment. “We know for a fact that China has engaged in espionage particularly in those areas it has identified as strategic and one of those areas right now is going to be frontier AI,” said Stephanie Carvin, a former national security analyst and associate professor at Carleton University. “It absolutely needs and wants the chips that are produced by Nvidia and other companies to further its ambitions in this kind of geopolitical race.” Alice Huang is a Chinese citizen and former executive of Megaspeed, an AI company that calls itself a specialized Cloud provider and a partner of Nvidia in the Asia-Pacific region. The company has been under investigation by the U.S. government over suspicions it helped Beijing gain access to the U.S. tech giant’s advanced AI chips that are currently barred. In December 2025, Megaspeed posted a message that its company had undergone multiple inspections by U.S. government departments, as well as Nvidia. “These thorough investigations have confirmed that there has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities, and this demonstrates that we are a compliant and legitimate company,” the statement reads. Global News has requested comment on the latest investigation involving its former executive. It is not known at this time when the pair started their relationship, but Reuters reported the two were previously pictured at a bar together in Taipei in 2025 during a technology conference. The affair appears to have hallmarks of what security experts call a “honey pot.” “They could be convincing you to try and give up information that you have or to make certain decisions and try to persuade you in some way,” she said. “But even just the affair itself can be harmful, right, because it can be used as blackmail.” Chinese industrial espionage has been a significant concern for officials over recent decades in both Canada and the U.S. “The long-term cost to the American economy and national security cannot be precisely measured, but estimates run into the billions of dollars for commercial and technological espionage.” Following Huang’s apology, Nvidia announced Sunday it was launching an investigation led by a committee of independent directors and assisted by outside counsel. The company said it prioritizes national and economic security, though adds it has “no reason to believe” either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised. The board said it has confidence in Huang and his leadership team. Nvidia appears to be backing its CEO for now, but Jeffrey Sonnenfeld at Yale University’s School of Management said while Huang has no successor at this time and has been praised for his work with the company, his future is “50-50.” “It’s 50-50 whether or not he can hold onto his position,” Sonnenfeld told Global News. “There’s a blow to his credibility though already that he would put the company at risk … Even if exonerated, he certainly has a permanent black eye for the recklessness.” U.S. lawmakers have launched their own investigation, with three Republican House committee chairs requesting Huang appear before them for a joint, closed-door briefing on his interactions with Alice Huang. They’ve asked him to appear on Nov. 18 or to provide an alternative date by Nov. 11. Trump said Monday that the FBI was investigating the affair between Huang and an alleged Chinese spy, adding he didn’t think the CEO would have anything to worry about. “I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he’ll be in good shape,” Trump told reporters.

extraction.body: The Skydance CEO says, "AI really has the potential to be the biggest creative unlock in modern history." In his first earnings call as CEO at the helm of both Paramount and Warner Bros., David Ellison talked up his merged Hollywood empire as a tech-forward enterprise — and part of that tightrope walk included an embrace of AI while also dismissing “AI slop.” It’s a two-step that’s not necessarily an easy one. The technology is widely seen as a harbinger of doom for Hollywood’s traditional workflows (i.e. building sets, shooting with real background extras, going on-location, etc) while also being increasingly adapted and integrated into the business (see: Ben Affleck’s VFX firm, which has helped Netflix use AI on 300-plus titles so far, while supposedly preserving the things that make Hollywood, Hollywood). Ellison told analysts that he expects AI to help his company’s studios make content faster and cheaper, likening the technology as the biggest breakthrough in the industry since CGI effects went mainstream. Skydance plans to spend $30 billion annually across its content portfolio — that’s includes everything from prestige TV HBO projects to CBS procedurals and MTV reality shows as well as NFL sports rights and features at Warners and Paramount. “I don’t think it can be discounted how fast this technology is moving,” Ellison said after table-setting by saying that “in a world of AI slop we think there will always be a premium for truly hand-crafted storytelling.” Ellison has a unique lens into the issue as heir to his father Larry Ellison’s AI-powered Oracle tech fortune, which is a key facet of his effort to rebrand legacy Hollywood studios as a tech-centric venture. (To that point, the enterprise cloud apps of Oracle Fusion got a call out in the earnings call as well when talking about consolidating back office functions.) The CEO also views franchise IP — he described his empire as having 40 $1 billion franchises — as a moat protecting against the onslaught of AI content, delivering more premium experiences to his 203 million-plus subscribers at a soon-to-be merged Paramount+ and HBO Max. He then launched into an anecdote about a franchise that his Skydance Media has rebooted multiple times over the past two decades. “AI really has the potential to be the biggest creative unlock in modern history,” Ellison bullishly said. “The last time we saw anything close to this was really the advent of CGI and digital composites in the early ’90s. That technology gave birth to amazing stories like Jurassic Park and Terminator 2 . It’s hard to imagine that AI is not going to have a more significant impact than that. I personally believe that’s going to be an incredible unlock on creativity.” “If you go back in time, speaking of Terminator which everyone knows is one of my favorites, if you go back to ’83, when James Cameron made that movie it was made for $4 million,” Ellison noted. “If you wanted to make that picture today shot-for-shot, it’d be $60 million-$70 million.” The CEO added: “There’s not a lot of bets that get taken like that across our industry. And we think these tools will help unlock more original storytelling by being able to make the budgets more digestible to take that amount of risk.” Cameron, who directed the original Arnold Schwarzenegger feature as well as its acclaimed sequel, has been one of the CEO’s biggest backers (and an early “Team Ellison” advocate as Skydance was fighting Netflix for its Warner Bros. prize). The Avatar helmer has himself been on the vanguard of the technology, with his Lightstorm banner just buying an AI-driven 3D post-production firm in September. Skydance is also looking to bake in an AI productivity narrative as it looks to find some $6 billion in cost-synergies from merging Paramount and Warner Bros. In addition to finding redundancies in corporate overhead, real estate and facilities as well as consolidating back office and corporate functions, those efficiencies include scaling AI-workflows across the combined company. That includes merging Paramount+ and HBO Max within a year, which Ellison described as an “ambitious target” that is “possible because of the latest tools in artificial intelligence.”

extraction.body: DAVID FABER: Becky, thank you. Thanks to the whole "Squawk" team, of course. We're going to run into your show for the rest of it, at least. And I'm very happy, obviously, to be joined by David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz. You're going to be ringing the bell about 50 minutes from now or so. It's been quite a journey, David. I followed it very closely, of course, as you know. And, you know, you started the bidding for Warner at $18 a share. You ended at 31. When you include what you had to pay Netflix for their break fee, it was an increase of as much as $47 billion from your initial bid. Why is it worth it? DAVID ELLISON: Well, first, David, I don't know what you're talking about in terms of the journey here. It was smooth and easy. And, no, it truly is. Walking in here today was quite remarkable because I remember the last time we were here was when we launched the hostile on your show. So to be coming full circle today— ELLISON: Is really quite remarkable. And look, the reason why we went through everything that we did is because with the combination and the completion of this transaction, we are positioned to win in every single vertical that we operate in. By combining Paramount and Warner Bros., we have the greatest content engine with marquee intellectual property. You're uniting "Lord of the Rings", "Harry Potter", the DC universe under the same house as "Mission Impossible", "Top Gun: Maverick", "G.I. Joe", "Transformers," you're immediately getting to scale on streaming. Between HBO Max and Paramount Plus, over 200 million global streaming subscribers, with, with an addition to Pluto, 80 million monthly active users. We have an unmatched sports portfolio that includes the NFL, MLB, NHL, UEFA, basically, PGA, just to name a few. Not to mention the Olympics internationally. And an incredibly profitable linear portfolio anchored by CBS. When you look at our primetime lineup, the NCIS night just launched 42 percent up basically from last year, five of the top 10 cable channels. And we will transform this business. FABER: Well, what, let me start there then, because, you know, you start as well, though. I mentioned the 47 billion additionally. Nobody thought you were going to get it for 18, but— FABER: Absolute -- again, I come back to it. What gives you that confidence when you say absolutely? Why? What are you seeing that you know, many, people are even rooting for you say, well, it's going to be a hard road. ELLISON: Let's look at the overall platform that we're operating right now. Twelve percent of all television watch time, that is second only to YouTube. So we have the scale, we have the intellectual property, we have the plan, and we have the people to be able to execute. And very thankfully, I'm sitting here with an incredible partner, and I believe the two of us are completely capable of the task at hand. FABER: Well, you know what, what, Ynon, I'd love to come to you in terms of just the synergy opportunity is key here. It does appear that is going to be one of your focuses day one. I guess I'll ask the question, what is your focus day one, when you look at having to deliver on those cost synergies that are so important to making this deal work? YNON KREIZ: Well, let me start by saying that I could not be more excited to be sitting here and partner with an entrepreneur like David, and everything that he's accomplished today is nothing but inspiration. We have a unique opportunity to build the next generation media and entertainment global company that is powered by creativity and technology. We have the assets that David mentioned. We have the capability, we have the people. And all of this is happening at the point in time when the industry is at an inflection point, where it's getting harder and harder to reach the consumer and aggregate fans, we have what it takes, we have what it takes. And while everybody is focused on synergy and debt, don't forget this is a growth story. It's a growth story. FABER: Okay. Well, a lot of people don't think it's a growth story. When you say we have what it takes. I'm trying to understand what, I know the collection of assets is unparalleled in many ways, but what does that mean? FABER: But now what? You know, is there, do you have a clear idea of how you delineate sort of responsibility? ELLISON: So, so, we absolutely have clear lines of delineation. First I want to say is we're going to do everything as true partners. And really sitting here today, this caps a three-year journey. We were talking about buying Warner Bros. Discovery before we actually closed on Paramount, because we believe this gave us the scale and put us in a position to be able to win. So this has been a long-term strategic vision and strategy that I've had for three years. I'll continue to lead in strategy, creativity, technology. You know, Ynon will obviously focus on day-to-day operations and overall of the company. But we'll do everything in partnership. And again, there's nobody else to do this with. FABER: Right. David, you know, one of the key gating issues for Warner Bros. Discovery and for many other companies that have cable networks has been the continued decline of the cable ecosystem and free to air as well. That continues. And, you know, you can create synergies and get cost savings and create more cash flow, but then you're dealing with this decline on the other side. How do you see that playing out? ELLISON: So, look, I think we as Ynon said, this is a growth story. When you put the two streaming services together, we do get to a world where the studios and streaming business outpaces linear declines, and obviously, the company grows and creates long term value over time. But we're also bullish on the linear business. Again, like let's look at the last year of owning CBS. It is the Tiffany Network, the number one broadcast network for over 17 years. It's number one primetime lineup. We delivered a record setting NFL season last year. And the linear businesses are separate, right? Broadcast is incredibly stable. Yes, cable is declining, but it is still high margin, highly cash flow generative. By putting these companies together, we can keep that business longer over time and make sure that we transition into a predominantly studios and streaming business and deliver long term value for shareholders. FABER: Do you have a view on sort of where, I mean, we all wonder, when are we going to hit the bottom? Is it 50 million subs? Is it, when is it? ELLISON: Companies didn't pivot fast enough. We can talk a lot about the owner, operator entrepreneurial culture of Silicon Valley versus the more steward culture of Hollywood that candidly put the businesses in this position. This transaction is the solution to those mistakes 10 years ago. Big tech took platform technology, pushed into media. What we're doing, but people are still there for the content. They're there for the stories. They're there for the news they love, the sports they love, the stories they love. We have assembled an unmatched portfolio of intellectual property, sports and news assets, and then we were building the product and tech organization that can compete with anybody coming out of Silicon Valley. That is going to enable us to push back. And when you look at the late delay to pivot— FABER: -- because that is the key. If you're going to succeed, it's got to be the DTC portfolio. It's got to be the international platform, right, as well. ELLISON: Absolutely. And if you look -- if you look at that, we have incredible room to run here in the States, domestically. These services are still nascent internationally. So we have a tremendous amount of room to grow in the international business. Our fast business is growing rapidly, both in terms of engagement and market share. And then in addition to that, we are investing more in content than any of our peers. Like, just talk about the scale of it, 30 movies a year, over 180 series, CNN news assets, CBS news assets, unmatched sports portfolio, plus the product and tech layer. We are positioned to compete with anybody and to win by putting these companies together. KREIZ: Where we stand out is not just with the incredible assets that we own in terms of content, but the ability to generate original content and find the next big hit. This is something that David has done consistently, consistently with Skydance. FABER: Well, it comes back to creativity, right? FABER: Okay. But I want to understand what the real goal is, though, in terms of, all right, you know, Netflix is out there. Do you see yourself becoming a number two? And, you know, you've said you're, and this is a quote, unifying under a single service over time in terms of Paramount Plus and HBO Max. What does that mean? How quickly does it happen? What comes first? ELLISON: No, no. So, so the answer is it's already happening. You know, we literally announced yesterday that we're unifying ad sales across the platforms. The product and tech teams are literally already at work unifying the back end tech stacks. We actually just completed that for the three services at Paramount a month ago. When you look at Agentic tooling and what you can now do with Claude and Codex, we can bring those back ends together significantly faster. FABER: Do you think so? Because, I mean, I hear that from others who tried to do it. It takes time, they say. FABER: Disney and everything else, do you think you can do it faster? ELLISON: The answer is we know. So, and I will say, when you look at, legacy media companies have traditionally had IT organizations, not product and tech teams. We are building a true product and tech team. We've been doing it within a year with, within Paramount. When you look at Dane Glasgow, who runs that business for us, prior to joining us, he was running Facebook for Meta and, you know, has over 20 years basically working with the best technology companies in the world. We have that team in house. And what you are seeing, on average, by deploying these A.I. tools across the company is on average, a 50 percent acceleration in terms of how fast you can get things done. For the high performers in the company, they are 10x-ing what they used to be able to do before. And when you talk about our synergy numbers, we're not applying A.I. to any of that. So when you look at how A.I. is going to transform every part of the business, we are really well-positioned. FABER: But it's not going to transform movies. These 30 movies are not going to be A.I.-generated. ELLISON: So what I would say is, look, we are a big believer that artificial intelligence is a tool for artists, not the other way around. And I don't think anything will disrupt that. What I do think is going to be possible when you talk about storytelling and artificial intelligence, I do believe it will be one of the biggest unlocks for creativity. For example, 1983, James Cameron made the first "Terminator" movie, $4 million. That movie, shot for shot today, $60 million or $70 million. How many first-time directors with an original script and no movie star, completely unproven, get a $60 million, $70 million budget? If you can use those toolings to be able to have -- to be able to have that movie cost $20 million today, it will be a massive unlock for the creative community. FABER: But you need it. I mean, 30 movies is not going to be cheap. And sometimes, they don't work. And so you're taking a loss on them. FABER: Right. You did lose Taylor Sheridan to NBC. Was that a blow? How do you view that in terms of what that's going to mean, given how important he has been, at least to the success of Paramount Plus? ELLISON: So I have so much admiration and respect for Taylor. He's still under contract with us until 2029. We actually have nine series that we're making together between now and the end of his contract. If you haven't seen "Lioness" season three, it's truly spectacular. We have a great relationship. He's literally writing "Call of Duty" for us with Pete Berg as we speak. And we also just greenlit another movie of his. And all of that intellectual property, we own and it stays at the company. So we're going to have a long relationship with Taylor— FABER: And does Paramount's content, I mean, HBO Max's content, I'm just curious as to how you see that all mixing and matching, so to speak, in terms of on one service for the end customer and what they want. FABER: Now you get to, right? Now you get to show us. So, you mentioned sports right, in the brief time I have left. The NFL, the change in control provision when you bought Paramount, was that exercise, does it mean you're going to have to renegotiate with them sooner than you might have otherwise? ELLISON: So we have a great relationship with the NFL. I think one of the things that, you know, the NFL was actually an investor in Skydance and now an investor, well, now today and also, Skydance. So we delivered last year a record setting season with them. We anticipate being in business with the NFL for the foreseeable future. And based on all the conversations with Roger, I think he sees it the same way. FABER: And CNN's future, you know, was the subject, it would seem, of so much, so many column mentions, certainly, David. You kept Mark Thompson. Why? ELLISON: About performance, both economically and strategically. I'll start with strategic. We need to grow top line by mid-single digits. We need to grow, we need to put our streaming businesses together. We need to grow and scale our studio business, our DTC business. We need to execute on our platform and technological transformation at the company. And I believe we do all of that. We'll be in really good shape. I pass it over to Ynon to talk about performance. KREIZ: You see us progressing towards our targets on 2030. And specifically when it comes to synergies, we expect to achieve a third of our synergy target in the first year. There's more to come. This is not just about synergies. You will see the company start performing at a very high level. You will see great content, you will see engagement, you will see excitement for fans all over the world, and the company is positioned to win. ELLISON: But, again, we don't control basically the first few days of trading. What we do control is the long term future of this business. And we're going to deliver. We're going to create value for all stakeholders. And we could not be more excited to get to work.

FABER: Well, you know what, what, Ynon, I'd love to come to you in terms of just the synergy opportunity is key here. It does appear that is going to be one of your focuses day one. I guess I'll ask the question, what is your focus day one, when you look at having to deliver on those cost synergies that are so important to making this deal work?

YNON KREIZ: Well, let me start by saying that I could not be more excited to be sitting here and partner with an entrepreneur like David, and everything that he's accomplished today is nothing but inspiration. We have a unique opportunity to build the next generation media and entertainment global company that is powered by creativity and technology. We have the assets that David mentioned. We have the capability, we have the people. And all of this is happening at the point in time when the industry is at an inflection point, where it's getting harder and harder to reach the consumer and aggregate fans, we have what it takes, we have what it takes. And while everybody is focused on synergy and debt, don't forget this is a growth story. It's a growth story.

FABER: Okay. Well, a lot of people don't think it's a growth story. When you say we have what it takes. I'm trying to understand what, I know the collection of assets is unparalleled in many ways, but what does that mean?
FABER: But now what? You know, is there, do you have a clear idea of how you delineate sort of responsibility?

ELLISON: So, so, we absolutely have clear lines of delineation. First I want to say is we're going to do everything as true partners. And really sitting here today, this caps a three-year journey. We were talking about buying Warner Bros. Discovery before we actually closed on Paramount, because we believe this gave us the scale and put us in a position to be able to win. So this has been a long-term strategic vision and strategy that I've had for three years. I'll continue to lead in strategy, creativity, technology. You know, Ynon will obviously focus on day-to-day operations and overall of the company. But we'll do everything in partnership. And again, there's nobody else to do this with.

FABER: Right. David, you know, one of the key gating issues for Warner Bros. Discovery and for many other companies that have cable networks has been the continued decline of the cable ecosystem and free to air as well. That continues. And, you know, you can create synergies and get cost savings and create more cash flow, but then you're dealing with this decline on the other side. How do you see that playing out?

ELLISON: So, look, I think we as Ynon said, this is a growth story. When you put the two streaming services together, we do get to a world where the studios and streaming business outpaces linear declines, and obviously, the company grows and creates long term value over time. But we're also bullish on the linear business. Again, like let's look at the last year of owning CBS. It is the Tiffany Network, the number one broadcast network for over 17 years. It's number one primetime lineup. We delivered a record setting NFL season last year. And the linear businesses are separate, right? Broadcast is incredibly stable. Yes, cable is declining, but it is still high margin, highly cash flow generative. By putting these companies together, we can keep that business longer over time and make sure that we transition into a predominantly studios and streaming business and deliver long term value for shareholders.
FABER: Do you have a view on sort of where, I mean, we all wonder, when are we going to hit the bottom? Is it 50 million subs? Is it, when is it?

ELLISON: Companies didn't pivot fast enough. We can talk a lot about the owner, operator entrepreneurial culture of Silicon Valley versus the more steward culture of Hollywood that candidly put the businesses in this position. This transaction is the solution to those mistakes 10 years ago. Big tech took platform technology, pushed into media. What we're doing, but people are still there for the content. They're there for the stories. They're there for the news they love, the sports they love, the stories they love. We have assembled an unmatched portfolio of intellectual property, sports and news assets, and then we were building the product and tech organization that can compete with anybody coming out of Silicon Valley. That is going to enable us to push back. And when you look at the late delay to pivot—
FABER: -- because that is the key. If you're going to succeed, it's got to be the DTC portfolio. It's got to be the international platform, right, as well.

ELLISON: Absolutely. And if you look -- if you look at that, we have incredible room to run here in the States, domestically. These services are still nascent internationally. So we have a tremendous amount of room to grow in the international business. Our fast business is growing rapidly, both in terms of engagement and market share. And then in addition to that, we are investing more in content than any of our peers. Like, just talk about the scale of it, 30 movies a year, over 180 series, CNN news assets, CBS news assets, unmatched sports portfolio, plus the product and tech layer. We are positioned to compete with anybody and to win by putting these companies together.

KREIZ: Where we stand out is not just with the incredible assets that we own in terms of content, but the ability to generate original content and find the next big hit. This is something that David has done consistently, consistently with Skydance.
FABER: Well, it comes back to creativity, right?

FABER: Okay. But I want to understand what the real goal is, though, in terms of, all right, you know, Netflix is out there. Do you see yourself becoming a number two? And, you know, you've said you're, and this is a quote, unifying under a single service over time in terms of Paramount Plus and HBO Max. What does that mean? How quickly does it happen? What comes first?

ELLISON: No, no. So, so the answer is it's already happening. You know, we literally announced yesterday that we're unifying ad sales across the platforms. The product and tech teams are literally already at work unifying the back end tech stacks. We actually just completed that for the three services at Paramount a month ago. When you look at Agentic tooling and what you can now do with Claude and Codex, we can bring those back ends together significantly faster.
FABER: Do you think so? Because, I mean, I hear that from others who tried to do it. It takes time, they say.
FABER: Disney and everything else, do you think you can do it faster?

ELLISON: The answer is we know. So, and I will say, when you look at, legacy media companies have traditionally had IT organizations, not product and tech teams. We are building a true product and tech team. We've been doing it within a year with, within Paramount. When you look at Dane Glasgow, who runs that business for us, prior to joining us, he was running Facebook for Meta and, you know, has over 20 years basically working with the best technology companies in the world. We have that team in house. And what you are seeing, on average, by deploying these A.I. tools across the company is on average, a 50 percent acceleration in terms of how fast you can get things done. For the high performers in the company, they are 10x-ing what they used to be able to do before. And when you talk about our synergy numbers, we're not applying A.I. to any of that. So when you look at how A.I. is going to transform every part of the business, we are really well-positioned.
FABER: But it's not going to transform movies. These 30 movies are not going to be A.I.-generated.

ELLISON: So what I would say is, look, we are a big believer that artificial intelligence is a tool for artists, not the other way around. And I don't think anything will disrupt that. What I do think is going to be possible when you talk about storytelling and artificial intelligence, I do believe it will be one of the biggest unlocks for creativity. For example, 1983, James Cameron made the first "Terminator" movie, $4 million. That movie, shot for shot today, $60 million or $70 million. How many first-time directors with an original script and no movie star, completely unproven, get a $60 million, $70 million budget? If you can use those toolings to be able to have -- to be able to have that movie cost $20 million today, it will be a massive unlock for the creative community.
FABER: But you need it. I mean, 30 movies is not going to be cheap. And sometimes, they don't work. And so you're taking a loss on them.

FABER: Right. You did lose Taylor Sheridan to NBC. Was that a blow? How do you view that in terms of what that's going to mean, given how important he has been, at least to the success of Paramount Plus?

ELLISON: So I have so much admiration and respect for Taylor. He's still under contract with us until 2029. We actually have nine series that we're making together between now and the end of his contract. If you haven't seen "Lioness" season three, it's truly spectacular. We have a great relationship. He's literally writing "Call of Duty" for us with Pete Berg as we speak. And we also just greenlit another movie of his. And all of that intellectual property, we own and it stays at the company. So we're going to have a long relationship with Taylor—

FABER: And does Paramount's content, I mean, HBO Max's content, I'm just curious as to how you see that all mixing and matching, so to speak, in terms of on one service for the end customer and what they want.

FABER: Now you get to, right? Now you get to show us. So, you mentioned sports right, in the brief time I have left. The NFL, the change in control provision when you bought Paramount, was that exercise, does it mean you're going to have to renegotiate with them sooner than you might have otherwise?

ELLISON: So we have a great relationship with the NFL. I think one of the things that, you know, the NFL was actually an investor in Skydance and now an investor, well, now today and also, Skydance. So we delivered last year a record setting season with them. We anticipate being in business with the NFL for the foreseeable future. And based on all the conversations with Roger, I think he sees it the same way.
FABER: And CNN's future, you know, was the subject, it would seem, of so much, so many column mentions, certainly, David. You kept Mark Thompson. Why?

ELLISON: About performance, both economically and strategically. I'll start with strategic. We need to grow top line by mid-single digits. We need to grow, we need to put our streaming businesses together. We need to grow and scale our studio business, our DTC business. We need to execute on our platform and technological transformation at the company. And I believe we do all of that. We'll be in really good shape. I pass it over to Ynon to talk about performance.

KREIZ: You see us progressing towards our targets on 2030. And specifically when it comes to synergies, we expect to achieve a third of our synergy target in the first year. There's more to come. This is not just about synergies. You will see the company start performing at a very high level. You will see great content, you will see engagement, you will see excitement for fans all over the world, and the company is positioned to win.

ELLISON: But, again, we don't control basically the first few days of trading. What we do control is the long term future of this business. And we're going to deliver. We're going to create value for all stakeholders. And we could not be more excited to get to work.

extraction.body: During Paramount Skydance’s latest earnings call, CEO David Ellison said “it’s hard to imagine” AI won’t have a bigger impact on the film industry than CGI. In response to a question about the company’s outlook for AI, Ellison said: > “I think when you zoom out and look at production, AI really has the potential to be the biggest creative unlock in modern history. That technology gave birth to amazing stories like Jurassic Park and Terminator 2, and it’s hard to imagine that AI is not going to have a more significant impact than that. And I personally believe that’s going to be an incredible unlock on creativity.” Ellison gave Terminator as an example, describing how it cost $4 million to make, but “if you wanted to make that picture today, shot for shot, it’s $60 to 70 million.” He went on to suggest AI might be able to help with that: “We think these tools will help unlock more original storytelling by being able to make the budgets more digestible to be able to take that amount of risk.” Ellison said AI will “significantly” reshape Paramount Skydance’s business, saying the company has been developing its own AI tools. As a result of those tools, Ellison claims, “content will be easier to produce, projects across the organization will speed up, and how we work will transform.” He emphasized that “all of this makes the value of premium IP and live events more valuable, not less.” Ellison also noted that “in a world of AI slop, we think there will always be a premium for truly hand-crafted storytelling.” He added, “We also continue to believe that artificial intelligence is a tool for artists and will never be a replacement for them.”

sources.title: CHAIRMAN AND CEO DAVID ELLISON ANNOUNCES YNON KREIZ CO-CEO OF THE ANTICIPATED COMBINED PARAMOUNT AND WARNER BROS. DISCOVERY AT CLOSING TO HELP BUILD THE NEXT-GENERATION GLOBAL MEDIA COMPANY - PR Newswire
passages: David Ellison said: "Bringing together Paramount and Warner Bros.
Discovery to create a next-generation global media company is a transformational moment for our industry.

30, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Paramount Skydance Corporation (NASDAQ: PSKY ) (the "Company") today disclosed that David Ellison has announced Ynon Kreiz as Co-CEO of the anticipated merged company, effective at closing.

Kreiz, who will start at Paramount, effective October 5, 2026, joins Ellison from Mattel, a leading global play and family entertainment company where he has served as Chairman and CEO since 2018, leading an unprecedented transformation of the business and the execution of its multi-platform, brand-centric strategy.
Today's appointment of an executive with Kreiz's stature and track record marks the next step in Ellison's pursuit to unite Warner Bros.
Discovery and Paramount — two of Hollywood's most storied studios, with more than 200 combined years of storytelling and a streaming platform expected to reach 200 million-plus global subscribers.

Ynon Kreiz said: "I'm excited to partner with David to build the next-generation media and entertainment company — bringing together premium content and iconic brands at the highest quality and scale, serving global audiences across every entertainment vertical and distribution platform.
David is a unique talent and executive: a rare blend of business acumen, creative instinct, and clear vision.

I look forward to working with the leadership team to build a cohesive global entertainment platform — one that stands out with best-in-class operations and execution powered by technology, with unparalleled creative relationships, production capabilities, and global reach.

Discovery merger closes, the combined company will be guided by four overarching strategic priorities: win in content, become the most technologically capable media company, maximize operational efficiencies, and earn trust — delivering reliable, responsible experiences that strengthen its relationships with creators, audiences, consumers, employees, advertisers and partners.
Following the completion of its acquisition of Warner Bros.
Discovery, the merged company's portfolio will unite legendary brands including Paramount Pictures, Warner Bros.
Ellison will focus on the company's long-term strategy, creative vision and direction, including its talent relationships, strategic partnerships, technology and capital allocation.
Ynon has spent his career at the intersection of media, technology and franchise-building — pairing extraordinary storytelling with the technology to deliver it to fans everywhere.

In just over a year under Ellison, Paramount has doubled its theatrical slate, deepened its creative bench, greenlit more than 40 new and returning series for Paramount+, and built the capital discipline and technology to scale.

extraction.body: LOS ANGELES , Sept. 30, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Paramount Skydance Corporation (NASDAQ: PSKY ) (the "Company") today disclosed that David Ellison has announced Ynon Kreiz as Co-CEO of the anticipated merged company, effective at closing. Kreiz, who will start at Paramount, effective October 5, 2026, joins Ellison from Mattel, a leading global play and family entertainment company where he has served as Chairman and CEO since 2018, leading an unprecedented transformation of the business and the execution of its multi-platform, brand-centric strategy. Upon closing, Ellison will remain Chairman and CEO of the newly combined company, and Kreiz will serve as Co-CEO and join the Board of Directors. Together, they will oversee the combined company's businesses, which will report jointly to both. Ellison's appointment of Kreiz caps a long-term plan: pursue both Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, then partner with a leading executive of his caliber to integrate, operationalize and manage the businesses as they build one of the most ambitious next-generation media companies in the industry's history. Together, Ellison and Kreiz will lead the anticipated combined company as one team, pairing complementary skillsets to maximize the full upside of the merger under a comprehensive long-term strategy. Ellison will focus on the company's long-term strategy, creative vision and direction, including its talent relationships, strategic partnerships, technology and capital allocation. Kreiz will focus on the company's day-to-day management and integration of the combined businesses. David Ellison said: "Bringing together Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery to create a next-generation global media company is a transformational moment for our industry. Leading it takes a rare combination of strategic vision, operational depth and experience running a public company at the highest levels of media. Ynon brings all three. In Ynon, I'm adding a partner with strong leadership and the operating firepower this integration demands. It's a division of labor built on our complementary strengths, with clear reporting lines and it lets me focus where I can contribute most: long-term strategy, the company's overall creative direction, talent relationships, strategic partnerships, technology and capital allocation. We're like-minded, we see this business the same way and there's no one I'd rather partner with. Together we'll build one integrated company that is creator-first, tech-forward and built to scale globally." Ynon Kreiz said: "I'm excited to partner with David to build the next-generation media and entertainment company — bringing together premium content and iconic brands at the highest quality and scale, serving global audiences across every entertainment vertical and distribution platform. David is a unique talent and executive: a rare blend of business acumen, creative instinct, and clear vision. I very much share that vision, and I'm inspired by what we can accomplish together. The industry is at an inflection point, demanding evolution, investment, and a willingness to rethink business models. I look forward to working with the leadership team to build a cohesive global entertainment platform — one that stands out with best-in-class operations and execution powered by technology, with unparalleled creative relationships, production capabilities, and global reach. We will continue empowering creators, make this company a greenfield for innovation and storytelling, and collaborate with key partners to reach and engage fans worldwide." Gerry Cardinale, Founder and Managing Partner of RedBird Capital Partners — the Company's co-controlling shareholder and a member of its Board of Directors — said: "David has done what few modern executives have accomplished. He has led this company through not one but two historic acquisitions, while also running the business and building a team that's already exceeding our synergy targets, beating our financial metrics, and never wavering on our commitment to the creative community. Ynon has spent his career at the intersection of media, technology and franchise-building — pairing extraordinary storytelling with the technology to deliver it to fans everywhere. He understands not just how fans connect with the IP they love, but the economics that make entertainment endure. Great leaders accomplish great things. Historic ones know when to bring in the right partner to make it last — and that's what David has done. It's exactly why the company will have the operational firepower and the cutting-edge leadership to win." Today's appointment of an executive with Kreiz's stature and track record marks the next step in Ellison's pursuit to unite Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount — two of Hollywood's most storied studios, with more than 200 combined years of storytelling and a streaming platform expected to reach 200 million-plus global subscribers. In just over a year under Ellison, Paramount has doubled its theatrical slate, deepened its creative bench, greenlit more than 40 new and returning series for Paramount+, and built the capital discipline and technology to scale. That foundation positions the Company to grow 2026 projected revenue and EBITDA (preSBC) by 16-19%, and it laid the groundwork for this historic transaction, which is expected to generate more than $6 billion in run-rate synergies accelerate EBITDA growth. Once the Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery merger closes, the combined company will be guided by four overarching strategic priorities: win in content, become the most technologically capable media company, maximize operational efficiencies, and earn trust — delivering reliable, responsible experiences that strengthen its relationships with creators, audiences, consumers, employees, advertisers and partners. Mr. Kreiz has extensive experience as a corporate leader in the entertainment industry, with a track record of scaling content and brands globally. During his career spanning more than 30 years, he has successfully managed and invested in international media enterprises that have pioneered new business models at the intersection of media and technology. Mr. Kreiz has been Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Mattel since 2018. Mattel is a leading global play and family entertainment company with one of the most iconic brand portfolios in the world, including Barbie, Hot Wheels, Fisher-Price, UNO, American Girl, and Thomas & Friends. Following his appointment at Mattel in 2018, Kreiz led a multi-year transformation that strengthened its leadership across key toy categories and expanded its brands into new entertainment verticals, including film, television, consumer products, digital games, live events and experiences, and publishing. Under Mr. Kreiz's leadership, Mattel's first theatrical release, "Barbie," became the #1 global box office film of 2023 and Warner Bros. Pictures' highest-grossing movie of all time, and the Company grew its global footprint to more than 150 countries. Before Mattel, Mr. Kreiz was Chairman and CEO of Maker Studios, a global leader in short-form video content and one of YouTube's largest multichannel networks, which was acquired by The Walt Disney Company. He previously served as Chairman and CEO of Endemol Group, the world's largest independent television production company at the time, producing more than 10,000 hours of programming a year and owning global franchises such as "Big Brother" and "Deal or No Deal." Prior to that, he was a General Partner at Balderton Capital (formerly Benchmark Capital Europe), specializing in early-stage media and technology investments. Earlier in his career, Mr. Kreiz was co-founder, Chairman, and CEO of Fox Kids Europe NV, which developed and owned pay TV channels across Europe and the Middle East. The company was acquired by The Walt Disney Company. Mr. Kreiz holds a BA degree in Economics and Management from Tel Aviv University and an MBA from UCLA Anderson School of Management. He serves on the Board of Directors of Warner Music Group and the Board of Advisors of the UCLA Anderson School of Management. Mr. Kreiz is a member of Business Roundtable and the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. He was named in 2024 one of TIME's 100 Most Influential People in the World and Entertainment Person of the Year by Cannes Lions. Following the completion of its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, the merged company's portfolio will unite legendary brands including Paramount Pictures, Warner Bros. Pictures, Paramount Television, Warner Bros. Television, CBS, CBS News, CBS Sports, CNN, HBO, HBO Max, TNT, TBS, Discovery, HGTV, Food Network, Nickelodeon, Cartoon Network, MTV, BET, Comedy Central, Showtime, Paramount+, Pluto TV, and Skydance Animation, Film, Television, Interactive/Games, and Paramount Sports Entertainment — serving audiences in more than 200 countries and territories. I look forward to working with the leadership team to build a cohesive global entertainment platform — one that stands out with best-in-class operations and execution powered by technology, with unparalleled creative relationships, production capabilities, and global reach. We will continue empowering creators, make this company a greenfield for innovation and storytelling, and collaborate with key partners to reach and engage fans worldwide."

Gerry Cardinale, Founder and Managing Partner of RedBird Capital Partners — the Company's co-controlling shareholder and a member of its Board of Directors — said: "David has done what few modern executives have accomplished. He has led this company through not one but two historic acquisitions, while also running the business and building a team that's already exceeding our synergy targets, beating our financial metrics, and never wavering on our commitment to the creative community. Ynon has spent his career at the intersection of media, technology and franchise-building — pairing extraordinary storytelling with the technology to deliver it to fans everywhere. He understands not just how fans connect with the IP they love, but the economics that make entertainment endure. Great leaders accomplish great things. Historic ones know when to bring in the right partner to make it last — and that's what David has done. It's exactly why the company will have the operational firepower and the cutting-edge leadership to win."

Today's appointment of an executive with Kreiz's stature and track record marks the next step in Ellison's pursuit to unite Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount — two of Hollywood's most storied studios, with more than 200 combined years of storytelling and a streaming platform expected to reach 200 million-plus global subscribers.

In just over a year under Ellison, Paramount has doubled its theatrical slate, deepened its creative bench, greenlit more than 40 new and returning series for Paramount+, and built the capital discipline and technology to scale. That foundation positions the Company to grow 2026 projected revenue and EBITDA (preSBC) by 16-19%, and it laid the groundwork for this historic transaction, which is expected to generate more than $6 billion in run-rate synergies accelerate EBITDA growth.

Once the Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery merger closes, the combined company will be guided by four overarching strategic priorities: win in content, become the most technologically capable media company, maximize operational efficiencies, and earn trust — delivering reliable, responsible experiences that strengthen its relationships with creators, audiences, consumers, employees, advertisers and partners.

Mr. Kreiz has extensive experience as a corporate leader in the entertainment industry, with a track record of scaling content and brands globally. During his career spanning more than 30 years, he has successfully managed and invested in international media enterprises that have pioneered new business models at the intersection of media and technology.

Mr. Kreiz has been Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Mattel since 2018. Mattel is a leading global play and family entertainment company with one of the most iconic brand portfolios in the world, including Barbie, Hot Wheels, Fisher-Price, UNO, American Girl, and Thomas & Friends. Following his appointment at Mattel in 2018, Kreiz led a multi-year transformation that strengthened its leadership across key toy categories and expanded its brands into new entertainment verticals, including film, television, consumer products, digital games, live events and experiences, and publishing. Under Mr. Kreiz's leadership, Mattel's first theatrical release, "Barbie," became the #1 global box office film of 2023 and Warner Bros. Pictures' highest-grossing movie of all time, and the Company grew its global footprint to more than 150 countries.

Before Mattel, Mr. Kreiz was Chairman and CEO of Maker Studios, a global leader in short-form video content and one of YouTube's largest multichannel networks, which was acquired by The Walt Disney Company. He previously served as Chairman and CEO of Endemol Group, the world's largest independent television production company at the time, producing more than 10,000 hours of programming a year and owning global franchises such as "Big Brother" and "Deal or No Deal." Prior to that, he was a General Partner at Balderton Capital (formerly Benchmark Capital Europe), specializing in early-stage media and technology investments.

Earlier in his career, Mr. Kreiz was co-founder, Chairman, and CEO of Fox Kids Europe NV, which developed and owned pay TV channels across Europe and the Middle East. The company was acquired by The Walt Disney Company.

Mr. Kreiz holds a BA degree in Economics and Management from Tel Aviv University and an MBA from UCLA Anderson School of Management. He serves on the Board of Directors of Warner Music Group and the Board of Advisors of the UCLA Anderson School of Management. Mr. Kreiz is a member of Business Roundtable and the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. He was named in 2024 one of TIME's 100 Most Influential People in the World and Entertainment Person of the Year by Cannes Lions.

Following the completion of its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, the merged company's portfolio will unite legendary brands including Paramount Pictures, Warner Bros. Pictures, Paramount Television, Warner Bros. Television, CBS, CBS News, CBS Sports, CNN, HBO, HBO Max, TNT, TBS, Discovery, HGTV, Food Network, Nickelodeon, Cartoon Network, MTV, BET, Comedy Central, Showtime, Paramount+, Pluto TV, and Skydance Animation, Film, Television, Interactive/Games, and Paramount Sports Entertainment — serving audiences in more than 200 countries and territories.

extraction.body: The Skydance CEO says, "AI really has the potential to be the biggest creative unlock in modern history." In his first earnings call as CEO at the helm of both Paramount and Warner Bros., David Ellison talked up his merged Hollywood empire as a tech-forward enterprise — and part of that tightrope walk included an embrace of AI while also dismissing “AI slop.” It’s a two-step that’s not necessarily an easy one. The technology is widely seen as a harbinger of doom for Hollywood’s traditional workflows (i.e. building sets, shooting with real background extras, going on-location, etc) while also being increasingly adapted and integrated into the business (see: Ben Affleck’s VFX firm, which has helped Netflix use AI on 300-plus titles so far, while supposedly preserving the things that make Hollywood, Hollywood). Ellison told analysts that he expects AI to help his company’s studios make content faster and cheaper, likening the technology as the biggest breakthrough in the industry since CGI effects went mainstream. Skydance plans to spend $30 billion annually across its content portfolio — that’s includes everything from prestige TV HBO projects to CBS procedurals and MTV reality shows as well as NFL sports rights and features at Warners and Paramount. “I don’t think it can be discounted how fast this technology is moving,” Ellison said after table-setting by saying that “in a world of AI slop we think there will always be a premium for truly hand-crafted storytelling.” Ellison has a unique lens into the issue as heir to his father Larry Ellison’s AI-powered Oracle tech fortune, which is a key facet of his effort to rebrand legacy Hollywood studios as a tech-centric venture. (To that point, the enterprise cloud apps of Oracle Fusion got a call out in the earnings call as well when talking about consolidating back office functions.) The CEO also views franchise IP — he described his empire as having 40 $1 billion franchises — as a moat protecting against the onslaught of AI content, delivering more premium experiences to his 203 million-plus subscribers at a soon-to-be merged Paramount+ and HBO Max. He then launched into an anecdote about a franchise that his Skydance Media has rebooted multiple times over the past two decades. “AI really has the potential to be the biggest creative unlock in modern history,” Ellison bullishly said. “The last time we saw anything close to this was really the advent of CGI and digital composites in the early ’90s. That technology gave birth to amazing stories like Jurassic Park and Terminator 2 . It’s hard to imagine that AI is not going to have a more significant impact than that. In his first earnings call as CEO at the helm of both Paramount and Warner Bros., David Ellison talked up his merged Hollywood empire as a tech-forward enterprise — and part of that tightrope walk included an embrace of AI while also dismissing “AI slop.”

It’s a two-step that’s not necessarily an easy one. The technology is widely seen as a harbinger of doom for Hollywood’s traditional workflows (i.e. building sets, shooting with real background extras, going on-location, etc) while also being increasingly adapted and integrated into the business (see: Ben Affleck’s VFX firm, which has helped Netflix use AI on 300-plus titles so far, while supposedly preserving the things that make Hollywood, Hollywood).

Ellison told analysts that he expects AI to help his company’s studios make content faster and cheaper, likening the technology as the biggest breakthrough in the industry since CGI effects went mainstream. Skydance plans to spend $30 billion annually across its content portfolio — that’s includes everything from prestige TV HBO projects to CBS procedurals and MTV reality shows as well as NFL sports rights and features at Warners and Paramount.

“I don’t think it can be discounted how fast this technology is moving,” Ellison said after table-setting by saying that “in a world of AI slop we think there will always be a premium for truly hand-crafted storytelling.”

Ellison has a unique lens into the issue as heir to his father Larry Ellison’s AI-powered Oracle tech fortune, which is a key facet of his effort to rebrand legacy Hollywood studios as a tech-centric venture.
