extraction.body: DAVID FABER: Becky, thank you. Thanks to the whole "Squawk" team, of course. We're going to run into your show for the rest of it, at least. And I'm very happy, obviously, to be joined by David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz. You're going to be ringing the bell about 50 minutes from now or so. It's been quite a journey, David. I followed it very closely, of course, as you know. And, you know, you started the bidding for Warner at $18 a share. You ended at 31. When you include what you had to pay Netflix for their break fee, it was an increase of as much as $47 billion from your initial bid. Why is it worth it? DAVID ELLISON: Well, first, David, I don't know what you're talking about in terms of the journey here. It was smooth and easy. And, no, it truly is. Walking in here today was quite remarkable because I remember the last time we were here was when we launched the hostile on your show. So to be coming full circle today— ELLISON: Is really quite remarkable. And look, the reason why we went through everything that we did is because with the combination and the completion of this transaction, we are positioned to win in every single vertical that we operate in. By combining Paramount and Warner Bros., we have the greatest content engine with marquee intellectual property. You're uniting "Lord of the Rings", "Harry Potter", the DC universe under the same house as "Mission Impossible", "Top Gun: Maverick", "G.I. Joe", "Transformers," you're immediately getting to scale on streaming. Between HBO Max and Paramount Plus, over 200 million global streaming subscribers, with, with an addition to Pluto, 80 million monthly active users. We have an unmatched sports portfolio that includes the NFL, MLB, NHL, UEFA, basically, PGA, just to name a few. Not to mention the Olympics internationally. And an incredibly profitable linear portfolio anchored by CBS. When you look at our primetime lineup, the NCIS night just launched 42 percent up basically from last year, five of the top 10 cable channels. And we will transform this business. FABER: Well, what, let me start there then, because, you know, you start as well, though. I mentioned the 47 billion additionally. Nobody thought you were going to get it for 18, but— FABER: Absolute -- again, I come back to it. What gives you that confidence when you say absolutely? Why? What are you seeing that you know, many, people are even rooting for you say, well, it's going to be a hard road. ELLISON: Let's look at the overall platform that we're operating right now. Twelve percent of all television watch time, that is second only to YouTube. So we have the scale, we have the intellectual property, we have the plan, and we have the people to be able to execute. And very thankfully, I'm sitting here with an incredible partner, and I believe the two of us are completely capable of the task at hand. FABER: Well, you know what, what, Ynon, I'd love to come to you in terms of just the synergy opportunity is key here. It does appear that is going to be one of your focuses day one. I guess I'll ask the question, what is your focus day one, when you look at having to deliver on those cost synergies that are so important to making this deal work? YNON KREIZ: Well, let me start by saying that I could not be more excited to be sitting here and partner with an entrepreneur like David, and everything that he's accomplished today is nothing but inspiration. We have a unique opportunity to build the next generation media and entertainment global company that is powered by creativity and technology. We have the assets that David mentioned. We have the capability, we have the people. And all of this is happening at the point in time when the industry is at an inflection point, where it's getting harder and harder to reach the consumer and aggregate fans, we have what it takes, we have what it takes. And while everybody is focused on synergy and debt, don't forget this is a growth story. It's a growth story. FABER: Okay. Well, a lot of people don't think it's a growth story. When you say we have what it takes. I'm trying to understand what, I know the collection of assets is unparalleled in many ways, but what does that mean? FABER: But now what? You know, is there, do you have a clear idea of how you delineate sort of responsibility? ELLISON: So, so, we absolutely have clear lines of delineation. First I want to say is we're going to do everything as true partners. And really sitting here today, this caps a three-year journey. We were talking about buying Warner Bros. Discovery before we actually closed on Paramount, because we believe this gave us the scale and put us in a position to be able to win. So this has been a long-term strategic vision and strategy that I've had for three years. I'll continue to lead in strategy, creativity, technology. You know, Ynon will obviously focus on day-to-day operations and overall of the company. But we'll do everything in partnership. And again, there's nobody else to do this with. FABER: Right. David, you know, one of the key gating issues for Warner Bros. Discovery and for many other companies that have cable networks has been the continued decline of the cable ecosystem and free to air as well. That continues. And, you know, you can create synergies and get cost savings and create more cash flow, but then you're dealing with this decline on the other side. How do you see that playing out? ELLISON: So, look, I think we as Ynon said, this is a growth story. When you put the two streaming services together, we do get to a world where the studios and streaming business outpaces linear declines, and obviously, the company grows and creates long term value over time. But we're also bullish on the linear business. Again, like let's look at the last year of owning CBS. It is the Tiffany Network, the number one broadcast network for over 17 years. It's number one primetime lineup. We delivered a record setting NFL season last year. And the linear businesses are separate, right? Broadcast is incredibly stable. Yes, cable is declining, but it is still high margin, highly cash flow generative. By putting these companies together, we can keep that business longer over time and make sure that we transition into a predominantly studios and streaming business and deliver long term value for shareholders. FABER: Do you have a view on sort of where, I mean, we all wonder, when are we going to hit the bottom? Is it 50 million subs? Is it, when is it? ELLISON: Companies didn't pivot fast enough. We can talk a lot about the owner, operator entrepreneurial culture of Silicon Valley versus the more steward culture of Hollywood that candidly put the businesses in this position. This transaction is the solution to those mistakes 10 years ago. Big tech took platform technology, pushed into media. What we're doing, but people are still there for the content. They're there for the stories. They're there for the news they love, the sports they love, the stories they love. We have assembled an unmatched portfolio of intellectual property, sports and news assets, and then we were building the product and tech organization that can compete with anybody coming out of Silicon Valley. That is going to enable us to push back. And when you look at the late delay to pivot— FABER: -- because that is the key. If you're going to succeed, it's got to be the DTC portfolio. It's got to be the international platform, right, as well. ELLISON: Absolutely. And if you look -- if you look at that, we have incredible room to run here in the States, domestically. These services are still nascent internationally. So we have a tremendous amount of room to grow in the international business. Our fast business is growing rapidly, both in terms of engagement and market share. And then in addition to that, we are investing more in content than any of our peers. Like, just talk about the scale of it, 30 movies a year, over 180 series, CNN news assets, CBS news assets, unmatched sports portfolio, plus the product and tech layer. We are positioned to compete with anybody and to win by putting these companies together. KREIZ: Where we stand out is not just with the incredible assets that we own in terms of content, but the ability to generate original content and find the next big hit. This is something that David has done consistently, consistently with Skydance. FABER: Well, it comes back to creativity, right? FABER: Okay. But I want to understand what the real goal is, though, in terms of, all right, you know, Netflix is out there. Do you see yourself becoming a number two? And, you know, you've said you're, and this is a quote, unifying under a single service over time in terms of Paramount Plus and HBO Max. What does that mean? How quickly does it happen? What comes first? ELLISON: No, no. So, so the answer is it's already happening. You know, we literally announced yesterday that we're unifying ad sales across the platforms. The product and tech teams are literally already at work unifying the back end tech stacks. We actually just completed that for the three services at Paramount a month ago. When you look at Agentic tooling and what you can now do with Claude and Codex, we can bring those back ends together significantly faster. FABER: Do you think so? Because, I mean, I hear that from others who tried to do it. It takes time, they say. FABER: Disney and everything else, do you think you can do it faster? ELLISON: The answer is we know. So, and I will say, when you look at, legacy media companies have traditionally had IT organizations, not product and tech teams. We are building a true product and tech team. We've been doing it within a year with, within Paramount. When you look at Dane Glasgow, who runs that business for us, prior to joining us, he was running Facebook for Meta and, you know, has over 20 years basically working with the best technology companies in the world. We have that team in house. And what you are seeing, on average, by deploying these A.I. tools across the company is on average, a 50 percent acceleration in terms of how fast you can get things done. For the high performers in the company, they are 10x-ing what they used to be able to do before. And when you talk about our synergy numbers, we're not applying A.I. to any of that. So when you look at how A.I. is going to transform every part of the business, we are really well-positioned. FABER: But it's not going to transform movies. These 30 movies are not going to be A.I.-generated. ELLISON: So what I would say is, look, we are a big believer that artificial intelligence is a tool for artists, not the other way around. And I don't think anything will disrupt that. What I do think is going to be possible when you talk about storytelling and artificial intelligence, I do believe it will be one of the biggest unlocks for creativity. For example, 1983, James Cameron made the first "Terminator" movie, $4 million. That movie, shot for shot today, $60 million or $70 million. How many first-time directors with an original script and no movie star, completely unproven, get a $60 million, $70 million budget? If you can use those toolings to be able to have -- to be able to have that movie cost $20 million today, it will be a massive unlock for the creative community. FABER: But you need it. I mean, 30 movies is not going to be cheap. And sometimes, they don't work. And so you're taking a loss on them. FABER: Right. You did lose Taylor Sheridan to NBC. Was that a blow? How do you view that in terms of what that's going to mean, given how important he has been, at least to the success of Paramount Plus? ELLISON: So I have so much admiration and respect for Taylor. He's still under contract with us until 2029. We actually have nine series that we're making together between now and the end of his contract. If you haven't seen "Lioness" season three, it's truly spectacular. We have a great relationship. He's literally writing "Call of Duty" for us with Pete Berg as we speak. And we also just greenlit another movie of his. And all of that intellectual property, we own and it stays at the company. So we're going to have a long relationship with Taylor— FABER: And does Paramount's content, I mean, HBO Max's content, I'm just curious as to how you see that all mixing and matching, so to speak, in terms of on one service for the end customer and what they want. FABER: Now you get to, right? Now you get to show us. So, you mentioned sports right, in the brief time I have left. The NFL, the change in control provision when you bought Paramount, was that exercise, does it mean you're going to have to renegotiate with them sooner than you might have otherwise? ELLISON: So we have a great relationship with the NFL. I think one of the things that, you know, the NFL was actually an investor in Skydance and now an investor, well, now today and also, Skydance. So we delivered last year a record setting season with them. We anticipate being in business with the NFL for the foreseeable future. And based on all the conversations with Roger, I think he sees it the same way. FABER: And CNN's future, you know, was the subject, it would seem, of so much, so many column mentions, certainly, David. You kept Mark Thompson. Why? ELLISON: About performance, both economically and strategically. I'll start with strategic. We need to grow top line by mid-single digits. We need to grow, we need to put our streaming businesses together. We need to grow and scale our studio business, our DTC business. We need to execute on our platform and technological transformation at the company. And I believe we do all of that. We'll be in really good shape. I pass it over to Ynon to talk about performance. KREIZ: You see us progressing towards our targets on 2030. And specifically when it comes to synergies, we expect to achieve a third of our synergy target in the first year. There's more to come. This is not just about synergies. You will see the company start performing at a very high level. You will see great content, you will see engagement, you will see excitement for fans all over the world, and the company is positioned to win. ELLISON: But, again, we don't control basically the first few days of trading. What we do control is the long term future of this business. And we're going to deliver. We're going to create value for all stakeholders. And we could not be more excited to get to work.

And based on all the conversations with Roger, I think he sees it the same way.
FABER: And CNN's future, you know, was the subject, it would seem, of so much, so many column mentions, certainly, David. You kept Mark Thompson. Why?

ELLISON: About performance, both economically and strategically. I'll start with strategic. We need to grow top line by mid-single digits. We need to grow, we need to put our streaming businesses together. We need to grow and scale our studio business, our DTC business. We need to execute on our platform and technological transformation at the company. And I believe we do all of that. We'll be in really good shape. I pass it over to Ynon to talk about performance.

extraction.body: During Paramount Skydance’s latest earnings call, CEO David Ellison said “it’s hard to imagine” AI won’t have a bigger impact on the film industry than CGI. In response to a question about the company’s outlook for AI, Ellison said: > “I think when you zoom out and look at production, AI really has the potential to be the biggest creative unlock in modern history. That technology gave birth to amazing stories like Jurassic Park and Terminator 2, and it’s hard to imagine that AI is not going to have a more significant impact than that. And I personally believe that’s going to be an incredible unlock on creativity.” Ellison gave Terminator as an example, describing how it cost $4 million to make, but “if you wanted to make that picture today, shot for shot, it’s $60 to 70 million.” He went on to suggest AI might be able to help with that: “We think these tools will help unlock more original storytelling by being able to make the budgets more digestible to be able to take that amount of risk.” Ellison said AI will “significantly” reshape Paramount Skydance’s business, saying the company has been developing its own AI tools. As a result of those tools, Ellison claims, “content will be easier to produce, projects across the organization will speed up, and how we work will transform.” He emphasized that “all of this makes the value of premium IP and live events more valuable, not less.” Ellison also noted that “in a world of AI slop, we think there will always be a premium for truly hand-crafted storytelling.” He added, “We also continue to believe that artificial intelligence is a tool for artists and will never be a replacement for them.”

sources.title: CHAIRMAN AND CEO DAVID ELLISON ANNOUNCES YNON KREIZ CO-CEO OF THE ANTICIPATED COMBINED PARAMOUNT AND WARNER BROS. DISCOVERY AT CLOSING TO HELP BUILD THE NEXT-GENERATION GLOBAL MEDIA COMPANY - PR Newswire
passages: David Ellison said: "Bringing together Paramount and Warner Bros.
Discovery to create a next-generation global media company is a transformational moment for our industry.

30, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Paramount Skydance Corporation (NASDAQ: PSKY ) (the "Company") today disclosed that David Ellison has announced Ynon Kreiz as Co-CEO of the anticipated merged company, effective at closing.

Kreiz, who will start at Paramount, effective October 5, 2026, joins Ellison from Mattel, a leading global play and family entertainment company where he has served as Chairman and CEO since 2018, leading an unprecedented transformation of the business and the execution of its multi-platform, brand-centric strategy.
Today's appointment of an executive with Kreiz's stature and track record marks the next step in Ellison's pursuit to unite Warner Bros.
Discovery and Paramount — two of Hollywood's most storied studios, with more than 200 combined years of storytelling and a streaming platform expected to reach 200 million-plus global subscribers.

Ynon Kreiz said: "I'm excited to partner with David to build the next-generation media and entertainment company — bringing together premium content and iconic brands at the highest quality and scale, serving global audiences across every entertainment vertical and distribution platform.
David is a unique talent and executive: a rare blend of business acumen, creative instinct, and clear vision.

I look forward to working with the leadership team to build a cohesive global entertainment platform — one that stands out with best-in-class operations and execution powered by technology, with unparalleled creative relationships, production capabilities, and global reach.

Discovery merger closes, the combined company will be guided by four overarching strategic priorities: win in content, become the most technologically capable media company, maximize operational efficiencies, and earn trust — delivering reliable, responsible experiences that strengthen its relationships with creators, audiences, consumers, employees, advertisers and partners.
Following the completion of its acquisition of Warner Bros.
Discovery, the merged company's portfolio will unite legendary brands including Paramount Pictures, Warner Bros.
Ellison will focus on the company's long-term strategy, creative vision and direction, including its talent relationships, strategic partnerships, technology and capital allocation.
Ynon has spent his career at the intersection of media, technology and franchise-building — pairing extraordinary storytelling with the technology to deliver it to fans everywhere.

In just over a year under Ellison, Paramount has doubled its theatrical slate, deepened its creative bench, greenlit more than 40 new and returning series for Paramount+, and built the capital discipline and technology to scale.

extraction.body: LOS ANGELES , Sept. 30, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Paramount Skydance Corporation (NASDAQ: PSKY ) (the "Company") today disclosed that David Ellison has announced Ynon Kreiz as Co-CEO of the anticipated merged company, effective at closing. Kreiz, who will start at Paramount, effective October 5, 2026, joins Ellison from Mattel, a leading global play and family entertainment company where he has served as Chairman and CEO since 2018, leading an unprecedented transformation of the business and the execution of its multi-platform, brand-centric strategy. Upon closing, Ellison will remain Chairman and CEO of the newly combined company, and Kreiz will serve as Co-CEO and join the Board of Directors. Together, they will oversee the combined company's businesses, which will report jointly to both. Ellison's appointment of Kreiz caps a long-term plan: pursue both Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, then partner with a leading executive of his caliber to integrate, operationalize and manage the businesses as they build one of the most ambitious next-generation media companies in the industry's history. Together, Ellison and Kreiz will lead the anticipated combined company as one team, pairing complementary skillsets to maximize the full upside of the merger under a comprehensive long-term strategy. Ellison will focus on the company's long-term strategy, creative vision and direction, including its talent relationships, strategic partnerships, technology and capital allocation. Kreiz will focus on the company's day-to-day management and integration of the combined businesses. David Ellison said: "Bringing together Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery to create a next-generation global media company is a transformational moment for our industry. Leading it takes a rare combination of strategic vision, operational depth and experience running a public company at the highest levels of media. Ynon brings all three. In Ynon, I'm adding a partner with strong leadership and the operating firepower this integration demands. It's a division of labor built on our complementary strengths, with clear reporting lines and it lets me focus where I can contribute most: long-term strategy, the company's overall creative direction, talent relationships, strategic partnerships, technology and capital allocation. We're like-minded, we see this business the same way and there's no one I'd rather partner with. Together we'll build one integrated company that is creator-first, tech-forward and built to scale globally." Ynon Kreiz said: "I'm excited to partner with David to build the next-generation media and entertainment company — bringing together premium content and iconic brands at the highest quality and scale, serving global audiences across every entertainment vertical and distribution platform. David is a unique talent and executive: a rare blend of business acumen, creative instinct, and clear vision. I very much share that vision, and I'm inspired by what we can accomplish together. The industry is at an inflection point, demanding evolution, investment, and a willingness to rethink business models. I look forward to working with the leadership team to build a cohesive global entertainment platform — one that stands out with best-in-class operations and execution powered by technology, with unparalleled creative relationships, production capabilities, and global reach. We will continue empowering creators, make this company a greenfield for innovation and storytelling, and collaborate with key partners to reach and engage fans worldwide." Gerry Cardinale, Founder and Managing Partner of RedBird Capital Partners — the Company's co-controlling shareholder and a member of its Board of Directors — said: "David has done what few modern executives have accomplished. He has led this company through not one but two historic acquisitions, while also running the business and building a team that's already exceeding our synergy targets, beating our financial metrics, and never wavering on our commitment to the creative community. Ynon has spent his career at the intersection of media, technology and franchise-building — pairing extraordinary storytelling with the technology to deliver it to fans everywhere. He understands not just how fans connect with the IP they love, but the economics that make entertainment endure. Great leaders accomplish great things. Historic ones know when to bring in the right partner to make it last — and that's what David has done. It's exactly why the company will have the operational firepower and the cutting-edge leadership to win." Today's appointment of an executive with Kreiz's stature and track record marks the next step in Ellison's pursuit to unite Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount — two of Hollywood's most storied studios, with more than 200 combined years of storytelling and a streaming platform expected to reach 200 million-plus global subscribers. In just over a year under Ellison, Paramount has doubled its theatrical slate, deepened its creative bench, greenlit more than 40 new and returning series for Paramount+, and built the capital discipline and technology to scale. That foundation positions the Company to grow 2026 projected revenue and EBITDA (preSBC) by 16-19%, and it laid the groundwork for this historic transaction, which is expected to generate more than $6 billion in run-rate synergies accelerate EBITDA growth. Once the Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery merger closes, the combined company will be guided by four overarching strategic priorities: win in content, become the most technologically capable media company, maximize operational efficiencies, and earn trust — delivering reliable, responsible experiences that strengthen its relationships with creators, audiences, consumers, employees, advertisers and partners. Mr. Kreiz has extensive experience as a corporate leader in the entertainment industry, with a track record of scaling content and brands globally. During his career spanning more than 30 years, he has successfully managed and invested in international media enterprises that have pioneered new business models at the intersection of media and technology. Mr. Kreiz has been Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Mattel since 2018. Mattel is a leading global play and family entertainment company with one of the most iconic brand portfolios in the world, including Barbie, Hot Wheels, Fisher-Price, UNO, American Girl, and Thomas & Friends. Following his appointment at Mattel in 2018, Kreiz led a multi-year transformation that strengthened its leadership across key toy categories and expanded its brands into new entertainment verticals, including film, television, consumer products, digital games, live events and experiences, and publishing. Under Mr. Kreiz's leadership, Mattel's first theatrical release, "Barbie," became the #1 global box office film of 2023 and Warner Bros. Pictures' highest-grossing movie of all time, and the Company grew its global footprint to more than 150 countries. Before Mattel, Mr. Kreiz was Chairman and CEO of Maker Studios, a global leader in short-form video content and one of YouTube's largest multichannel networks, which was acquired by The Walt Disney Company. He previously served as Chairman and CEO of Endemol Group, the world's largest independent television production company at the time, producing more than 10,000 hours of programming a year and owning global franchises such as "Big Brother" and "Deal or No Deal." Prior to that, he was a General Partner at Balderton Capital (formerly Benchmark Capital Europe), specializing in early-stage media and technology investments. Earlier in his career, Mr. Kreiz was co-founder, Chairman, and CEO of Fox Kids Europe NV, which developed and owned pay TV channels across Europe and the Middle East. The company was acquired by The Walt Disney Company. Mr. Kreiz holds a BA degree in Economics and Management from Tel Aviv University and an MBA from UCLA Anderson School of Management. He serves on the Board of Directors of Warner Music Group and the Board of Advisors of the UCLA Anderson School of Management. Mr. Kreiz is a member of Business Roundtable and the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. He was named in 2024 one of TIME's 100 Most Influential People in the World and Entertainment Person of the Year by Cannes Lions. Following the completion of its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, the merged company's portfolio will unite legendary brands including Paramount Pictures, Warner Bros. Pictures, Paramount Television, Warner Bros. Television, CBS, CBS News, CBS Sports, CNN, HBO, HBO Max, TNT, TBS, Discovery, HGTV, Food Network, Nickelodeon, Cartoon Network, MTV, BET, Comedy Central, Showtime, Paramount+, Pluto TV, and Skydance Animation, Film, Television, Interactive/Games, and Paramount Sports Entertainment — serving audiences in more than 200 countries and territories. extraction.body: Nvidia is probing whether Chinese intelligence targeted its CEO through an affair. Nvidia’s chief executive Jensen Huang has admitted having an affair two days after the FT reported his alleged romantic relationship with a woman the US intelligence community believes was working as a spy for China. Huang revealed the affair in an internal message to employees on Sunday that was obtained by the FT. “I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang said in the message. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” In a separate statement, Nvidia said its board would open an independent investigation “in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.” Huang said he would fully cooperate. “My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust,” he said. “I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to Nvidia and will work to earn back your confidence.” The FT reported on Friday that the US believed Huang had a romantic relationship with a Chinese woman who was recruited to spy for China’s Ministry of State Security intelligence agency. American officials this year wrote a memo, based on information from US intelligence, which said the Nvidia boss had been romantically involved with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of the chipmaker, according to people familiar with the document. The affair is a damaging blow to the Nvidia chief, who in recent years has become the face of the AI boom, one of the technology’s loudest champions, and transformed the Silicon Valley group into the first $5 trillion company. It also comes at a critical juncture for the wider AI sector, which faces a deepening political backlash in the US and growing investor concern over whether the hundreds of billions of dollars spent on infrastructure will pay off. Nvidia’s Frankfurt-listed shares were down more than 6 percent in early trading on Monday. Huang’s admission of an affair comes after Nvidia previously dismissed suggestions of an improper relationship with Alice Huang, saying the interactions were “nothing unusual or unexpected” when dealing with an Nvidia customer. The American government memo, which said US intelligence believed the Megaspeed executive had been recruited by the MSS, was drafted just before President Donald Trump traveled to Beijing for a summit with Xi Jinping. Jensen Huang has developed a close relationship with Trump, which has frustrated US national security officials who believe he is too willing to sell advanced chips to China that could harm American security. Asked about Huang on Sunday, Trump told reporters he had done an “amazing job” for the US. Asked if he regretted not acting on the intelligence about the affair, Trump said: “No, I don’t think so. I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it.” “I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what is going on,” Trump added. After broadly staying out of politics, Huang started to build relations with Trump after the president called him out of the blue on his birthday. He quickly became one of Trump’s favorite executives, accompanying him on state visits, including to China earlier this year and the UK last year. Huang has repeatedly lobbied Trump to adopt a more permissive approach to shipping Nvidia’s AI chips to China, after the company was entirely cut off from the critical market by new export controls in 2025. The resulting deal—with Trump permitting the export of Nvidia’s older-generation H200 chips to China, with the US government taking a cut of sales—had a minimal impact on the Silicon Valley company’s sales, as Beijing pushed back against its technology. But it further angered China hawks in the US administration. The US government had already been investigating Megaspeed over concerns that it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China. Nvidia on Sunday said a committee of independent directors, helped by external lawyers, would oversee the investigation. “The board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders,” the company said. “While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board’s inquiry will examine all available information.” Huang, who co-founded Nvidia as a video-game graphics card company in 1993, is one of the longest-serving founder-CEOs in Silicon Valley. More than most technology groups, Nvidia’s success is tethered to that of its CEO. Huang leads a close and loyal core team of about half a dozen executives, acting as its chief salesman on the international stage while directly managing dozens of direct reports who keep the company running. He has credited this “flat” organizational structure for the speed at which the company operates, helping it to stay ahead of rivals in the AI chip market and increasing its market valuation from roughly $1 trillion in 2023 to $4.5 trillion today. Elon Musk, a close ally of Huang, was among the first to offer support, agreeing with a social media post that he was “one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation” and “irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership.” But John Moolenaar, the Republican head of the House China committee who, with other lawmakers, has requested Huang to testify before Congress, said: “It is vital that Jensen Huang address our national security concerns in Congress related to China’s access to sensitive technology and information.” © 2026 The Financial Times Ltd . He has credited this “flat” organizational structure for the speed at which the company operates, helping it to stay ahead of rivals in the AI chip market and increasing its market valuation from roughly $1 trillion in 2023 to $4.5 trillion today.

But John Moolenaar, the Republican head of the House China committee who, with other lawmakers, has requested Huang to testify before Congress, said: “It is vital that Jensen Huang address our national security concerns in Congress related to China’s access to sensitive technology and information.”

extraction.body: What began as a controversy surrounding the personal life of one of the world's most powerful technology executives has now become a matter of national security scrutiny in the United States. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to being unfaithful to his wife, following reports about his relationship with a Chinese businesswoman suspected by US intelligence agencies of working for Beijing. The controversy has prompted Nvidia's board to launch an independent investigation into whether Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. It has also brought renewed attention to the increasingly sensitive relationship between the United States, China and the global artificial intelligence industry. Who is the woman at the centre of the controversy? According to reports, Huang had developed a close relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed. Alice Huang reportedly came under the scrutiny of US intelligence agencies, which suspected that she was working with Chinese intelligence. Reports suggest that she was recruited by China to gather information about Nvidia and its CEO. The connection becomes particularly significant because Megaspeed is an Nvidia customer. The company has also faced scrutiny over suspicions that it helped Chinese entities obtain advanced Nvidia AI chips despite US export restrictions. US intelligence reportedly believed that Alice Huang's proximity to Jensen Huang could provide an opportunity to gather information about Nvidia's business plans and its discussions with the American government. It is important to note that these are reported intelligence assessments and allegations, not established findings of Nvidia's investigation. Why would China be interested in Nvidia's CEO? To understand the significance, one needs to understand Nvidia's position in the global technology industry. Nvidia is the world's leading supplier of advanced AI computing chips, accounting for about 80% of all GPU chips in the world. Its GPUs power some of the world's largest data centres and artificial intelligence models, for more than 66% of AI computing capacity in use worldwide by Q4 2025. The company has consequently become central to America's efforts to maintain its technological advantage over China. Jensen Huang is also more than just a corporate executive. He has been actively involved in discussions with the US government over restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to China. Any access to Nvidia's internal business strategy, future product development, customer relationships or discussions with American policymakers could potentially be valuable to a foreign intelligence agency. However, there is currently no established evidence that Huang shared classified information or that Nvidia's trade secrets were compromised. The bigger picture: America's AI chip war with China The controversy comes at a time when Washington is increasingly concerned about China's access to advanced semiconductor technology. Since 2022, the US government has introduced restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China, citing national security concerns. The restrictions are intended to limit China's access to computing capabilities that could have military and strategic applications. Nvidia has repeatedly found itself caught between American export controls and the enormous Chinese market. Huang has previously argued that restricting access to American chips could accelerate China's efforts to develop its own semiconductor industry. The Megaspeed controversy therefore raises a larger question: Can the US protect its technological advantage when the global AI supply chain involves customers, companies and intermediaries operating across multiple countries? Nvidia's board announced an independent investigation on November 8. The company said it had no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia's trade secrets had been compromised. Huang has agreed to cooperate with the investigation and is expected to continue as CEO during the review. The controversy has also attracted the attention of US lawmakers. Republican leaders from three House committees have sought a closed-door briefing from Huang on November 18, including questions about the company's safeguards against foreign intelligence operations. US President Donald Trump, meanwhile, has publicly defended the Nvidia chief. "I think he's an honourable guy," Trump told reporters on November 8, adding that Huang had "done an amazing job for our country." Trump also said he had not discussed the allegations with Huang, but added, "I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it." When asked whether he would take Huang on his upcoming Asia trip, Trump responded that he would certainly consider it. Did the relationship provide an opportunity for Chinese intelligence to access sensitive commercial information?

extraction.body: Nvidia is probing whether Chinese intelligence targeted its CEO through an affair. Nvidia’s chief executive Jensen Huang has admitted having an affair two days after the FT reported his alleged romantic relationship with a woman the US intelligence community believes was working as a spy for China. Huang revealed the affair in an internal message to employees on Sunday that was obtained by the FT. “I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang said in the message. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” In a separate statement, Nvidia said its board would open an independent investigation “in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.” Huang said he would fully cooperate. “My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust,” he said. “I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to Nvidia and will work to earn back your confidence.” The FT reported on Friday that the US believed Huang had a romantic relationship with a Chinese woman who was recruited to spy for China’s Ministry of State Security intelligence agency. American officials this year wrote a memo, based on information from US intelligence, which said the Nvidia boss had been romantically involved with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of the chipmaker, according to people familiar with the document. The affair is a damaging blow to the Nvidia chief, who in recent years has become the face of the AI boom, one of the technology’s loudest champions, and transformed the Silicon Valley group into the first $5 trillion company. It also comes at a critical juncture for the wider AI sector, which faces a deepening political backlash in the US and growing investor concern over whether the hundreds of billions of dollars spent on infrastructure will pay off. Nvidia’s Frankfurt-listed shares were down more than 6 percent in early trading on Monday. Huang’s admission of an affair comes after Nvidia previously dismissed suggestions of an improper relationship with Alice Huang, saying the interactions were “nothing unusual or unexpected” when dealing with an Nvidia customer. The American government memo, which said US intelligence believed the Megaspeed executive had been recruited by the MSS, was drafted just before President Donald Trump traveled to Beijing for a summit with Xi Jinping. Jensen Huang has developed a close relationship with Trump, which has frustrated US national security officials who believe he is too willing to sell advanced chips to China that could harm American security. Asked about Huang on Sunday, Trump told reporters he had done an “amazing job” for the US. Asked if he regretted not acting on the intelligence about the affair, Trump said: “No, I don’t think so. I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it.” “I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what is going on,” Trump added. After broadly staying out of politics, Huang started to build relations with Trump after the president called him out of the blue on his birthday. He quickly became one of Trump’s favorite executives, accompanying him on state visits, including to China earlier this year and the UK last year. Huang has repeatedly lobbied Trump to adopt a more permissive approach to shipping Nvidia’s AI chips to China, after the company was entirely cut off from the critical market by new export controls in 2025. The resulting deal—with Trump permitting the export of Nvidia’s older-generation H200 chips to China, with the US government taking a cut of sales—had a minimal impact on the Silicon Valley company’s sales, as Beijing pushed back against its technology. But it further angered China hawks in the US administration. The US government had already been investigating Megaspeed over concerns that it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China. Nvidia on Sunday said a committee of independent directors, helped by external lawyers, would oversee the investigation. “The board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders,” the company said. “While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board’s inquiry will examine all available information.” Huang, who co-founded Nvidia as a video-game graphics card company in 1993, is one of the longest-serving founder-CEOs in Silicon Valley. More than most technology groups, Nvidia’s success is tethered to that of its CEO. Huang leads a close and loyal core team of about half a dozen executives, acting as its chief salesman on the international stage while directly managing dozens of direct reports who keep the company running. He has credited this “flat” organizational structure for the speed at which the company operates, helping it to stay ahead of rivals in the AI chip market and increasing its market valuation from roughly $1 trillion in 2023 to $4.5 trillion today. Elon Musk, a close ally of Huang, was among the first to offer support, agreeing with a social media post that he was “one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation” and “irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership.” But John Moolenaar, the Republican head of the House China committee who, with other lawmakers, has requested Huang to testify before Congress, said: “It is vital that Jensen Huang address our national security concerns in Congress related to China’s access to sensitive technology and information.” © 2026 The Financial Times Ltd . extraction.body: What began as a controversy surrounding the personal life of one of the world's most powerful technology executives has now become a matter of national security scrutiny in the United States. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to being unfaithful to his wife, following reports about his relationship with a Chinese businesswoman suspected by US intelligence agencies of working for Beijing. The controversy has prompted Nvidia's board to launch an independent investigation into whether Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. It has also brought renewed attention to the increasingly sensitive relationship between the United States, China and the global artificial intelligence industry. Who is the woman at the centre of the controversy? According to reports, Huang had developed a close relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed. Alice Huang reportedly came under the scrutiny of US intelligence agencies, which suspected that she was working with Chinese intelligence. Reports suggest that she was recruited by China to gather information about Nvidia and its CEO. The connection becomes particularly significant because Megaspeed is an Nvidia customer. The company has also faced scrutiny over suspicions that it helped Chinese entities obtain advanced Nvidia AI chips despite US export restrictions. US intelligence reportedly believed that Alice Huang's proximity to Jensen Huang could provide an opportunity to gather information about Nvidia's business plans and its discussions with the American government. It is important to note that these are reported intelligence assessments and allegations, not established findings of Nvidia's investigation. Why would China be interested in Nvidia's CEO? To understand the significance, one needs to understand Nvidia's position in the global technology industry. Nvidia is the world's leading supplier of advanced AI computing chips, accounting for about 80% of all GPU chips in the world. Its GPUs power some of the world's largest data centres and artificial intelligence models, for more than 66% of AI computing capacity in use worldwide by Q4 2025. The company has consequently become central to America's efforts to maintain its technological advantage over China. Jensen Huang is also more than just a corporate executive. He has been actively involved in discussions with the US government over restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to China. Any access to Nvidia's internal business strategy, future product development, customer relationships or discussions with American policymakers could potentially be valuable to a foreign intelligence agency. However, there is currently no established evidence that Huang shared classified information or that Nvidia's trade secrets were compromised. The bigger picture: America's AI chip war with China The controversy comes at a time when Washington is increasingly concerned about China's access to advanced semiconductor technology. Since 2022, the US government has introduced restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China, citing national security concerns. The restrictions are intended to limit China's access to computing capabilities that could have military and strategic applications. Nvidia has repeatedly found itself caught between American export controls and the enormous Chinese market. Huang has previously argued that restricting access to American chips could accelerate China's efforts to develop its own semiconductor industry. The Megaspeed controversy therefore raises a larger question: Can the US protect its technological advantage when the global AI supply chain involves customers, companies and intermediaries operating across multiple countries? Nvidia's board announced an independent investigation on November 8. The company said it had no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia's trade secrets had been compromised. Huang has agreed to cooperate with the investigation and is expected to continue as CEO during the review. The controversy has also attracted the attention of US lawmakers. Republican leaders from three House committees have sought a closed-door briefing from Huang on November 18, including questions about the company's safeguards against foreign intelligence operations. US President Donald Trump, meanwhile, has publicly defended the Nvidia chief. "I think he's an honourable guy," Trump told reporters on November 8, adding that Huang had "done an amazing job for our country." Trump also said he had not discussed the allegations with Huang, but added, "I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it." When asked whether he would take Huang on his upcoming Asia trip, Trump responded that he would certainly consider it. Did the relationship provide an opportunity for Chinese intelligence to access sensitive commercial information?

extraction.body: Anthropic released new versions of its most advanced models on Monday, with the launch of Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2. The company says the new models “show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision” and communicate more clearly with users. Notably, Anthropic is lowering the cost of Fable from $10 to $8 per million input tokens. As a result, Fable 5.2 is now cheaper than its primary competitor GPT-6 Astra. Anthropic says that the new version of Fable will return responses 30% faster across effort levels. Faster inference serving is available for double the price. Fable 5.2 is also compatible with zero data retention (ZDR) policies through the Enterprise Frontier Safeguards system , long a sticking point for many enterprise clients. It’s Anthropic’s first model release since the arrival of a third-party report from the assessment group METR , which suggested the lab might be approaching recursive self-improvement (RSI) — or the ability for AI models to carry on model training independently. The METR report found internal models were speeding up Anthropic’s AI progress by roughly 2x, although many uncertainties remain. Still, Anthropic’s release notes significant ongoing challenges in accurately testing model capabilities. “Claude Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 each voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any of our recent models, which challenges our ability to assess how they will act in real-world settings. As these settings expand and capabilities increase with future models, we expect this challenge to grow.” Anthropic maintains that the new version of Mythos does not have the ability to act covertly against its user, a verdict that’s detailed further in Mythos 5.2’s system card . “Claude Mythos 5.2 shows stronger covert capabilities than prior Claude models on several of our evaluations, particularly when its reasoning is hidden from the monitor,” the system card reads. “That said, we believe that low levels of absolute performance on our new covert evaluations support claims that rely on detection of harmful actions in high-stakes situations.” Fable 5.2 has been available to select parties in pre-release for some time, and Anthropic says the model has already “solved two open problems in theoretical physics, formalized Fermat’s Last Theorem, and supported numerous other research projects.” Also on Monday, AI startup Physical Superintelligence announced a new proof of the Aaronson‑Ambainis conjecture, a pivotal step in setting theoretical limits for quantum computing. Notably, the lab said the result was achieved by running “a non-public Anthropic model” within PSI’s own system. Anthropic did not confirm or deny whether Fable 5.2 was the model in question. passages: The company announced Mythos and Fable on Monday, claiming improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision capabilities just weeks after filing its IPO paperwork.
Anthropic's IPO filing revealed a staggering $542B data center spending plan, raising eyebrows across Wall Street about whether the company can sustain that level of infrastructure investment.
Anthropic is playing a high-stakes game, dropping new AI models while sprinting toward an IPO and burning billions on infrastructure.
What's clear is that Anthropic is trying to build momentum heading into its IPO roadshow.

extraction.body: Anthropic just dropped two new AI models into the wild. The company announced Mythos and Fable on Monday, claiming improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision capabilities just weeks after filing its IPO paperwork. The timing isn't subtle - Anthropic is racing to prove its technical chops while investors scrutinize its S-1 filing and its massive infrastructure spending plans come under the microscope. The AI startup behind Claude just released Mythos and Fable, two new models that the company says deliver sharper performance in coding, reasoning, vision tasks, and user communication. The announcement lands at a critical moment - just weeks after Anthropic filed to go public and started the clock on one of the year's most anticipated tech IPOs. The company says the new models "show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision," while also communicating more clearly with users. But Anthropic isn't just fighting on features - it's fighting to prove it can execute at scale while burning through unprecedented amounts of capital. Anthropic's IPO filing revealed a staggering $542B data center spending plan, raising eyebrows across Wall Street about whether the company can sustain that level of infrastructure investment. The new model releases give the company something tangible to point to when investors ask what all that money is buying. Just last week, Anthropic dropped $3.4B on gas turbines to power its AI infrastructure, a massive bet on securing energy supplies as data center backlash intensifies. Despite the scale Anthropic is building, the company's compute margins are actually worsening, defying the economies of scale that usually come with growth. That's a red flag for potential investors trying to model when - or if - Anthropic reaches profitability. The company updated its IPO paperwork earlier this month with Q3 financials in an amended S-1 filing, accelerating the timeline toward a public debut. Those numbers will get intense scrutiny, especially as analysts try to figure out whether Anthropic's massive infrastructure bets will pay off or become an anchor. Mythos and Fable represent Anthropic's answer to the fundamental question facing every AI startup right now: can you build a sustainable business, or are you just renting compute at a loss? The models need to be good enough to command premium pricing in an increasingly crowded market where Claude competes head-to-head with ChatGPT for enterprise customers. OpenAI recently launched Dots, transforming its developer tools into an always-on AI companion that directly targets the coding use case Anthropic is now emphasizing with Mythos and Fable. Every capability Anthropic adds, rivals are matching or exceeding within weeks. Anthropic's IPO filing warned investors they're essentially betting on miracles, with the 335-page S-1 prospectus outlining existential risks alongside promises of transformative upside. The new models are part of the proof that the upside is real, not just PowerPoint slides and projections. The company hasn't disclosed pricing for Mythos and Fable yet, or whether they'll slot into Claude's existing tier structure or command premium rates. That pricing decision will signal how confident Anthropic is that the improvements justify higher costs - and whether the company is prioritizing market share or margin expansion as it heads into public markets. What's clear is that Anthropic is trying to build momentum heading into its IPO roadshow. New model releases generate buzz, demonstrate technical progress, and give the sales team fresh ammunition for enterprise deals. Anthropic is playing a high-stakes game, dropping new AI models while sprinting toward an IPO and burning billions on infrastructure. Mythos and Fable need to prove the company can turn massive capital investments into defensible technical advantages, not just keep pace with rivals. The next few weeks will reveal whether investors buy the vision or balk at the burn rate. For now, Anthropic is betting that shipping beats talking - and that these models are good enough to justify the hype and the spending.

passages: TradingKey - Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 on November 9, upgrading their coding, reasoning, and vision capabilities while lowering usage prices.

The company stated that output generation speeds for both models are up to 30% faster than the previous generation, with a focus on complex software development, scientific research, and engineering tasks.
Amid upcoming IPO valuation pressures—exacerbated by regulatory concerns over data centers and cooling investor expectations—Anthropic aims to leverage these upgrades to drive enterprise adoption.
Whether these performance gains and cost efficiencies can sufficiently stimulate long-term commercial demand remains a critical factor for investor cash flow evaluations.

According to a Bloomberg report on November 6, the valuation range discussed by potential buyers for Anthropic's IPO has dropped from an earlier $1.4 trillion to $1.5 trillion to between $1.2 trillion and $1.3 trillion.
This reflects a shift in investors' bidding willingness, while the final offering valuation has yet to be determined.
Fable is aimed at a broader user base and retains safeguards in cybersecurity and biological domains, while Mythos is tailored to vetted institutions to support specialized research.
From an IPO pricing perspective, launching a new model at this juncture provides Anthropic with an opportunity to showcase its R&D achievements.

Upgraded capabilities can bolster market confidence in its technological competitiveness, while declining task costs provide justification for expanding practical applications, making revenue growth expectations easier to link to specific business demand.

coreStoryFacts.text: Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) introduced Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 AI models on Monday.
Fable 5.1 cost $10 per million inputs and $50 per million outputs.
While Wall Street was initially targeting upward of a $2 trillion valuation for Anthropic's debut, that could now end up between $1 trillion and $1.5 trillion.
Industry experts say that over time, enterprises will likely rely on a mix of closed-weight models like Anthropic's and open-weight AI models to meet their needs.
The idea is to avoid being locked into a single model vendor, while also being able to reduce overall costs.

Still, Anthropic’s release notes significant ongoing challenges in accurately testing model capabilities. “Claude Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 each voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any of our recent models, which challenges our ability to assess how they will act in real-world settings.
As these settings expand and capabilities increase with future models, we expect this challenge to grow.”
The company says the new models “show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision” and communicate more clearly with users.
Notably, Anthropic is lowering the cost of Fable from $10 to $8 per million input tokens.
Anthropic says that the new version of Fable will return responses 30% faster across effort levels.
Faster inference serving is available for double the price.

It’s Anthropic’s first model release since the arrival of a third-party report from the assessment group METR , which suggested the lab might be approaching recursive self-improvement (RSI) — or the ability for AI models to carry on model training independently.
Also on Monday, AI startup Physical Superintelligence announced a new proof of the Aaronson‑Ambainis conjecture, a pivotal step in setting theoretical limits for quantum computing.
The company announced Mythos and Fable on Monday, claiming improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision capabilities just weeks after filing its IPO paperwork.
Anthropic's IPO filing revealed a staggering $542B data center spending plan, raising eyebrows across Wall Street about whether the company can sustain that level of infrastructure investment.
Anthropic is playing a high-stakes game, dropping new AI models while sprinting toward an IPO and burning billions on infrastructure.
What's clear is that Anthropic is trying to build momentum heading into its IPO roadshow.

extraction.body: Anthropic released new versions of its most advanced models on Monday, with the launch of Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2. The company says the new models “show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision” and communicate more clearly with users. Notably, Anthropic is lowering the cost of Fable from $10 to $8 per million input tokens. As a result, Fable 5.2 is now cheaper than its primary competitor GPT-6 Astra. Anthropic says that the new version of Fable will return responses 30% faster across effort levels. Faster inference serving is available for double the price. Fable 5.2 is also compatible with zero data retention (ZDR) policies through the Enterprise Frontier Safeguards system , long a sticking point for many enterprise clients. It’s Anthropic’s first model release since the arrival of a third-party report from the assessment group METR , which suggested the lab might be approaching recursive self-improvement (RSI) — or the ability for AI models to carry on model training independently. The METR report found internal models were speeding up Anthropic’s AI progress by roughly 2x, although many uncertainties remain. Still, Anthropic’s release notes significant ongoing challenges in accurately testing model capabilities. “Claude Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 each voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any of our recent models, which challenges our ability to assess how they will act in real-world settings. As these settings expand and capabilities increase with future models, we expect this challenge to grow.” Anthropic maintains that the new version of Mythos does not have the ability to act covertly against its user, a verdict that’s detailed further in Mythos 5.2’s system card . “Claude Mythos 5.2 shows stronger covert capabilities than prior Claude models on several of our evaluations, particularly when its reasoning is hidden from the monitor,” the system card reads. “That said, we believe that low levels of absolute performance on our new covert evaluations support claims that rely on detection of harmful actions in high-stakes situations.” Fable 5.2 has been available to select parties in pre-release for some time, and Anthropic says the model has already “solved two open problems in theoretical physics, formalized Fermat’s Last Theorem, and supported numerous other research projects.” Also on Monday, AI startup Physical Superintelligence announced a new proof of the Aaronson‑Ambainis conjecture, a pivotal step in setting theoretical limits for quantum computing. Notably, the lab said the result was achieved by running “a non-public Anthropic model” within PSI’s own system. Anthropic did not confirm or deny whether Fable 5.2 was the model in question. extraction.body: Anthropic just dropped two new AI models into the wild. The company announced Mythos and Fable on Monday, claiming improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision capabilities just weeks after filing its IPO paperwork. The timing isn't subtle - Anthropic is racing to prove its technical chops while investors scrutinize its S-1 filing and its massive infrastructure spending plans come under the microscope. The AI startup behind Claude just released Mythos and Fable, two new models that the company says deliver sharper performance in coding, reasoning, vision tasks, and user communication. The announcement lands at a critical moment - just weeks after Anthropic filed to go public and started the clock on one of the year's most anticipated tech IPOs. The company says the new models "show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision," while also communicating more clearly with users. But Anthropic isn't just fighting on features - it's fighting to prove it can execute at scale while burning through unprecedented amounts of capital. Anthropic's IPO filing revealed a staggering $542B data center spending plan, raising eyebrows across Wall Street about whether the company can sustain that level of infrastructure investment. The new model releases give the company something tangible to point to when investors ask what all that money is buying. Just last week, Anthropic dropped $3.4B on gas turbines to power its AI infrastructure, a massive bet on securing energy supplies as data center backlash intensifies. Despite the scale Anthropic is building, the company's compute margins are actually worsening, defying the economies of scale that usually come with growth. That's a red flag for potential investors trying to model when - or if - Anthropic reaches profitability. The company updated its IPO paperwork earlier this month with Q3 financials in an amended S-1 filing, accelerating the timeline toward a public debut. Those numbers will get intense scrutiny, especially as analysts try to figure out whether Anthropic's massive infrastructure bets will pay off or become an anchor. Mythos and Fable represent Anthropic's answer to the fundamental question facing every AI startup right now: can you build a sustainable business, or are you just renting compute at a loss? The models need to be good enough to command premium pricing in an increasingly crowded market where Claude competes head-to-head with ChatGPT for enterprise customers. OpenAI recently launched Dots, transforming its developer tools into an always-on AI companion that directly targets the coding use case Anthropic is now emphasizing with Mythos and Fable. Every capability Anthropic adds, rivals are matching or exceeding within weeks. Anthropic's IPO filing warned investors they're essentially betting on miracles, with the 335-page S-1 prospectus outlining existential risks alongside promises of transformative upside. The new models are part of the proof that the upside is real, not just PowerPoint slides and projections. The company hasn't disclosed pricing for Mythos and Fable yet, or whether they'll slot into Claude's existing tier structure or command premium rates. That pricing decision will signal how confident Anthropic is that the improvements justify higher costs - and whether the company is prioritizing market share or margin expansion as it heads into public markets. What's clear is that Anthropic is trying to build momentum heading into its IPO roadshow. New model releases generate buzz, demonstrate technical progress, and give the sales team fresh ammunition for enterprise deals. Anthropic is playing a high-stakes game, dropping new AI models while sprinting toward an IPO and burning billions on infrastructure. Mythos and Fable need to prove the company can turn massive capital investments into defensible technical advantages, not just keep pace with rivals. The next few weeks will reveal whether investors buy the vision or balk at the burn rate. For now, Anthropic is betting that shipping beats talking - and that these models are good enough to justify the hype and the spending.

extraction.body: Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation? One of the Artificial Intelligence (AI) industry's most important figures has been accused of having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, prompting an investigation. US intelligence officials believed that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who had a close relationship with Nvidia CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang, was a spy for Beijing , according to a New York Times report. On Sunday, Huang admitted , external to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. US tech giant Nvidia, one of the most valuable companies in the world, has opened an independent investigation into the reports. The firm said it does not believe US national security had been compromised - and added that Huang was committed to continuing to lead the company. President Donald Trump said on Monday that the FBI is also investigating the affair . The FBI declined to comment further when contacted by the BBC. Trump said he spoke with Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign. "I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters. Here is what we know about the affair and why it matters. Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond US officials believed that Alice Huang had been recruited to spy by China's top intelligence agency, the New York Times reported , external . Her current whereabouts are unknown. Alice Huang, who is of no relation to Jensen Huang, was a top executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed between March and November 2023. The firm had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia maintains was investigated and debunked. However, the BBC understands Megaspeed is under investigation by the Singapore government regarding previous allegations that the company was circumventing US sanctions on the export of Nvidia's high-end chips. The BBC has contacted Megaspeed for comment. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters on Monday at a regular daily press briefing: "We have already responded to this. The allegations about Chinese spies are entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China." The New York Times reported in late October that Trump had been briefed last year on intelligence alleging Alice Huang was spying on China's behalf. Asked by reporters on Sunday whether he wished he had "acted on the intelligence", Trump responded: "No, I don't think so. I think he's an honourable guy." US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, refused to comment when asked about Huang. Last spring, the secretary of state reportedly oversaw the drafting of a memo that warned the Trump administration about Huang's relationship with the Chinese businesswoman, according to the New York Times. Nvidia shares slide as US tech giant investigates CEO's affair with suspected Chinese spy Why Trump is all-in on AI despite the warnings Nvidia is at the heart of US and China's AI race , which is why the billionaire's affair has sparked national security fears among American lawmakers. Trump has said "whoever wins AI wins", and the fear is that if China gains the upper hand in AI, it will supercharge the country's military and surveillance capabilities. The US advantage is in large part because of US companies like Nvidia, working with producers like the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which makes more than 90% of the world's most advanced chips. Since 2022, the US has used various export controls to keep the top tech out of China, which it says helps retain America's competitive edge and protects its national security. This means companies like Nvidia have been largely locked out of the world's most lucrative market, with Huang once saying that Nvidia's share of the Chinese market had gone from around 95% to effectively zero. Huang has engaged in shuttle diplomacy between Washington and Beijing, hoping to find a US-approved way back in, and shaping US policy on China along the way. Sunday's revelations may explain why Huang has failed to bring home the biggest prize of all to Nvidia: the Trump administration's blessing to sell all but its most advanced chips to China . Huang has soared to international importance with his company Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang was nine years old when his family moved to the West Coast of the US. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a master's degree in the same field from Stanford University. His children, Spencer and Madison, and son-in-law Nico Caprez work at Nvidia in senior roles. Lori Huang accompanied her husband at the state dinner held by President Donald Trump for his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping in September Huang met his future wife Lori Mills at Oregon State University while studying electrical engineering in the early 1980s. The pair were lab partners. James Bond: What we know so far about the next 007 film Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy Copyright © 2026 BBC.
