extraction.body: Nvidia’s board of directors said Sunday that it is opening an independent investigation after CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. The announcement followed recent reporting by The New York Times and the Financial Times about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who the newspapers reported had been recruited to spy for China. A person familiar with the matter told NBC News late Sunday that U.S. intelligence agencies had determined that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy and had a relationship with Nvidia’s Jensen Huang. “The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort,” the company said in a statement. “A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation. The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders.” The company added that while it “has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information.” In a memo to Nvidia employees that the company shared with NBC News, Huang said: “I was unfaithful to my wife. There is no excuse for what I did.” The New York Times and the Financial Times reported that Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen whose Singapore-based company was buying Nvidia’s advanced chips, had been under surveillance by U.S. intelligence agencies. Those agencies, the reports said, found that she had been recruited to spy by China’s top intelligence agency. Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Monday that “the so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China.” Jensen Huang and Nvidia, for years, have been at the forefront of the artificial intelligence boom. Nvidia’s products are the most highly sought-after chips in the world; however its top-tier products are mostly restricted from being sold to customers in China because of national security fears. Huang, 63, essentially serves as an ambassador for the industry, regularly appearing alongside the likes of President Donald Trump and King Charles III of Great Britain and at conferences to tout his company and what he says will be immense payoff in the future from AI. In October, Trump awarded Huang the National Medal of Science, one of the nation’s highest honors for achievement in science and technology. Nvidia is the world’s second-largest publicly traded company as of Friday, worth nearly $4.5 trillion. Nvidia shares fell more than 4% , erasing almost $200 billion in value. But the drop did not immediately spill over into other major tech stocks or to Nvidia’s peers, all of which appeared largely unaffected. The broader stock market, as tracked by the S&P 500 and Nasdaq, were sharply higher for the day. “Given Huang’s central role in Nvidia’s success and the wider AI investment narrative, even speculation about leadership uncertainty could unsettle investors,” wrote Capital.com senior market analyst Daniela Hathorn in a note. Huang’s wealth has also ballooned as he has led the company. His net worth has soared from around $25 billion at the start of 2022 to almost $160 billion, making him the world’s 10th-richest person, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. In the latest series of reports, published Sunday afternoon, The New York Times reported that concerns inside the U.S. government about Alice Huang and Jensen Huang rose as high as Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Speaking Sunday to reporters in Florida shortly after Nvidia’s announcement, Rubio said, “I just can’t comment because of the nature of it, and I also can’t comment on an internal corporate matter that’s going on with Nvidia.” A short time later, Trump gave Huang his complete support, telling reporters that he thinks Huang is a “fine person” who should remain CEO of Nvidia. “I think he’s an honorable guy,” the president said. “He’s done an amazing job for our country,” Trump added, while touting recent stock market gains. The president also said he would support bringing Huang on his upcoming trip through Asia. Asked by reporters if Trump wished that he had acted on intelligence about Alice Huang, he said, “no, I don’t think so.” On Friday, the FT reported that the U.S. government believed Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang. In response to the article, the FT reported that Nvidia declined to comment and said Jensen Huang meets “thousands of customer executives every year,” as any CEO normally does. Huang previously defended his interactions with Alice Huang, describing them as business-related in a recent statement: “Our relationship, our interactions, have been related to Megaspeed, and it was all completely normal and not unusual.” In Sunday’s memo, Huang wrote: “To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust.” The email to employees continued: “To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence.” A spokesperson for Nvidia told NBC News that “today’s news will not slow” the company and that Huang is “committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption.” Before Sunday’s announcement, Nvidia and Huang were already facing congressional scrutiny over the reports about Megaspeed and its executive. On Thursday, top House Republicans requested a briefing from Huang about the reports. “Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC’s access to sensitive U.S. technology and information,” said Rep. “It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk,” a letter to Nvidia read.

extraction.body: Nvidia’s board of directors said Sunday that it is opening an independent investigation after CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. The announcement followed recent reporting by The New York Times and the Financial Times about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who the newspapers reported had been recruited to spy for China. A person familiar with the matter told NBC News late Sunday that U.S. intelligence agencies had determined that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy and had a relationship with Nvidia’s Jensen Huang. “The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort,” the company said in a statement. “A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation. The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders.” The company added that while it “has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information.” In a memo to Nvidia employees that the company shared with NBC News, Huang said: “I was unfaithful to my wife. There is no excuse for what I did.” The New York Times and the Financial Times reported that Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen whose Singapore-based company was buying Nvidia’s advanced chips, had been under surveillance by U.S. intelligence agencies. Those agencies, the reports said, found that she had been recruited to spy by China’s top intelligence agency. Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Monday that “the so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China.” Jensen Huang and Nvidia, for years, have been at the forefront of the artificial intelligence boom. Nvidia’s products are the most highly sought-after chips in the world; however its top-tier products are mostly restricted from being sold to customers in China because of national security fears. Huang, 63, essentially serves as an ambassador for the industry, regularly appearing alongside the likes of President Donald Trump and King Charles III of Great Britain and at conferences to tout his company and what he says will be immense payoff in the future from AI. In October, Trump awarded Huang the National Medal of Science, one of the nation’s highest honors for achievement in science and technology. Nvidia is the world’s second-largest publicly traded company as of Friday, worth nearly $4.5 trillion. Nvidia shares fell more than 4% , erasing almost $200 billion in value. But the drop did not immediately spill over into other major tech stocks or to Nvidia’s peers, all of which appeared largely unaffected. The broader stock market, as tracked by the S&P 500 and Nasdaq, were sharply higher for the day. “Given Huang’s central role in Nvidia’s success and the wider AI investment narrative, even speculation about leadership uncertainty could unsettle investors,” wrote Capital.com senior market analyst Daniela Hathorn in a note. Huang’s wealth has also ballooned as he has led the company. His net worth has soared from around $25 billion at the start of 2022 to almost $160 billion, making him the world’s 10th-richest person, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. In the latest series of reports, published Sunday afternoon, The New York Times reported that concerns inside the U.S. government about Alice Huang and Jensen Huang rose as high as Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Speaking Sunday to reporters in Florida shortly after Nvidia’s announcement, Rubio said, “I just can’t comment because of the nature of it, and I also can’t comment on an internal corporate matter that’s going on with Nvidia.” A short time later, Trump gave Huang his complete support, telling reporters that he thinks Huang is a “fine person” who should remain CEO of Nvidia. “I think he’s an honorable guy,” the president said. “He’s done an amazing job for our country,” Trump added, while touting recent stock market gains. The president also said he would support bringing Huang on his upcoming trip through Asia. Asked by reporters if Trump wished that he had acted on intelligence about Alice Huang, he said, “no, I don’t think so.” On Friday, the FT reported that the U.S. government believed Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang. In response to the article, the FT reported that Nvidia declined to comment and said Jensen Huang meets “thousands of customer executives every year,” as any CEO normally does. Huang previously defended his interactions with Alice Huang, describing them as business-related in a recent statement: “Our relationship, our interactions, have been related to Megaspeed, and it was all completely normal and not unusual.” In Sunday’s memo, Huang wrote: “To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust.” The email to employees continued: “To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence.” A spokesperson for Nvidia told NBC News that “today’s news will not slow” the company and that Huang is “committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption.” Before Sunday’s announcement, Nvidia and Huang were already facing congressional scrutiny over the reports about Megaspeed and its executive. On Thursday, top House Republicans requested a briefing from Huang about the reports. “Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC’s access to sensitive U.S. technology and information,” said Rep. “It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk,” a letter to Nvidia read.

An independent investigation of the founder who runs a company reads as a warning about key-person risk, the one risk Nvidia’s rise never asked you to price; the limit is that the board says it has confidence in Huang, he is cooperating, and the precedent where the board kept its founder is the one where the stock went up. passages: Anthropic is announcing two new models today: Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, which it says are designed to take on “daunting” technical challenges.
The company claims the new models show improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision, and can generate outputs faster than the 5.1 versions of the Fable and Mythos models.

During prerelease testing, the two models have “helped our engineers complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours,” Anthropic says.

passages: Anthropic’s latest AI models, Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, promise faster responses, improved coding capabilities and lower API pricing.
With a reported 49.1% score on FrontierCode 2.0, the launch marks a significant update in AI-powered software development.
Read the full report for pricing details, benchmark comparisons and new features.
Their primary difference lies in access restrictions and safety policies.
The company continues to recommend Claude Opus 5.5 for most everyday coding and knowledge-work requirements.
Anthropic is limiting access to organisations participating in its Cyber and Life Sciences verification programmes.
However, the results do not show Anthropic leading every evaluation.
According to the company, they can generate output up to 30% faster than the previous Fable 5.1 model and deliver stronger results across several technical benchmarks.
Anthropic has reduced the standard API pricing for both models to $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens.
Its testing also included designing three electronic devices, investigating two open problems involving black-hole physics and formalising a proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem.
The model coordinated more than 1,000 subagents over eight days to produce a system capable of booting on a laptop.
Lower standard pricing could make the models more accessible to developers and organisations that rely on large-scale API usage.
Meanwhile, the restricted Mythos programme highlights the company’s approach to managing access to AI systems with advanced capabilities in sensitive research areas.
Both share the same underlying model, but Mythos has more restrictive access policies.
Anthropic said the resulting service started approximately 26 times faster.
Anthropic further reported that more than 90% of changes merged into its core codebase are now written by Claude with human guidance.

Anthropic has launched Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, introducing upgrades in software development, reasoning and visual understanding alongside lower API prices and faster response generation. Announced on Monday, November 9, the new models represent the latest versions of Anthropic’s flagship AI systems. According to the company, they can generate output up to 30% faster than the previous Fable 5.1 model and deliver stronger results across several technical benchmarks. The launch also introduces a revised pricing structure that makes the models less expensive to use than their predecessors. Anthropic has reduced the standard API pricing for both models to $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. The previous Fable 5.1 pricing was $10 and $50, respectively. The company has also introduced an optional Fast mode, designed to increase token generation speeds by up to 2.5 times. Fast mode costs $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens. Fable 5.2 is available through the Claude API, Claude Code, Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure. Mythos 5.2, however, has restricted availability. Anthropic is limiting access to organisations participating in its Cyber and Life Sciences verification programmes. Anthropic’s latest AI models, Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, promise faster responses, improved coding capabilities and lower API pricing. With a reported 49.1% score on FrontierCode 2.0, the launch marks a significant update in AI-powered software development. Read the full report for pricing details, benchmark comparisons and new features. Anthropic says Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 share the same underlying model architecture. Their primary difference lies in access restrictions and safety policies. Fable 5.2 includes cybersecurity and biological safety safeguards and is available to regular customers. Mythos 5.2 is intended for organisations working in sensitive dual-use research areas and is accessible only through Anthropic’s verification programmes. The company continues to recommend Claude Opus 5.5 for most everyday coding and knowledge-work requirements. Fable 5.2 is positioned for more demanding, open-ended technical tasks. Both versions support a context window of up to one million tokens and can generate up to 128,000 output tokens. Anthropic reports that Fable 5.2 has achieved its strongest results so far on several internal evaluation benchmarks, particularly those measuring software engineering capabilities. On FrontierCode 2.0, Fable 5.2 recorded a score of 49.1%, compared with 45.5% for Opus 5.5, 42.8% for OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, 41.1% for Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon and 32.4% for Fable 5.1. The model also recorded 69.9% on FrontierSWE v2, 41.3% on the Remote Labor Index and 64.9% on RoboDojo Sim. However, the results do not show Anthropic leading every evaluation. Gemini 4 Carbon scored 53.9% on AutomationBench, ahead of Fable 5.2’s 51.4%. Opus 5.5 also retained a slight advantage on the AA-Briefcase knowledge-work evaluation. Anthropic said Fable 5.2 operating at High effort matched the best FrontierCode performance of Opus 5.5 at approximately half the cost per task. Separately, Cursor reported scores of 56.9% at default effort and 60% at maximum effort on its CursorBench evaluation after adding Fable 5.2 to its platform. The benchmark figures cited here come from company-reported evaluations and should not be treated as independent comparisons. Anthropic has also shared several examples from its internal testing to demonstrate the capabilities of the new models. The company said Fable 5.2 helped engineers complete software migrations that had previously been considered impractical. Its testing also included designing three electronic devices, investigating two open problems involving black-hole physics and formalising a proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem. According to Anthropic, the Fermat’s Last Theorem exercise involved a team of approximately 1,000 AI agents and took 30 hours. The company compared this with an earlier research effort that required 11 days, specialised tooling and human guidance. Anthropic further reported that more than 90% of changes merged into its core codebase are now written by Claude with human guidance. In another engineering exercise, a team of AI agents migrated a critical production service from Python to Rust. Anthropic said the resulting service started approximately 26 times faster. One particularly extensive experiment involved asking Fable 5.2 to build an operating system from an empty directory. The model coordinated more than 1,000 subagents over eight days to produce a system capable of booting on a laptop. The resulting prototype reportedly included its own kernel, drivers, file storage, window management, login screen and installer. Alongside performance upgrades, Anthropic says it has improved the way Fable 5.2 handles cybersecurity and biological safety restrictions. The company claims that the new safeguards maintain the protection levels of Fable 5.1 while reducing unnecessary refusals by approximately 55% during early testing across Claude.ai, Claude Code and Cowork. Developers upgrading from Fable 5.1 will also need to account for four breaking changes outlined in Anthropic’s migration documentation. These include account-level prefix checks, changes to the compatibility of thinking blocks, retirement of the computer_20251124 tool and updated advisor pairing rules. The release of Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 reflects Anthropic’s continued focus on improving the capabilities of AI systems for complex software engineering and technical research. Lower standard pricing could make the models more accessible to developers and organisations that rely on large-scale API usage. Meanwhile, the restricted Mythos programme highlights the company’s approach to managing access to AI systems with advanced capabilities in sensitive research areas. Although Anthropic’s reported benchmark results show substantial improvements in several coding evaluations, independent testing will be important in establishing how the models compare with competing systems in everyday development environments. For developers already using Claude, the combination of faster generation, increased context capacity and revised pricing makes Fable 5.2 a significant update to consider. They are Anthropic’s latest AI models, designed to improve coding, reasoning and visual understanding. Both share the same underlying model, but Mythos has more restrictive access policies. 4. extraction.body: Nvidia’s board of directors said Sunday that it is opening an independent investigation after CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. The announcement followed recent reporting by The New York Times and the Financial Times about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who the newspapers reported had been recruited to spy for China. A person familiar with the matter told NBC News late Sunday that U.S. intelligence agencies had determined that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy and had a relationship with Nvidia’s Jensen Huang. “The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort,” the company said in a statement. “A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation. The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders.” The company added that while it “has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information.” In a memo to Nvidia employees that the company shared with NBC News, Huang said: “I was unfaithful to my wife. There is no excuse for what I did.” The New York Times and the Financial Times reported that Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen whose Singapore-based company was buying Nvidia’s advanced chips, had been under surveillance by U.S. intelligence agencies. Those agencies, the reports said, found that she had been recruited to spy by China’s top intelligence agency. Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Monday that “the so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China.” Jensen Huang and Nvidia, for years, have been at the forefront of the artificial intelligence boom. Nvidia’s products are the most highly sought-after chips in the world; however its top-tier products are mostly restricted from being sold to customers in China because of national security fears. Huang, 63, essentially serves as an ambassador for the industry, regularly appearing alongside the likes of President Donald Trump and King Charles III of Great Britain and at conferences to tout his company and what he says will be immense payoff in the future from AI. In October, Trump awarded Huang the National Medal of Science, one of the nation’s highest honors for achievement in science and technology. Nvidia is the world’s second-largest publicly traded company as of Friday, worth nearly $4.5 trillion. Nvidia shares fell more than 4% , erasing almost $200 billion in value. But the drop did not immediately spill over into other major tech stocks or to Nvidia’s peers, all of which appeared largely unaffected. The broader stock market, as tracked by the S&P 500 and Nasdaq, were sharply higher for the day. “Given Huang’s central role in Nvidia’s success and the wider AI investment narrative, even speculation about leadership uncertainty could unsettle investors,” wrote Capital.com senior market analyst Daniela Hathorn in a note. Huang’s wealth has also ballooned as he has led the company. His net worth has soared from around $25 billion at the start of 2022 to almost $160 billion, making him the world’s 10th-richest person, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. In the latest series of reports, published Sunday afternoon, The New York Times reported that concerns inside the U.S. government about Alice Huang and Jensen Huang rose as high as Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Speaking Sunday to reporters in Florida shortly after Nvidia’s announcement, Rubio said, “I just can’t comment because of the nature of it, and I also can’t comment on an internal corporate matter that’s going on with Nvidia.” A short time later, Trump gave Huang his complete support, telling reporters that he thinks Huang is a “fine person” who should remain CEO of Nvidia. “I think he’s an honorable guy,” the president said. “He’s done an amazing job for our country,” Trump added, while touting recent stock market gains. The president also said he would support bringing Huang on his upcoming trip through Asia. Asked by reporters if Trump wished that he had acted on intelligence about Alice Huang, he said, “no, I don’t think so.” On Friday, the FT reported that the U.S. government believed Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang. In response to the article, the FT reported that Nvidia declined to comment and said Jensen Huang meets “thousands of customer executives every year,” as any CEO normally does. Huang previously defended his interactions with Alice Huang, describing them as business-related in a recent statement: “Our relationship, our interactions, have been related to Megaspeed, and it was all completely normal and not unusual.” In Sunday’s memo, Huang wrote: “To my wife and family: I love you. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust.” The email to employees continued: “To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence.” A spokesperson for Nvidia told NBC News that “today’s news will not slow” the company and that Huang is “committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption.” Before Sunday’s announcement, Nvidia and Huang were already facing congressional scrutiny over the reports about Megaspeed and its executive. On Thursday, top House Republicans requested a briefing from Huang about the reports. “Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC’s access to sensitive U.S. technology and information,” said Rep. “It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk,” a letter to Nvidia read.

Vice Minister of Science and ICT Ryu Jemyung told a parliamentary budget committee that 10,000 GPUs funded under a 2025 supplementary budget had already arrived and were in use. Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo told the Times on Sunday that “today’s news will not slow Nvidia”. “Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption.” Nvidia is one of the hottest companies in the stock market right now, given the popularity of its chips. It has a market capitalization of roughly 4.5 trillion and was trading at nearly $240 per share early last month. However, the investigation adds to pressure on Nvidia at a time investors are already pulling back amid uncertainty over the sustainability of the booming AI market. Nvidia shares fell in out-of-hours trading on Monday and extended to South Korea, where Madison Huang, Huang's daughter and an Nvidia executive, cancelled a planned visit to Seoul for an Nvidia conference set to begin this week. The Nvidia leader and his wife, Lori Huang, attended a state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House in September. The company said that while its board had no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, its inquiry would examine all available information. Billionaire investor Bill Ackman said on X that the Nvidia CEO was an "incredible human," but if "indeed this is more ⁠than an affair, then it is obviously a real problem." Tesla CEO Elon Musk commented "I agree" on a post by Sequoia partner Shaun Maguire that said Huang "did something incredibly dumb" that was "bad for America" but that "Jensen is irreplaceable for America's AI leadership".

It said that the board has confidence in Huang and his ⁠leadership team, adding that the CEO fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it. Late last month, the New York Times reported that Huang had formed a close relationship with Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a Chinese executive at a Singapore-based data center. Alice Huang is considered by U.S. officials to be a Chinese spy, feeding information to Beijing, according to the report, which cited sources briefed on the surveillance of Alice Huang and other officials and industry experts. When asked about Alice Huang being suspected of spying for China, Liu Chang, the spokesman for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, told the Times the U.S. was pursuing a campaign of “groundless smears and slanders” against the Asian country. Trump said on Sunday he had not spoken to Huang about ​the allegations, but ⁠called him a fine person. "I hope everything's fine. He's done such an ‌incredible job," he added. Vice Minister of Science and ICT Ryu Jemyung told a parliamentary budget committee that 10,000 GPUs funded under a 2025 supplementary budget had already arrived and were in use. The Nvidia leader and his wife, Lori Huang, attended a state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House in September. His attendance wasn’t unusual, given that OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg were also there. "I am hoping for a simple affair, not a risk to our national security," he added. Nvidia’s Jensen Huang apologized for the extramarital relationship and the company is investigating him over concerns he’s a ‘target of a foreign intelligence effort’
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to having an affair with a woman whom U.S. intelligence reportedly suspects is a Chinese spy.

Huang, who heads a leading AI chipmaker and is an ally of President Donald Trump , apologized in a message to the company, saying, “I was unfaithful to my wife” and took "full responsibility" for his actions.
“My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

Nvidia announced in a press release Sunday that its board was opening an independent investigation “in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.”
The company said that while its board had no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, its inquiry would examine all available information.
It said that the board has confidence in Huang and his ⁠leadership team, adding that the CEO fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it.
Late last month, the New York Times reported that Huang had formed a close relationship with Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a Chinese executive at a Singapore-based data center.

Alice Huang is considered by U.S. officials to be a Chinese spy, feeding information to Beijing, according to the report, which cited sources briefed on the surveillance of Alice Huang and other officials and industry experts.

When asked about Alice Huang being suspected of spying for China, Liu Chang, the spokesman for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, told the Times the U.S. was pursuing a campaign of “groundless smears and slanders” against the Asian country.
Trump said on Sunday he had not spoken to Huang about ​the allegations, but ⁠called him a fine person.
"I hope everything's fine. He's done such an ‌incredible job," he added.

When asked if he believed he should have acted on intelligence when he was briefed about it, Trump said: "No, I don't think so. I think he's an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it."

Nvidia is one of the hottest companies in the stock market right now, given the popularity of its chips. It has a market capitalization of roughly 4.5 trillion and was trading at nearly $240 per share early last month.
However, the investigation adds to pressure on Nvidia at a time investors are already pulling back amid uncertainty over the sustainability of the booming AI market.

Nvidia shares fell in out-of-hours trading on Monday and extended to South Korea, where Madison Huang, Huang's daughter and an Nvidia executive, cancelled a planned visit to Seoul for an Nvidia conference set to begin this week.

But Seoul expects contracted deliveries of Nvidia graphics processing units (GPUs) to proceed without disruption despite a controversy surrounding Huang. Vice Minister of Science and ICT Ryu Jemyung told a parliamentary budget committee that 10,000 GPUs funded under a 2025 supplementary budget had already arrived and were in use.
Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo told the Times on Sunday that “today’s news will not slow Nvidia”. “Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption.”

Huang, like other tech leaders, has flocked to Trump as the president embraces AI. The Nvidia leader and his wife, Lori Huang, attended a state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House in September. His attendance wasn’t unusual, given that OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg were also there.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio refused to say whether Huang was excluded from U.S. briefings in light of the recent reporting. He told reporters Sunday before departing for France, “I just can’t comment because of the nature of it.”
Trump is a major backer of AI, trying to rebrand the technology as SI for “Super Intelligence” and loosen regulations.
While Huang may be an ally to the president, it will be hard to overlook a potential security breach from not only a U.S. adversary, but also its top competitor in the AI race.

“We’re leading China in AI,” the president said in September amid concerns that AI could pose an existential threat to humans . “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world. And frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins.”
Billionaire investor Bill Ackman said on X that the Nvidia CEO was an "incredible human," but if "indeed this is more ⁠than an affair, then it is obviously a real problem."
"I am hoping for a simple affair, not a risk to our national security," he added.

Tesla CEO Elon Musk commented "I agree" on a post by Sequoia partner Shaun Maguire that said Huang "did something incredibly dumb" that was "bad for America" but that "Jensen is irreplaceable for America's AI leadership".
The Independent has reached out to the State Department and the White House for comment.

But Seoul expects contracted deliveries of Nvidia graphics processing units (GPUs) to proceed without disruption despite a controversy surrounding Huang.

An Nvidia spokesperson said that Huang was committed to continuing as CEO of Nvidia without interruption. The allegations come as Nvidia has become the center of a trade dispute between China and the U.S. as AI is seen as increasingly critical to national security. The announcement followed recent reporting by The New York Times and the Financial Times about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who the newspapers reported had been recruited to spy for China. A person familiar with the matter told NBC News late Sunday that U.S. intelligence agencies had determined that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy and had a relationship with Nvidia’s Jensen Huang. “The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort,” the company said in a statement. “A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation. The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders.” The company added that while it “has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information.” In a memo to Nvidia employees that the company shared with NBC News, Huang said: “I was unfaithful to my wife. There is no excuse for what I did.” The New York Times and the Financial Times reported that Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen whose Singapore-based company was buying Nvidia’s advanced chips, had been under surveillance by U.S. intelligence agencies. Those agencies, the reports said, found that she had been recruited to spy by China’s top intelligence agency. Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Monday that “the so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China.” Jensen Huang and Nvidia, for years, have been at the forefront of the artificial intelligence boom. Nvidia’s products are the most highly sought-after chips in the world; however its top-tier products are mostly restricted from being sold to customers in China because of national security fears. Huang, 63, essentially serves as an ambassador for the industry, regularly appearing alongside the likes of President Donald Trump and King Charles III of Great Britain and at conferences to tout his company and what he says will be immense payoff in the future from AI. In October, Trump awarded Huang the National Medal of Science, one of the nation’s highest honors for achievement in science and technology. Nvidia is the world’s second-largest publicly traded company as of Friday, worth nearly $4.5 trillion. Nvidia shares fell more than 4% , erasing almost $200 billion in value. But the drop did not immediately spill over into other major tech stocks or to Nvidia’s peers, all of which appeared largely unaffected. The broader stock market, as tracked by the S&P 500 and Nasdaq, were sharply higher for the day. “Given Huang’s central role in Nvidia’s success and the wider AI investment narrative, even speculation about leadership uncertainty could unsettle investors,” wrote Capital.com senior market analyst Daniela Hathorn in a note. Huang’s wealth has also ballooned as he has led the company. His net worth has soared from around $25 billion at the start of 2022 to almost $160 billion, making him the world’s 10th-richest person, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. In the latest series of reports, published Sunday afternoon, The New York Times reported that concerns inside the U.S. government about Alice Huang and Jensen Huang rose as high as Secretary of State Marco Rubio. In response to the article, the FT reported that Nvidia declined to comment and said Jensen Huang meets “thousands of customer executives every year,” as any CEO normally does. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust.” The email to employees continued: “To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence.” A spokesperson for Nvidia told NBC News that “today’s news will not slow” the company and that Huang is “committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption.” Before Sunday’s announcement, Nvidia and Huang were already facing congressional scrutiny over the reports about Megaspeed and its executive. On Thursday, top House Republicans requested a briefing from Huang about the reports. “Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC’s access to sensitive U.S. technology and information,” said Rep. “It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk,” a letter to Nvidia read.

There is no excuse for what I did.” The New York Times and the Financial Times reported that Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen whose Singapore-based company was buying Nvidia’s advanced chips, had been under surveillance by U.S. intelligence agencies. Those agencies, the reports said, found that she had been recruited to spy by China’s top intelligence agency. Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Monday that “the so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China.” Jensen Huang and Nvidia, for years, have been at the forefront of the artificial intelligence boom. Nvidia’s products are the most highly sought-after chips in the world; however its top-tier products are mostly restricted from being sold to customers in China because of national security fears. Huang, 63, essentially serves as an ambassador for the industry, regularly appearing alongside the likes of President Donald Trump and King Charles III of Great Britain and at conferences to tout his company and what he says will be immense payoff in the future from AI. In October, Trump awarded Huang the National Medal of Science, one of the nation’s highest honors for achievement in science and technology. Nvidia is the world’s second-largest publicly traded company as of Friday, worth nearly $4.5 trillion. Nvidia shares fell more than 4% , erasing almost $200 billion in value. But the drop did not immediately spill over into other major tech stocks or to Nvidia’s peers, all of which appeared largely unaffected. The broader stock market, as tracked by the S&P 500 and Nasdaq, were sharply higher for the day. “Given Huang’s central role in Nvidia’s success and the wider AI investment narrative, even speculation about leadership uncertainty could unsettle investors,” wrote Capital.com senior market analyst Daniela Hathorn in a note. Huang’s wealth has also ballooned as he has led the company. His net worth has soared from around $25 billion at the start of 2022 to almost $160 billion, making him the world’s 10th-richest person, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. In the latest series of reports, published Sunday afternoon, The New York Times reported that concerns inside the U.S. government about Alice Huang and Jensen Huang rose as high as Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Speaking Sunday to reporters in Florida shortly after Nvidia’s announcement, Rubio said, “I just can’t comment because of the nature of it, and I also can’t comment on an internal corporate matter that’s going on with Nvidia.” A short time later, Trump gave Huang his complete support, telling reporters that he thinks Huang is a “fine person” who should remain CEO of Nvidia. “I think he’s an honorable guy,” the president said. “He’s done an amazing job for our country,” Trump added, while touting recent stock market gains. Asked by reporters if Trump wished that he had acted on intelligence about Alice Huang, he said, “no, I don’t think so.” On Friday, the FT reported that the U.S. government believed Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang. In response to the article, the FT reported that Nvidia declined to comment and said Jensen Huang meets “thousands of customer executives every year,” as any CEO normally does. Huang previously defended his interactions with Alice Huang, describing them as business-related in a recent statement: “Our relationship, our interactions, have been related to Megaspeed, and it was all completely normal and not unusual.” In Sunday’s memo, Huang wrote: “To my wife and family: I love you. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust.” The email to employees continued: “To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence.” A spokesperson for Nvidia told NBC News that “today’s news will not slow” the company and that Huang is “committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption.” Before Sunday’s announcement, Nvidia and Huang were already facing congressional scrutiny over the reports about Megaspeed and its executive. On Thursday, top House Republicans requested a briefing from Huang about the reports. “Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC’s access to sensitive U.S. technology and information,” said Rep. “It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk,” a letter to Nvidia read.

Apple has made it clear for a while that Siri AI is bound by daily usage limits and that it will offer expanded access via iCloud+ plans. The company hasn't shed more light on exactly how that will work, but it has revealed how Creator Studio users can continue wielding the AI features of those apps after they reach the regular limits. It has started selling $50 intelligence usage packs for Creator Studio, and Logic Pro is the first app to support these. Apple updated Logic Pro last month to include an assistant that's powered by its own models as well as those from third parties. The company said the chatbot can help "creators and producers navigate production workflows, start a new song, set up a vocal track from a single prompt or refine an active project." As noted by 9to5Mac , folks can view their AI usage in the app by going to Logic Pro on the menu bar, then Intelligence Features > Show Usage . The window that pops up includes a Buy More Usage button — clicking this takes you to the option to buy an intelligence usage pack. A support page explains that users with active Apple Creator Studio subscriptions in the US, UK, Canada, Brazil, France, Germany, India and Mexico can buy intelligence usage packs to keep using AI features after they reach their monthly usage limit. A pack is tied to the Apple Account used to purchase it — there's no Family Sharing support. "Unused additional usage purchased with intelligence usage packs roll over from month to month and expire 12 months after purchase," Apple added. "Additional usage gets consumed for relevant features only after you've reached your monthly limit in any given month." It seems likely that Apple will expand intelligence usage packs to other Creator Studio apps, such as Final Cut Pro and Pixelmator Pro. It's interesting that Apple is opting for this approach over a regular subscription, but perhaps the company has other offerings planned for the future. For what it's worth, Creator Studio apps are available via a subscription or one-time purchase .

passages: It has a built-in AI assistant to do things like “start a new song, set up a vocal track from a single prompt, or refine an active project.” These Intelligence Usage Packs, as Apple calls them, will allow users to continue accessing certain Apple Intelligence features that have usage limits because they rely on cloud-based AI models from OpenAI or Google Gemini.

For Logic Pro, Apple says the usage limit is “impacted by the complexity of conversations you have with the assistant.” Users finding themselves running out of access can find the option to buy an Intelligence Usage Pack in the Intelligence Features > Show Usage section of the app’s main menu.

The Usage Packs can only be used by the Apple Account that purchased them (Family Sharing isn’t supported) and, as Apple explains on its website, any unused additional usage will roll over from month to month, but will expire 12 months after it was purchased.

"Unused additional usage purchased with intelligence usage packs roll over from month to month and expire 12 months after purchase," Apple added. For what it's worth, Creator Studio apps are available via a subscription or one-time purchase .

This affair has also raised questions among outsiders about whether Jensen Huang will continue to serve as CEO of the $4.5 trillion artificial intelligence chipmaker, though the company’s board has expressed confidence in his leadership. The New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, the woman at the center of this scandal who previously held an executive position at NVIDIA client Megaspeed, was recruited to gather information on the company’s operations for the Chinese government. Here is the timeline of events leading to Huang Renxun's "explosive disclosure" and the subsequent developments: The New York Times reported that U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the drafting of a "highly classified" memo this spring warning about issues related to Jensen Huang. Jensen Huang was not initially on the list of top executives accompanying U.S. President Donald Trump on his visit to China in May. News outlets noted that his absence was unusual, given that the NVIDIA CEO had previously accompanied Trump on similar occasions. On May 12, Trump posted: "Huang Renxun is currently on Air Force One, and unless I make him get off—which is extremely unlikely—CNBC’s report is wrong, or, in political terms, fake news!" At the time, Huang Renxun’s name was not on the list of U.S. business executives sent by White House officials to Business Insider. Subsequently, according to CNBC, the NVIDIA CEO told reporters that Trump “invited me.” Questions regarding Huang Renxun surfaced in October. On October 29, The New York Times reported that U.S. officials have concluded that Alice Huang, or Huang Le, is a "CCP intelligence asset" and has "established close ties with Jensen Huang." The report included photos of the two at a party in June 2024, claiming the images were posted on LinkedIn. It also mentioned that in May 2025, Alice Huang waited outside a restaurant in Taipei behind Jensen Huang, shortly after he spoke to reporters. The New York Times quoted NVIDIA spokesperson John Rizzo as saying: "Mr. Huang's interactions with Ms. Huang are neither unusual nor surprising. Huang also told the outlet that the U.S. government did not notify him regarding its concerns about Alice Huang, corroborating another part of the New York Times report. The paper’s original article mentioned that Huang had not received what is known as a “defensive briefing”—a formal warning sometimes delivered to business leaders. On November 4, three House Republican committee chairs wrote to Jensen Huang, requesting that he attend a closed-door joint hearing to discuss his interactions with Alice Huang. The letter states: "Recent reports have raised significant national security concerns regarding the People's Republic of China's acquisition of sensitive U.S. technologies and information. The infiltration and acquisition of cutting-edge U.S. technologies by China have been at the core of our three committees' investigations this Congress. Congress must determine the extent to which U.S. national security is at risk." This letter describes Alice Huang as a "publicly reported intelligence asset of the People's Republic of China (PRC)" and requests a meeting on November 18. Later on Sunday, Trump defended the NVIDIA CEO, calling him "a decent person." Trump told the reporters, "I think he might have his own interpretation. You have to listen first." The withdrawals come after Huang admitted to an extramarital affair over the weekend, and Nvidia opened an investigation into his relationship with a possible Chinese spy. “I owe my family and all of you an apology. I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” Huang said in a memo to the company. The incident has rattled the AI industry, raising questions about Huang’s staying power as CEO and Nvidia’s own China ambitions.

extraction.body: Jensen Huang was scheduled to speak at two tech events this week. Then the CEO disclosed he had an affair, and Nvidia's board opened an investigation. Ahead of its expected IPO next week, Anthropic is hosting a private CEO forum this week in Montecito. Huang was set to be interviewed by an Anthropic executive on Monday evening, a person familiar with the event told Business Insider. He is no longer expected to attend, according to a second person familiar with the matter. Huang is also no longer set to speak at the ElevenLabs Summit in NYC later this week, a spokesperson for the AI voice technology startup confirmed to Business Insider. On Monday, Huang's name and image disappeared from the speaker list for ElevenLabs' conference before later reappearing and vanishing once more. The Nvidia CEO had been scheduled for a fireside chat with ElevenLabs CEO Mati Staniszewski on Wednesday, where the two would have a "conversation on the future of AI." The agenda now lists a closing keynote from Staniszewski alone. Nvidia did not immediately respond to requests for comment. In a Sunday note to staff, Huang said that he had been "unfaithful" to his wife. He apologized to his wife and kids, and said that his Nvidia colleagues deserved better. "I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence," Huang wrote. That same day, Nvidia said that its board of directors opened an investigation into whether Huang had been the target of a "foreign intelligence effort." The investigation followed an October report by The New York Times, which said that Megaspeed executive Alice Huang had developed a close relationship with Nvidia's CEO. US officials believed Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset, the Times reported. In his memo to staff, Huang said that he intended to cooperate fully with the investigation. Other speakers at ElevanLabs' Wednesday conference include several of the AI company's other executives, as well as leaders from Ramp, McKinsey, and AWS. Update November 9, 2026 — Added ElevenLabs' statement confirming Huang is no longer speaking at its conference.

extraction.body: Following NVIDIA's CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang's acknowledgment of an extramarital affair, an independent investigation into the billionaire businessman has been initiated. This affair has also raised questions among outsiders about whether Jensen Huang will continue to serve as CEO of the $4.5 trillion artificial intelligence chipmaker, though the company’s board has expressed confidence in his leadership. The New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, the woman at the center of this scandal who previously held an executive position at NVIDIA client Megaspeed, was recruited to gather information on the company’s operations for the Chinese government. Here is the timeline of events leading to Huang Renxun's "explosive disclosure" and the subsequent developments: The New York Times reported that U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the drafting of a "highly classified" memo this spring warning about issues related to Jensen Huang. Jensen Huang was not initially on the list of top executives accompanying U.S. President Donald Trump on his visit to China in May. News outlets noted that his absence was unusual, given that the NVIDIA CEO had previously accompanied Trump on similar occasions. On May 12, Trump posted: "Huang Renxun is currently on Air Force One, and unless I make him get off—which is extremely unlikely—CNBC’s report is wrong, or, in political terms, fake news!" At the time, Huang Renxun’s name was not on the list of U.S. business executives sent by White House officials to Business Insider. Subsequently, according to CNBC, the NVIDIA CEO told reporters that Trump “invited me.” Questions regarding Huang Renxun surfaced in October. On October 29, The New York Times reported that U.S. officials have concluded that Alice Huang, or Huang Le, is a "CCP intelligence asset" and has "established close ties with Jensen Huang." The report included photos of the two at a party in June 2024, claiming the images were posted on LinkedIn. It also mentioned that in May 2025, Alice Huang waited outside a restaurant in Taipei behind Jensen Huang, shortly after he spoke to reporters. The New York Times quoted NVIDIA spokesperson John Rizzo as saying: "Mr. Huang's interactions with Ms. Huang are neither unusual nor surprising. Meeting with clients is part of the CEO's job; Mr. Huang speaks with tens of thousands of client executives each year." Huang also echoed the company’s statement, downplaying his interactions with Alice Huang as routine business dealings. Huang also told the outlet that the U.S. government did not notify him regarding its concerns about Alice Huang, corroborating another part of the New York Times report. The paper’s original article mentioned that Huang had not received what is known as a “defensive briefing”—a formal warning sometimes delivered to business leaders. On November 4, three House Republican committee chairs wrote to Jensen Huang, requesting that he attend a closed-door joint hearing to discuss his interactions with Alice Huang. The letter states: "Recent reports have raised significant national security concerns regarding the People's Republic of China's acquisition of sensitive U.S. technologies and information. The infiltration and acquisition of cutting-edge U.S. technologies by China have been at the core of our three committees' investigations this Congress. Congress must determine the extent to which U.S. national security is at risk." This letter describes Alice Huang as a "publicly reported intelligence asset of the People's Republic of China (PRC)" and requests a meeting on November 18. On the same day, NVIDIA's board announced that it had launched an investigation into whether Jensen Huang was a target of foreign intelligence operations. The board stated that a committee composed of independent directors will oversee the investigation with the assistance of external independent legal counsel. The board stated: “Although the board has no reason to believe that national security or NVIDIA secrets have been compromised, the board’s investigation will review all available information.” Huang Renxun stated that he supports the investigation and "will fully cooperate." Later on Sunday, Trump defended the NVIDIA CEO, calling him "a decent person." Trump told the reporters, "I think he might have his own interpretation. You have to listen first." The president also said he believes Jensen Huang should continue serving as NVIDIA's CEO. Trump said, "He has done an outstanding job for our country." NVIDIA's CEO has been removed from the list of tech events. Following the scandal, Jensen Huang no longer plans to attend the private CEO forum hosted by Anthropic on Monday in Montecito, California. A person familiar with the event told Business Insider that an Anthropic executive was originally scheduled to interview Jensen Huang. Another source said Huang no longer plans to attend. NVIDIA’s CEO will no longer speak at the ElevenLabs summit in New York later this week. A spokesperson for the AI voice technology startup has confirmed this to Business Insider. Huang was originally scheduled for a fireside chat with ElevenLabs CEO Mati Staniszewski. The Chinese government has refuted the claim that Alice Huang is a spy. At a press conference on Monday, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said, "The accusations of 'Chinese spies' are entirely baseless and intended to smear China."

sources.title: Bitcoin and Ethereum Just Hit Their Lowest Prices Since August After $1 Billion in Liquidations. Where Do Analysts Say They Bottom? - Yahoo Finance
passages: Over $1 billion in liquidations, mostly forced long sales, triggered a cascade that pushed Bitcoin and Ethereum to their lowest closes since August.
In the last 24 hours, Ethereum has dropped 4.6%, while Bitcoin has decreased by 1.2%.
So where do analysts see a Bitcoin bottom, and what could stop the selling pressure on Ethereum?
Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) closed at $74,740 on November 8, 2026, marking its lowest daily close since it finished at $73,021 on August 20.
Compared to other major cryptocurrencies, Bitcoin has shown relative resilience.
This chain reaction, known as a liquidation cascade, ceases when the excess long positions are closed.
Bitcoin has faced two of these cascades in under two weeks, following a $1.3 billion long liquidation that pushed it to a five-week low on October 30.
The small rebound since then appears to reflect forced selling slowing down, with new buyers yet to enter the market.
FxPro analyst Alex Kuptsikevich believes that the market will test the 200-day moving average, describing it as an essential target for bearish sentiment.

Going further, analyst Beth Kindig expressed a more pessimistic view, stating, "We believe that one more large drop is coming over the next several months," although she did not specify a price level.
When losses use up a trader's collateral, an exchange closes the position.
Each forced sale can push prices down further, potentially triggering a cascade of additional liquidations.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
A moving average represents a coin's average closing price over a specific time frame.
Bitcoin is currently trading 5% below its 20-day average of $79,005 and around 8.2% below its 50-day average of $81,760.
Market reports indicate that Bitcoin has also lost its 50-week moving average, which tracks the average weekly close for the past year.
The on-chain data firm CryptoQuant noted that coins recently traded by short-term holders are currently moving down on average.
As such, the $79,000 area, just 5% above Bitcoin's current price, may prove to be a tougher level to break.
Bitcoin's stronger performance may be attributed to support from spot ETFs and corporate treasuries, which contribute to more stable buying.
In contrast, smaller cryptocurrencies involve more leveraged positions, leading to more significant impacts during sell-offs.

Both prints feed the December rate decision the market now leans toward as a hike. The selling was heaviest in Ethereum, which absorbed nearly $500 million of the liquidations against $305.3 million for Bitcoin, per CoinGlass. On 6 November, Ethereum's decline triggered about $210 million in liquidations, $179 million of them from leveraged longs.

US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $1.28 billion in net outflows last week, their largest weekly withdrawals since late June, per SoSoValue. That took the funds' net outflows for the year to about $919 million, after $515 million of outflows in October.

IBIT carried most of it: its outflows ran to six consecutive trading sessions and about $1.44 billion since 30 October, roughly 95% of the weekly total, per SoSoValue. Fidelity's FBTC went the other way, drawing about $93 million in net inflows for the week. On 5 November, US spot Bitcoin and Ethereum ETFs together posted $530.1 million in net outflows.

The macro calendar did as much as the flows. US nonfarm payrolls added 165,000 jobs in October, well above the 65,000 expected, and September's figure was revised up to 60,000. After the release, the odds of a 25 basis point Fed rate hike in December rose from 66.9% to 76.8%, per CME Group's FedWatch Tool, and market pricing reached 78.8%.
Tech shares sold off alongside crypto: the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.5% on Thursday, its biggest single-day decline since April 2025.

The US Bureau of Labor Statistics will release October's Consumer Price Index on Tuesday and the Producer Price Index on Friday, both at 8:30 am ET. Both prints feed the December rate decision the market now leans toward as a hike.

Bitfire Research described the market as being in a "breakdown and bottom-seeking phase", pointing to the inflation data and Federal Reserve signals as the factors to watch. The firm said a sustained break below the $74,400 to $75,000 support range could lead to further selling.

The first hard number of the week lands Tuesday at 8:30 am ET with the CPI print. Bitcoin holding above the 21-week average at $73,078 keeps the weekend low as the bottom so far; a close back through the 50-week average at $75,492 would put the price back above the line it lost.

extraction.body: Big Tech sees a culture war over progress. But the real fault line is electricity: drawing it from the grid and generating it onsite provoke different kinds of backlash, neither easily solved by public relations. This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape. Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ. It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words. But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity. Here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid. One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy. Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables). The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts. That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport . Elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she says—that is, electricity. Some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg, to be fair. But it’s the particular consequences of drawing so much power from the grid that have done the most to shape how the backlash has played out. Recent protests have led to new rules from the state that data centers must pay fully for the cost of new transmission lines to the grid and make sure they’re not spread among everyone else. Data center developers told me they’re preparing for new rules that would cut them off from grid power during peak demand. Schlossberg also worries about the downstream effects of a strained grid—for example, that data centers will run more diesel generators or that Dominion Energy will expand fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables to meet demand. The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way. The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to. Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines. Companies also build diesel generators for backup. Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company. Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded. The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts. It’s a lot of power for one industrial site, but not unprecedented: One data center developer told me he’s eyeing a former steel mill already equipped to draw that much electricity from the grid. But the ideal facilities are more like 6,000 megawatts. That’s the estimated draw of the city of Chicago, which is powered by more than 20 power plants within the city alone (and dozens farther out). The notion of data center companies’ bringing their own power might seem attractive at first, because they wouldn’t be straining the grid. But generating electricity at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and when public utilities build infrastructure of this magnitude, communities have traditionally expected a say in where it goes. Now, private companies are undertaking projects on a similar scale. Natural-gas turbines of any scale release air pollutants. When diesel generators are used, it’s even worse. And in the unprecedented rush to get these facilities operating, companies have become horrible neighbors (recall that Elon Musk violated air quality laws when he set up dozens of turbines to power a data center in Memphis, according to the Environmental Protection Agency). Big Tech’s tendency to chalk the backlash up to a culture war obfuscates one simple fact: There’s only so pleasant you can make a small city of computers to live around. Sure, companies can pursue better deals that raise tax revenues, hire local workers, and get more community involvement, as the protests are leading them to do . But if a small town is asked to welcome a Walt Disney World, an international airport, a steel plant, and the power plants to run them all, should we be surprised by its trepidation? Again, that’s not to say this is the sole reason for opposition to data centers. Fears of job losses, existential risks, and concentrated corporate power all fuel the backlash, as does misinformation (most facilities use far less water than many people think). Nor is consuming enormous amounts of electricity inherently bad: Many of the advances that have improved modern life have required just that. But as one developer recently told me, industry insiders see their ambitions as constrained less by public opposition than by a lack of electricity. That should tell us something. So what happens next? It’s possible that newly elected politicians’ actual stances on data centers won’t be as negative as the ones they campaigned on. But what seems true regardless is that if new data centers need their own power generated onsite, they’ll go where there are the fewest people able to resist them. That might mean the Permian Basin , where a network of natural-gas lines can be easy for developers to connect to and populations are sparse. Companies might also try their chances abroad; Google, in fact, announced the day after the elections that it will spend $15 billion on data center projects in Malaysia. But there’s one place where Big Tech may find virtually no limits at all, as Elon Musk posted just hours after the midterms results came rolling in: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.” Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.
