passages: Big Tech sees a culture war over progress. But the real fault line is electricity: drawing it from the grid and generating it onsite provoke different kinds of backlash, neither easily solved by public relations.
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here .

As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape.
Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ.

It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words.

But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity.

Here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid.

One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy. Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables).
The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts. That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport .

Elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she says—that is, electricity.

Some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg, to be fair. But it’s the particular consequences of drawing so much power from the grid that have done the most to shape how the backlash has played out.

Recent protests have led to new rules from the state that data centers must pay fully for the cost of new transmission lines to the grid and make sure they’re not spread among everyone else. Data center developers told me they’re preparing for new rules that would cut them off from grid power during peak demand. Schlossberg also worries about the downstream effects of a strained grid—for example, that data centers will run more diesel generators or that Dominion Energy will expand fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables to meet demand.

The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way. The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to. Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines. Companies also build diesel generators for backup. Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company.

Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded. The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts. It’s a lot of power for one industrial site, but not unprecedented: One data center developer told me he’s eyeing a former steel mill already equipped to draw that much electricity from the grid.
But the ideal facilities are more like 6,000 megawatts. That’s the estimated draw of the city of Chicago, which is powered by more than 20 power plants within the city alone (and dozens farther out).

The notion of data center companies’ bringing their own power might seem attractive at first, because they wouldn’t be straining the grid. But generating electricity at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and when public utilities build infrastructure of this magnitude, communities have traditionally expected a say in where it goes. Now, private companies are undertaking projects on a similar scale.

Natural-gas turbines of any scale release air pollutants. When diesel generators are used, it’s even worse. And in the unprecedented rush to get these facilities operating, companies have become horrible neighbors (recall that Elon Musk violated air quality laws when he set up dozens of turbines to power a data center in Memphis, according to the Environmental Protection Agency).

Big Tech’s tendency to chalk the backlash up to a culture war obfuscates one simple fact: There’s only so pleasant you can make a small city of computers to live around. Sure, companies can pursue better deals that raise tax revenues, hire local workers, and get more community involvement, as the protests are leading them to do . But if a small town is asked to welcome a Walt Disney World, an international airport, a steel plant, and the power plants to run them all, should we be surprised by its trepidation?

Again, that’s not to say this is the sole reason for opposition to data centers. Fears of job losses, existential risks, and concentrated corporate power all fuel the backlash, as does misinformation (most facilities use far less water than many people think). Nor is consuming enormous amounts of electricity inherently bad: Many of the advances that have improved modern life have required just that.
But as one developer recently told me, industry insiders see their ambitions as constrained less by public opposition than by a lack of electricity. That should tell us something.

So what happens next? It’s possible that newly elected politicians’ actual stances on data centers won’t be as negative as the ones they campaigned on. But what seems true regardless is that if new data centers need their own power generated onsite, they’ll go where there are the fewest people able to resist them. That might mean the Permian Basin , where a network of natural-gas lines can be easy for developers to connect to and populations are sparse. Companies might also try their chances abroad; Google, in fact, announced the day after the elections that it will spend $15 billion on data center projects in Malaysia.

But there’s one place where Big Tech may find virtually no limits at all, as Elon Musk posted just hours after the midterms results came rolling in: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”
Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.

The backlash to data centers isn’t really about water or electricity. In most cases, it’s not about noise concerns. It’s not even primarily a response to alarming developments in artificial intelligence anymore. No, questions about building massive facilities to hold the servers powering the AI revolution are mainly a relief valve for frustration after two decades of dizzying technological change. It’s about screen time, social media, economic disruption and our fears of a world evolving so fast we feel we cannot keep up. Consider the newest front in the tech wars. Flock cameras, a brand of license-plate readers that police use to hunt for suspects, have become the focus of protest across the country and from various parts of the political spectrum. Americans have a robust tradition of bowing up to invasions of privacy. But we’ve also been steadily surrendering our own information and photos — voluntarily — to tech companies and assenting to a world where any public activity is likely to be caught on camera. So, why this, why now? The cameras are readily visible and subject to pressure on the mechanisms of public policy. For the same reasons, data centers have become the focal point of concerns about AI and its effect on life. These worries are legitimate and widespread. A Pew poll released in March found that half of Americans fear the impact of AI on their lives more than they are excited about its possibilities. Proposals to build data centers require state and local approval, so there’s something tangible for people to protest. It’s hard to sway Google, Amazon or any of the other big companies plunging into AI development. But when Texans tell pollsters they oppose a data center in their community , 56% to 29%, officeholders pay attention. Concerns about AI can seem apocalyptic, too. It’s hard to find a scarier sentence than this recent New York Times report that “scientists have used artificial intelligence to create new kinds of viruses , raising hopes for medical advances while also raising the disturbing possibility that the technology could someday be used to invent dangerous pathogens.” Our nature is to skip over that first part, the positive possibilities, while imagining every terrible pandemic-outbreak movie we’ve ever seen. We don’t even think about the potential improvement in diagnosing medical conditions, even though AI is already showing the ability to outperform human doctors in some cases. Add in concerns that AI will eliminate jobs, make us all too stupid to meaningfully read or write and maybe even go rogue a la the “Terminator” movies and suddenly, preventing a data center seems like the highest priority. We’re scarcely 20 years into the smartphone boom. That’s a smidgen of time in the human experience, and we are still adapting to a world of endless information and life spent on screens. Our brains don’t evolve at the pace of change, so we’re ill-equipped for the stream of misery, jealousy and distraction that we hold in our hands. People are looking for ways to break away from tech, even as it insinuates itself more into daily life. Giant buildings full of humming servers owned by shadowy corporate interests vying for big tax breaks represent a villainy we otherwise can’t get our arms around. If there’s an upside, perhaps it proves that our political system is more responsive than we think. In the span of less than a year, Gov. Greg Abbott has moved from cutting ribbons for big data center projects to issuing a list of demands about their power usage, location and economic contributions . In business-friendly Fort Worth, a majority of City Council members seems prepared to embrace a moratorium on new data center projects. As with so many populist outrage bubbles, though, facts and tradeoffs are getting short shrift. A common tactic to cause alarm is to add up every possible gigawatt that projects might use. But not all planned centers will bear fruit. Governments are already requiring the industry to generate its own electricity, and policymakers are even pushing data centers to provide a net increase in power. No one likes what’s happening with energy costs, but the cause is complex. Research indicates that data centers can actually help cut electricity prices because higher demand means more production. Big numbers about water use sound scary, too. Economic analyst James Pethokoukis has calculated that even if water consumption by data centers quadruples in 2030, they’ll still take just 1% of our supply. Cooling technology continues to advance, and smart negotiations with developers will demand that they use more efficient methods. If you’re really that worked up about our future water supply, tear out your lawn, quit playing golf and get rid of lush youth-sports fields. That would save far more water than shutting down every data center. Remember, too, we’re in a fierce AI race with China, which is not above meddling with American public opinion through TikTok or even funding political movements here. With affinity for socialism on the rise on the left, plenty of useful idiots will work against their own country’s national security interests on behalf of the Chinese communist behemoth. After all, isn’t it odd that many of the progressives raising alarm about electricity usage would gleefully force Americans to convert to electric cars? AI development will not be derailed. America’s four tech behemoths — Google, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft — have spent more than $1 trillion on AI in less than four years. Companies don’t walk away from such investments. Data centers will be built somewhere. There will be benefits, too. Building and maintaining data centers demands high-level trade work , a tremendous opportunity for lucrative working-class jobs and entrepreneurs to start businesses. Local governments, particularly in economically stagnant areas, can realize tremendous tax benefits that will fund public safety, healthcare and infrastructure. An obvious common-sense agenda would address the real concerns that Americans have over data centers and AI. Protect the power supply. Demand efficient cooling technology. Enforce transparency about power and water usage . Give communities tools to enforce noise limits and protect environmental standards. And refuse indulgent tax breaks for an industry that, as noted, is going to build itself out no matter what. Our energy is better spent grappling with our relationship with technology, now and in the future. Disruption that cannot be avoided can be channeled into improving the human condition. Maybe there’s even an app for that. sources.title: Is the Data Center Backlash Just NIMBY Run Amok? - Talking Points Memo
passages: In response to my post about this data center backlash outside of Kansas City (specifically Independence, Missouri), I’ve been fielding the range of ideas people have about hyperscale AI data centers.
sources.body: In response to my post about this data center backlash outside of Kansas City (specifically Independence, Missouri), I’ve been fielding the range of ideas people have about hyperscale AI data centers.

extraction.body: In response to my post about this data center backlash outside of Kansas City (specifically Independence, Missouri), I’ve been fielding the range of ideas people have about hyperscale AI data centers. As you’d probably expect, the vast majority of people are against them and excited to see this kind of backlash through the architecture of local government. But there’s a small but vocal group saying: no, this is all a kind of NIMBY moral panic driven by anger at Big Tech when a lot of these deals, maybe most, actually are good deals for the local communities. The last part isn’t totally crazy. Or at least they’re certainly on to something that a big part of the punch behind the data center backlash is fueled by a broad politico-economy anger about tech platforms, AI, and nascent oligarchy which in this one set of circumstances people can actually fight back against. I discussed this in a post at the end of last month. Part of the big sour mood that seems to pervade every nook and cranny of our society today is focused on Big Tech, the central and most visible moneyed power in the U.S. today. Everyone has this sense that these guys can simply do anything and there’s no accountability — no democratic control — over any of it. It’s their world and we’re just living in it. But here you have a case where you need to build a super big data center, where finally you have to come and ask permission from some sleepy town council or county commission. And all that pent up powerlessness just comes out as, No! Or, really, Fuck no! And along with that is comment that amounts to, I don’t even care what you’re doing. The answer’s still no. Because you guys have way too much power and someone has to say no to you. I’m not saying that’s all there is to the backlash by any means. But I’m pretty sure the potency of it draws a lot from that sentiment, as opposed to just a more mundane weighing of the pros and cons. And if a lot of it is just that, I’m not sure that’s necessarily a bad thing. Someone does have to say no to people. And the frameworks of economics and government don’t always provide the most straightforward way to do that. The general crisis of oligarchy and an increasingly freebooting, out-of-control tech sector isn’t something people are imagining. It’s real. Sometimes people need to clamp down where they can just to force big money to the table, to start renegotiating the social contract. On all these big questions, I find myself both uncertain and agnostic. I’ve thought for a while that the issue is less with AI itself than the economic and political context in which it is being introduced into society. It matters a lot that guys calling almost all the shots are unaccustomed to and unwilling to accept almost any kind of oversight of their society-shaping work. And over the course of the last half dozen years, they’ve gravitated toward a politics that we must broadly called authoritarian and even fascistic, as well as an extreme contempt for a broad range of liberal (in the broad sense) values. I’ve seen decent arguments that a lot of these fears are overblown, that big data centers can provide a sizable economic boost for declining rural communities, that the environmental and economic externalities are manageable. I think the big problem with this theory or assumption is the broader AI gold rush. Everything about the AI boom is operating in a gold rush fashion. Domestic behemoths are competing with each other. The U.S. is competing with China. Everyone wants to get there first. And these data centers are coming online with almost unimaginable demands for power on a utility grid that is already strained and creaky. Over time, with aggressive building-out of renewables, there’s probably enough energy for everyone, and clean energy at that. But when you’re trying to bring everything on line in the next two or three years, it all starts to look very different. Here’s just one data point — illustrative rather than proving a general point — from just the last few days. There’s an AI data center about 40 miles outside of the Philadelphia, on the New Jersey side of the border in Vineland. It’s being built to service Microsoft but it’s being run by Nebius, the same firm involved in Independence, Missouri. It’s currently under construction, and there are already lots of complaints about noise and other issues. Using thermal imagery and other forms of reporting, a non-profit newsroom called Floodlight was able to determine that the facility has allegedly set up an array of 62 trailer-sized gas generators which lack any permits, either state or federal, for their use. It’s like setting up a small and seemingly illegal power plant and … assuming no one will notice, or maybe the facility has enough clout to stop anyone from doing anything about it. This is just one facility. Nebius might eventually be able to get permits for these generators. They appear to be a stop-gap until they can get a different kind of generator up and working. But what I take away from this is just the totally Wild West atmosphere in which this is all happening. Move fast and break things and all that. You see lots of this stuff, and it’s enough to give even a city or county council that is sold on the concept of data centers to be very wary of letting one get started in their jurisdiction. My main point in writing this is to say that I — we — are basically agnostic on these details: are they good deals for localities, how bad are they for the environment, how much are they driving a return to gas or even coal to provide the needed scale of power? What is interesting and important about this as a story is the way it captures one of the central clashes of our era: untrammeled oligarchic tech power versus local self-government, and really all self-government. It doesn’t cease to be that just because we might disagree about the longterm tax benefits for the municipality or the precise amount of noise pollution or water contamination. There’s a reason this story — the big AI data center metastory — has the whole country electrified. Because big, big, big things are happening, and about a half dozen guys in Silicon Valley are deciding how they happen. The rest of us, mostly accurately, don’t think we have any say in the matter.

I’ve seen decent arguments that a lot of these fears are overblown, that big data centers can provide a sizable economic boost for declining rural communities, that the environmental and economic externalities are manageable.

I think the big problem with this theory or assumption is the broader AI gold rush. Everything about the AI boom is operating in a gold rush fashion. Domestic behemoths are competing with each other. The U.S. is competing with China. Everyone wants to get there first. And these data centers are coming online with almost unimaginable demands for power on a utility grid that is already strained and creaky. Over time, with aggressive building-out of renewables, there’s probably enough energy for everyone, and clean energy at that. But when you’re trying to bring everything on line in the next two or three years, it all starts to look very different.

Here’s just one data point — illustrative rather than proving a general point — from just the last few days. There’s an AI data center about 40 miles outside of the Philadelphia, on the New Jersey side of the border in Vineland. It’s being built to service Microsoft but it’s being run by Nebius, the same firm involved in Independence, Missouri. It’s currently under construction, and there are already lots of complaints about noise and other issues. Using thermal imagery and other forms of reporting, a non-profit newsroom called Floodlight was able to determine that the facility has allegedly set up an array of 62 trailer-sized gas generators which lack any permits, either state or federal, for their use. It’s like setting up a small and seemingly illegal power plant and … assuming no one will notice, or maybe the facility has enough clout to stop anyone from doing anything about it.

This is just one facility. Nebius might eventually be able to get permits for these generators. They appear to be a stop-gap until they can get a different kind of generator up and working. But what I take away from this is just the totally Wild West atmosphere in which this is all happening. Move fast and break things and all that. You see lots of this stuff, and it’s enough to give even a city or county council that is sold on the concept of data centers to be very wary of letting one get started in their jurisdiction.

My main point in writing this is to say that I — we — are basically agnostic on these details: are they good deals for localities, how bad are they for the environment, how much are they driving a return to gas or even coal to provide the needed scale of power? What is interesting and important about this as a story is the way it captures one of the central clashes of our era: untrammeled oligarchic tech power versus local self-government, and really all self-government. It doesn’t cease to be that just because we might disagree about the longterm tax benefits for the municipality or the precise amount of noise pollution or water contamination. There’s a reason this story — the big AI data center metastory — has the whole country electrified. Because big, big, big things are happening, and about a half dozen guys in Silicon Valley are deciding how they happen. The rest of us, mostly accurately, don’t think we have any say in the matter.

extraction.body: When Laura Beth moved to Coweta County, Ga., in 2023, she was drawn to her new home’s rural location––it was far from any major roads or highways and had sprawling open land behind it. “Our last home, the surrounding area was becoming very overdeveloped. We had a distribution center less than a mile from our house, and it was just kind of this urban encroachment,” she says. “We knew about the land behind us, and [thought] the worst thing it could be was a subdivision, because who in their right mind would want to build anything out here?” Then, at the start of 2025, she saw an article announcing that a new data center would be coming to her hometown. As she read it, a realization dawned on her. A hyperscale data center , spanning more than 4.9 million sq. ft., had been proposed—and was expected to run right through her backyard. “I didn't know who to reach out to, who to talk to, who could give me some more information,” she says. So she decided to start a Facebook group called “Stop Project Sail” to connect with her neighbors and discuss the proposed plan. More than 8,000 people have now joined the group, and have been organizing petition signings, installing yard signs, and mounting a legal fight against Coweta County and Atlas Development, the company behind the project. “The Board’s responsibility is to serve the entire community, thoughtfully considering all feedback as decisions are weighed that affect Coweta County's more than 160,000 residents and its long-term future.The Board values the principles of democracy and recognizes the importance of our citizens speaking up on all issues that affect our County,” Coweta County Administrator Michael Fouts said in a statement to TIME. “The Board ultimately voted in favor, 3-2, of Project Sail, with those who approved stating its long-term financial benefits it will provide to Coweta County.” Atlas Development did not respond to TIME’s request for comment ahead of publication. The Georgia town is not alone. If there’s one thing most Americans across the country agree on, it’s that they hate data centers. A June Reuters poll found that just a third of Americans approve of the pace of data-center construction, and only 14% are comfortable with a data center being built nearby. On July 18, a national day of protest against data centers saw 142 protests across 42 states. According to one count by The Information , more than 300 cities, towns, and counties—including Monterey Park, Calif., Dekalb County, Ga., and Jefferson County, Pa.—have placed bans or moratoriums on the construction of hyperscale data centers. In the first three months of 2026, 75 major projects worth more than $130 billion were delayed or canceled in part due to organized local opposition. And on July 14, New York governor Kathy Hochul signed an executive order to create the nation's first moratorium on new hyperscale data centers, while several other states, including Pennsylvania, Michigan, and South Carolina are considering similar pauses. Data centers have long been used to store and process our digital information—whether that be photos in the cloud or the videos we stream online. But the rise of hyperscale data centers in recent years—which are higher performing and often used to power AI—began to change things. “We've been aware of data center development as early as 2010, but they were much smaller in scale,” says John Farner, executive director of land and water at the Lincoln Institute of Land Policy, a non-profit which has been researching the land and water use of data centers over the last few years. “What we're seeing now, especially with the advent of hyperscale data centers, is that they're much larger, much more powerful. They're much more resource intensive.” More than 160 new AI data centers have popped up across the U.S. in the past three years—a 70% increase from the last three year period, according to a Bloomberg News analysis . In many instances, they’ve landed in communities with high competition for scarce water resources. A mid-sized data center consumes as much water as a small town , while larger ones require up to 5 million gallons of water every day—as much as a city of 50,000 people. They also consume massive amounts of electricity. Data centers accounted for 4% of total U.S. electricity use in 2024 , and their energy demand is expected to more than double by 2030. In many cases, the additional electricity costs are passed on to nearby residents; in states with a high concentration of data centers electricity prices have increased by up to 267% over the last five years. Steve Swope, another Coweta County resident, relies on wellwater, and is concerned that the construction of the data center could damage septic tanks or leak into the groundwater. “Our wells will either run dry or they'll become polluted and caked with sediment and mud,” he says. Residents in other rural areas around the country have already reported that nearby data centers are making well water undrinkable. When Meta began construction on a $750 million data center in nearby Newton County, Ga. in 2018, the construction damaged local wells, caused municipal water prices to soar, and could cause the county to face a water deficit by 2030, according to reporting from the New York Times . Meta said that according to a study it commissioned, its data center project was unlikely to have impacted the water supply. Soon after Project Sail was approved, four more data centers were proposed in Coweta County. In May, Coweta County approved a data center moratorium on any future projects, but residents say it’s too little, too late. “It's kind of like, well, the horses are all out of the barn, let's be sure to close the door now,” says Swope. The fight has left Beth and her family in limbo. They bought their home intending it to be a fixer-upper—the house is drafty, the windows need replacing. But they're hesitant to invest in a home they’re not sure they’ll stay in. “The unknown drives this cycle of [asking] do we move? I don't really want to move. Where do we move to?” she says. “They're everywhere. We'd want to move somewhere that also has a little bit of land, but all of that is that threat. We feel like there's no safe place to move.” But, as of now, remaining put comes with its own set of problems. “If we stay here, this is going to be in our backyard.” TIME may receive compensation for some links to products and services on this website. coreStoryFacts.text: But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes.
I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits.
The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity.
The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way.
The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to.
Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines.
Companies also build diesel generators for backup.
Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company.
Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded.
The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts.
The notion of data center companies’ bringing their own power might seem attractive at first, because they wouldn’t be straining the grid.

But generating electricity at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and when public utilities build infrastructure of this magnitude, communities have traditionally expected a say in where it goes.
Now, private companies are undertaking projects on a similar scale.
Companies might also try their chances abroad; Google, in fact, announced the day after the elections that it will spend $15 billion on data center projects in Malaysia.
The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts.
That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport .
But the real fault line is electricity: drawing it from the grid and generating it onsite provoke different kinds of backlash, neither easily solved by public relations.
The backlash to data centers isn’t really about water or electricity.
Greg Abbott has moved from cutting ribbons for big data center projects to issuing a list of demands about their power usage, location and economic contributions .
Economic analyst James Pethokoukis has calculated that even if water consumption by data centers quadruples in 2030, they’ll still take just 1% of our supply.
Enforce transparency about power and water usage .
Governments are already requiring the industry to generate its own electricity, and policymakers are even pushing data centers to provide a net increase in power.

On July 18, a national day of protest against data centers saw 142 protests across 42 states.

As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape. Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ. It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words. But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity. Here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid. One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy. Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables). The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts. That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport . Elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she says—that is, electricity. Some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg, to be fair. But it’s the particular consequences of drawing so much power from the grid that have done the most to shape how the backlash has played out. Recent protests have led to new rules from the state that data centers must pay fully for the cost of new transmission lines to the grid and make sure they’re not spread among everyone else. Data center developers told me they’re preparing for new rules that would cut them off from grid power during peak demand. Schlossberg also worries about the downstream effects of a strained grid—for example, that data centers will run more diesel generators or that Dominion Energy will expand fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables to meet demand. The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way. The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to. Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines. Companies also build diesel generators for backup. Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company. Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded. The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts. It’s a lot of power for one industrial site, but not unprecedented: One data center developer told me he’s eyeing a former steel mill already equipped to draw that much electricity from the grid. But the ideal facilities are more like 6,000 megawatts. That’s the estimated draw of the city of Chicago, which is powered by more than 20 power plants within the city alone (and dozens farther out). The notion of data center companies’ bringing their own power might seem attractive at first, because they wouldn’t be straining the grid. But generating electricity at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and when public utilities build infrastructure of this magnitude, communities have traditionally expected a say in where it goes. Now, private companies are undertaking projects on a similar scale. Natural-gas turbines of any scale release air pollutants. When diesel generators are used, it’s even worse. And in the unprecedented rush to get these facilities operating, companies have become horrible neighbors (recall that Elon Musk violated air quality laws when he set up dozens of turbines to power a data center in Memphis, according to the Environmental Protection Agency). Big Tech’s tendency to chalk the backlash up to a culture war obfuscates one simple fact: There’s only so pleasant you can make a small city of computers to live around. Sure, companies can pursue better deals that raise tax revenues, hire local workers, and get more community involvement, as the protests are leading them to do . But if a small town is asked to welcome a Walt Disney World, an international airport, a steel plant, and the power plants to run them all, should we be surprised by its trepidation? Again, that’s not to say this is the sole reason for opposition to data centers. Fears of job losses, existential risks, and concentrated corporate power all fuel the backlash, as does misinformation (most facilities use far less water than many people think). Nor is consuming enormous amounts of electricity inherently bad: Many of the advances that have improved modern life have required just that. But as one developer recently told me, industry insiders see their ambitions as constrained less by public opposition than by a lack of electricity. That should tell us something. So what happens next? It’s possible that newly elected politicians’ actual stances on data centers won’t be as negative as the ones they campaigned on. The backlash to data centers isn’t really about water or electricity. In most cases, it’s not about noise concerns. It’s not even primarily a response to alarming developments in artificial intelligence anymore. No, questions about building massive facilities to hold the servers powering the AI revolution are mainly a relief valve for frustration after two decades of dizzying technological change. It’s about screen time, social media, economic disruption and our fears of a world evolving so fast we feel we cannot keep up. Consider the newest front in the tech wars. Flock cameras, a brand of license-plate readers that police use to hunt for suspects, have become the focus of protest across the country and from various parts of the political spectrum. Americans have a robust tradition of bowing up to invasions of privacy. But we’ve also been steadily surrendering our own information and photos — voluntarily — to tech companies and assenting to a world where any public activity is likely to be caught on camera. So, why this, why now? The cameras are readily visible and subject to pressure on the mechanisms of public policy. For the same reasons, data centers have become the focal point of concerns about AI and its effect on life. These worries are legitimate and widespread. A Pew poll released in March found that half of Americans fear the impact of AI on their lives more than they are excited about its possibilities. Proposals to build data centers require state and local approval, so there’s something tangible for people to protest. It’s hard to sway Google, Amazon or any of the other big companies plunging into AI development. But when Texans tell pollsters they oppose a data center in their community , 56% to 29%, officeholders pay attention. Concerns about AI can seem apocalyptic, too. It’s hard to find a scarier sentence than this recent New York Times report that “scientists have used artificial intelligence to create new kinds of viruses , raising hopes for medical advances while also raising the disturbing possibility that the technology could someday be used to invent dangerous pathogens.” Our nature is to skip over that first part, the positive possibilities, while imagining every terrible pandemic-outbreak movie we’ve ever seen. We don’t even think about the potential improvement in diagnosing medical conditions, even though AI is already showing the ability to outperform human doctors in some cases. Add in concerns that AI will eliminate jobs, make us all too stupid to meaningfully read or write and maybe even go rogue a la the “Terminator” movies and suddenly, preventing a data center seems like the highest priority. We’re scarcely 20 years into the smartphone boom. That’s a smidgen of time in the human experience, and we are still adapting to a world of endless information and life spent on screens. Our brains don’t evolve at the pace of change, so we’re ill-equipped for the stream of misery, jealousy and distraction that we hold in our hands. People are looking for ways to break away from tech, even as it insinuates itself more into daily life. Giant buildings full of humming servers owned by shadowy corporate interests vying for big tax breaks represent a villainy we otherwise can’t get our arms around. If there’s an upside, perhaps it proves that our political system is more responsive than we think. In the span of less than a year, Gov. Greg Abbott has moved from cutting ribbons for big data center projects to issuing a list of demands about their power usage, location and economic contributions . In business-friendly Fort Worth, a majority of City Council members seems prepared to embrace a moratorium on new data center projects. As with so many populist outrage bubbles, though, facts and tradeoffs are getting short shrift. A common tactic to cause alarm is to add up every possible gigawatt that projects might use. But not all planned centers will bear fruit. Governments are already requiring the industry to generate its own electricity, and policymakers are even pushing data centers to provide a net increase in power. No one likes what’s happening with energy costs, but the cause is complex. Research indicates that data centers can actually help cut electricity prices because higher demand means more production. Big numbers about water use sound scary, too. Economic analyst James Pethokoukis has calculated that even if water consumption by data centers quadruples in 2030, they’ll still take just 1% of our supply. Cooling technology continues to advance, and smart negotiations with developers will demand that they use more efficient methods. If you’re really that worked up about our future water supply, tear out your lawn, quit playing golf and get rid of lush youth-sports fields. That would save far more water than shutting down every data center. Remember, too, we’re in a fierce AI race with China, which is not above meddling with American public opinion through TikTok or even funding political movements here. With affinity for socialism on the rise on the left, plenty of useful idiots will work against their own country’s national security interests on behalf of the Chinese communist behemoth. After all, isn’t it odd that many of the progressives raising alarm about electricity usage would gleefully force Americans to convert to electric cars? AI development will not be derailed. America’s four tech behemoths — Google, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft — have spent more than $1 trillion on AI in less than four years. Companies don’t walk away from such investments. Data centers will be built somewhere. There will be benefits, too. Building and maintaining data centers demands high-level trade work , a tremendous opportunity for lucrative working-class jobs and entrepreneurs to start businesses. Local governments, particularly in economically stagnant areas, can realize tremendous tax benefits that will fund public safety, healthcare and infrastructure. An obvious common-sense agenda would address the real concerns that Americans have over data centers and AI. Protect the power supply. Demand efficient cooling technology. Enforce transparency about power and water usage . Give communities tools to enforce noise limits and protect environmental standards. And refuse indulgent tax breaks for an industry that, as noted, is going to build itself out no matter what. Our energy is better spent grappling with our relationship with technology, now and in the future. Disruption that cannot be avoided can be channeled into improving the human condition. Maybe there’s even an app for that. extraction.body: In response to my post about this data center backlash outside of Kansas City (specifically Independence, Missouri), I’ve been fielding the range of ideas people have about hyperscale AI data centers. As you’d probably expect, the vast majority of people are against them and excited to see this kind of backlash through the architecture of local government. But there’s a small but vocal group saying: no, this is all a kind of NIMBY moral panic driven by anger at Big Tech when a lot of these deals, maybe most, actually are good deals for the local communities. The last part isn’t totally crazy. Or at least they’re certainly on to something that a big part of the punch behind the data center backlash is fueled by a broad politico-economy anger about tech platforms, AI, and nascent oligarchy which in this one set of circumstances people can actually fight back against. I discussed this in a post at the end of last month. Part of the big sour mood that seems to pervade every nook and cranny of our society today is focused on Big Tech, the central and most visible moneyed power in the U.S. today. Everyone has this sense that these guys can simply do anything and there’s no accountability — no democratic control — over any of it. It’s their world and we’re just living in it. But here you have a case where you need to build a super big data center, where finally you have to come and ask permission from some sleepy town council or county commission. And all that pent up powerlessness just comes out as, No! Or, really, Fuck no! And along with that is comment that amounts to, I don’t even care what you’re doing. The answer’s still no. Because you guys have way too much power and someone has to say no to you. I’m not saying that’s all there is to the backlash by any means. But I’m pretty sure the potency of it draws a lot from that sentiment, as opposed to just a more mundane weighing of the pros and cons. And if a lot of it is just that, I’m not sure that’s necessarily a bad thing. Someone does have to say no to people. And the frameworks of economics and government don’t always provide the most straightforward way to do that. The general crisis of oligarchy and an increasingly freebooting, out-of-control tech sector isn’t something people are imagining. It’s real. Sometimes people need to clamp down where they can just to force big money to the table, to start renegotiating the social contract. On all these big questions, I find myself both uncertain and agnostic. I’ve thought for a while that the issue is less with AI itself than the economic and political context in which it is being introduced into society. It matters a lot that guys calling almost all the shots are unaccustomed to and unwilling to accept almost any kind of oversight of their society-shaping work. And over the course of the last half dozen years, they’ve gravitated toward a politics that we must broadly called authoritarian and even fascistic, as well as an extreme contempt for a broad range of liberal (in the broad sense) values. I’ve seen decent arguments that a lot of these fears are overblown, that big data centers can provide a sizable economic boost for declining rural communities, that the environmental and economic externalities are manageable. I think the big problem with this theory or assumption is the broader AI gold rush. Everything about the AI boom is operating in a gold rush fashion. Domestic behemoths are competing with each other. The U.S. is competing with China. Everyone wants to get there first. And these data centers are coming online with almost unimaginable demands for power on a utility grid that is already strained and creaky. Over time, with aggressive building-out of renewables, there’s probably enough energy for everyone, and clean energy at that. But when you’re trying to bring everything on line in the next two or three years, it all starts to look very different. Here’s just one data point — illustrative rather than proving a general point — from just the last few days. There’s an AI data center about 40 miles outside of the Philadelphia, on the New Jersey side of the border in Vineland. It’s being built to service Microsoft but it’s being run by Nebius, the same firm involved in Independence, Missouri. It’s currently under construction, and there are already lots of complaints about noise and other issues. Using thermal imagery and other forms of reporting, a non-profit newsroom called Floodlight was able to determine that the facility has allegedly set up an array of 62 trailer-sized gas generators which lack any permits, either state or federal, for their use. It’s like setting up a small and seemingly illegal power plant and … assuming no one will notice, or maybe the facility has enough clout to stop anyone from doing anything about it. This is just one facility. Nebius might eventually be able to get permits for these generators. They appear to be a stop-gap until they can get a different kind of generator up and working. But what I take away from this is just the totally Wild West atmosphere in which this is all happening. Move fast and break things and all that. You see lots of this stuff, and it’s enough to give even a city or county council that is sold on the concept of data centers to be very wary of letting one get started in their jurisdiction. My main point in writing this is to say that I — we — are basically agnostic on these details: are they good deals for localities, how bad are they for the environment, how much are they driving a return to gas or even coal to provide the needed scale of power? What is interesting and important about this as a story is the way it captures one of the central clashes of our era: untrammeled oligarchic tech power versus local self-government, and really all self-government. It doesn’t cease to be that just because we might disagree about the longterm tax benefits for the municipality or the precise amount of noise pollution or water contamination. There’s a reason this story — the big AI data center metastory — has the whole country electrified. Because big, big, big things are happening, and about a half dozen guys in Silicon Valley are deciding how they happen. The rest of us, mostly accurately, don’t think we have any say in the matter.

In many instances, they’ve landed in communities with high competition for scarce water resources.
A mid-sized data center consumes as much water as a small town , while larger ones require up to 5 million gallons of water every day—as much as a city of 50,000 people.
They also consume massive amounts of electricity.
On July 18, a national day of protest against data centers saw 142 protests across 42 states.

extraction.body: When Laura Beth moved to Coweta County, Ga., in 2023, she was drawn to her new home’s rural location––it was far from any major roads or highways and had sprawling open land behind it. “Our last home, the surrounding area was becoming very overdeveloped. We had a distribution center less than a mile from our house, and it was just kind of this urban encroachment,” she says. “We knew about the land behind us, and [thought] the worst thing it could be was a subdivision, because who in their right mind would want to build anything out here?” Then, at the start of 2025, she saw an article announcing that a new data center would be coming to her hometown. As she read it, a realization dawned on her. A hyperscale data center , spanning more than 4.9 million sq. ft., had been proposed—and was expected to run right through her backyard. “I didn't know who to reach out to, who to talk to, who could give me some more information,” she says. So she decided to start a Facebook group called “Stop Project Sail” to connect with her neighbors and discuss the proposed plan. More than 8,000 people have now joined the group, and have been organizing petition signings, installing yard signs, and mounting a legal fight against Coweta County and Atlas Development, the company behind the project. “The Board’s responsibility is to serve the entire community, thoughtfully considering all feedback as decisions are weighed that affect Coweta County's more than 160,000 residents and its long-term future.The Board values the principles of democracy and recognizes the importance of our citizens speaking up on all issues that affect our County,” Coweta County Administrator Michael Fouts said in a statement to TIME. “The Board ultimately voted in favor, 3-2, of Project Sail, with those who approved stating its long-term financial benefits it will provide to Coweta County.” Atlas Development did not respond to TIME’s request for comment ahead of publication. The Georgia town is not alone. If there’s one thing most Americans across the country agree on, it’s that they hate data centers. A June Reuters poll found that just a third of Americans approve of the pace of data-center construction, and only 14% are comfortable with a data center being built nearby. On July 18, a national day of protest against data centers saw 142 protests across 42 states. According to one count by The Information , more than 300 cities, towns, and counties—including Monterey Park, Calif., Dekalb County, Ga., and Jefferson County, Pa.—have placed bans or moratoriums on the construction of hyperscale data centers. In the first three months of 2026, 75 major projects worth more than $130 billion were delayed or canceled in part due to organized local opposition. And on July 14, New York governor Kathy Hochul signed an executive order to create the nation's first moratorium on new hyperscale data centers, while several other states, including Pennsylvania, Michigan, and South Carolina are considering similar pauses. Data centers have long been used to store and process our digital information—whether that be photos in the cloud or the videos we stream online. But the rise of hyperscale data centers in recent years—which are higher performing and often used to power AI—began to change things. “We've been aware of data center development as early as 2010, but they were much smaller in scale,” says John Farner, executive director of land and water at the Lincoln Institute of Land Policy, a non-profit which has been researching the land and water use of data centers over the last few years. “What we're seeing now, especially with the advent of hyperscale data centers, is that they're much larger, much more powerful. They're much more resource intensive.” More than 160 new AI data centers have popped up across the U.S. in the past three years—a 70% increase from the last three year period, according to a Bloomberg News analysis . In many instances, they’ve landed in communities with high competition for scarce water resources. A mid-sized data center consumes as much water as a small town , while larger ones require up to 5 million gallons of water every day—as much as a city of 50,000 people. They also consume massive amounts of electricity. Data centers accounted for 4% of total U.S. electricity use in 2024 , and their energy demand is expected to more than double by 2030. In many cases, the additional electricity costs are passed on to nearby residents; in states with a high concentration of data centers electricity prices have increased by up to 267% over the last five years. Steve Swope, another Coweta County resident, relies on wellwater, and is concerned that the construction of the data center could damage septic tanks or leak into the groundwater. “Our wells will either run dry or they'll become polluted and caked with sediment and mud,” he says. Residents in other rural areas around the country have already reported that nearby data centers are making well water undrinkable. When Meta began construction on a $750 million data center in nearby Newton County, Ga. in 2018, the construction damaged local wells, caused municipal water prices to soar, and could cause the county to face a water deficit by 2030, according to reporting from the New York Times . Meta said that according to a study it commissioned, its data center project was unlikely to have impacted the water supply. Soon after Project Sail was approved, four more data centers were proposed in Coweta County. In May, Coweta County approved a data center moratorium on any future projects, but residents say it’s too little, too late. “It's kind of like, well, the horses are all out of the barn, let's be sure to close the door now,” says Swope. The fight has left Beth and her family in limbo. They bought their home intending it to be a fixer-upper—the house is drafty, the windows need replacing. But they're hesitant to invest in a home they’re not sure they’ll stay in. “The unknown drives this cycle of [asking] do we move? I don't really want to move. Where do we move to?” she says. “They're everywhere. We'd want to move somewhere that also has a little bit of land, but all of that is that threat. We feel like there's no safe place to move.” But, as of now, remaining put comes with its own set of problems. “If we stay here, this is going to be in our backyard.” TIME may receive compensation for some links to products and services on this website. Offers may be subject to change without notice.

The New York Stock Exchange is turning to Avalanche to power the behind-the-scenes plumbing of its forthcoming tokenized securities platform, one of the clearest signs yet that Wall Street's oldest institutions are moving core market infrastructure onto public blockchains.

The New York Stock Exchange is turning to Avalanche to power the behind-the-scenes plumbing of its forthcoming tokenized securities platform, one of the clearest signs yet that Wall Street's oldest institutions are moving core market infrastructure onto public blockchains. Ava Labs, the company behind Avalanche, said Monday that the blockchain will serve as the "core ledger technology" for the clearing firm behind an NYSE-affiliated digital trading venue. The platform, which the NYSE's parent Intercontinental Exchange previously said it was developing, is designed to allow 24/7 trading, clearing and settlement of tokenized securities, subject to regulatory approval. Running on Avalanche, it aims to bring the clearing of tokenized equities onchain at institutional scale. Tokenization, the practice of issuing traditional assets as blockchain-based tokens, has become one of Wall Street's buzziest pursuits, but most efforts so far have centered on individual products rather than the market machinery itself. The NYSE's move is notable because it puts a blockchain underneath the clearing and settlement layer, the plumbing that finalizes trades, rather than just wrapping a single fund or stock in a token. Dennis Lee, the NYSE's head of digital issuance, said the exchange is "picking the right technology for each job," and that while its planned platform will support equities listed across a range of blockchains, the ledger recording and settling trades needs to be fast, reliable and able to control who participates. Emin Gün Sirer, Ava Labs' CEO and founder, framed the deal as proof that blockchains can support not just products but the infrastructure they trade on, citing Avalanche's "24/7 atomic settlement" and predictable costs. The announcement adds to a frenetic race to put stocks and their underlying infrastructure onchain. The NYSE separately tapped Blockchain.com to reach crypto investors with tokenized stocks and ETFs, while ICE and crypto exchange OKX are planning a 24/7 tokenized stock venue under an SEC exemption, and Morgan Stanley has moved to tokenize securities. Apple Completes the Set: Every Magnificent Seven Stock Opts Out of OKX-ICE Venue That OKX-ICE effort has hit friction, though: Every Magnificent Seven stock, including Apple and Meta , opted out of having its shares tokenized on the venue, with 67 companies in all joining them. Research shows the appetite for tokenized stocks is real but uneven. The New York Stock Exchange is turning to Avalanche to power the behind-the-scenes plumbing of its forthcoming tokenized securities platform, one of the clearest signs yet that Wall Street's oldest institutions are moving core market infrastructure onto public blockchains.
Ava Labs, the company behind Avalanche, said Monday that the blockchain will serve as the "core ledger technology" for the clearing firm behind an NYSE-affiliated digital trading venue.

The platform, which the NYSE's parent Intercontinental Exchange previously said it was developing, is designed to allow 24/7 trading, clearing and settlement of tokenized securities, subject to regulatory approval. Running on Avalanche, it aims to bring the clearing of tokenized equities onchain at institutional scale.

Tokenization, the practice of issuing traditional assets as blockchain-based tokens, has become one of Wall Street's buzziest pursuits, but most efforts so far have centered on individual products rather than the market machinery itself.
The NYSE's move is notable because it puts a blockchain underneath the clearing and settlement layer, the plumbing that finalizes trades, rather than just wrapping a single fund or stock in a token.

Dennis Lee, the NYSE's head of digital issuance, said the exchange is "picking the right technology for each job," and that while its planned platform will support equities listed across a range of blockchains, the ledger recording and settling trades needs to be fast, reliable and able to control who participates.

Emin Gün Sirer, Ava Labs' CEO and founder, framed the deal as proof that blockchains can support not just products but the infrastructure they trade on, citing Avalanche's "24/7 atomic settlement" and predictable costs.
The announcement adds to a frenetic race to put stocks and their underlying infrastructure onchain.

The NYSE separately tapped Blockchain.com to reach crypto investors with tokenized stocks and ETFs, while ICE and crypto exchange OKX are planning a 24/7 tokenized stock venue under an SEC exemption, and Morgan Stanley has moved to tokenize securities.
Apple Completes the Set: Every Magnificent Seven Stock Opts Out of OKX-ICE Venue
That OKX-ICE effort has hit friction, though: Every Magnificent Seven stock, including Apple and Meta , opted out of having its shares tokenized on the venue, with 67 companies in all joining them.

Research shows the appetite for tokenized stocks is real but uneven. An IMF study found tokenized stocks show genuine demand yet remain volatile and illiquid, a reminder that the infrastructure may be arriving faster than the markets to fill it.

The New York Stock Exchange is turning to Avalanche to power the behind-the-scenes plumbing of its forthcoming tokenized securities platform, one of the clearest signs yet that Wall Street's oldest institutions are moving core market infrastructure onto public blockchains. Ava Labs, the company behind Avalanche, said Monday that the blockchain will serve as the "core ledger technology" for the clearing firm behind an NYSE-affiliated digital trading venue. The platform, which the NYSE's parent Intercontinental Exchange previously said it was developing, is designed to allow 24/7 trading, clearing and settlement of tokenized securities, subject to regulatory approval. Running on Avalanche, it aims to bring the clearing of tokenized equities onchain at institutional scale. Tokenization, the practice of issuing traditional assets as blockchain-based tokens, has become one of Wall Street's buzziest pursuits, but most efforts so far have centered on individual products rather than the market machinery itself. The NYSE's move is notable because it puts a blockchain underneath the clearing and settlement layer, the plumbing that finalizes trades, rather than just wrapping a single fund or stock in a token. Dennis Lee, the NYSE's head of digital issuance, said the exchange is "picking the right technology for each job," and that while its planned platform will support equities listed across a range of blockchains, the ledger recording and settling trades needs to be fast, reliable and able to control who participates. Emin Gün Sirer, Ava Labs' CEO and founder, framed the deal as proof that blockchains can support not just products but the infrastructure they trade on, citing Avalanche's "24/7 atomic settlement" and predictable costs. The announcement adds to a frenetic race to put stocks and their underlying infrastructure onchain. The NYSE separately tapped Blockchain.com to reach crypto investors with tokenized stocks and ETFs, while ICE and crypto exchange OKX are planning a 24/7 tokenized stock venue under an SEC exemption, and Morgan Stanley has moved to tokenize securities. Apple Completes the Set: Every Magnificent Seven Stock Opts Out of OKX-ICE Venue That OKX-ICE effort has hit friction, though: Every Magnificent Seven stock, including Apple and Meta , opted out of having its shares tokenized on the venue, with 67 companies in all joining them. Research shows the appetite for tokenized stocks is real but uneven. An IMF study found tokenized stocks show genuine demand yet remain volatile and illiquid, a reminder that the infrastructure may be arriving faster than the markets to fill it.

sources.title: Meta releases Muse Ember, a new lightweight model for agent execution
passages: Meta Superintelligence Lab released a new AI model on Monday called Muse Ember, the lab’s lightest and most cost-efficient AI model yet.
In its release, Meta said Ember was “designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing.”
Given the emphasis on low cost and accuracy at scale, Ember is designed to pair with a larger model like Meta’s Muse Wonder in an agentic harness.

In the case of a customer-support agent, for instance, you might see a heavier model establishing rules for how to handle a particular issue, then sending a lighter-weight model to apply the rules across tens of thousands of cases.
As Meta puts it in the announcement, “Muse Wonder plans, Muse Ember handles the volume.”
The flagship consumer AI product, the Muse Agent, was released in September to unexpected success , with new features like Spaces and video chat rolling out earlier this month.
With volume-heavy use cases in mind, Meta also trained Ember to work well across different types of media, including text, images, and audio.
The result makes the model surprisingly flexible in what kind of inputs it can handle.

Meta particularly emphasized Ember’s cost-per-task, using Artificial Analysis’s composite benchmark score to show Ember as cheaper and smarter than competitors like Anthropic’s Haiku and OpenAI’s Luna.
Meta acquires AI coding startup Conductor Lucas Ropek

coreStoryFacts.text: Meta Superintelligence Lab released a new AI model on Monday called Muse Ember, the lab’s lightest and most cost-efficient AI model yet.
In its release, Meta said Ember was “designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing.”
Given the emphasis on low cost and accuracy at scale, Ember is designed to pair with a larger model like Meta’s Muse Wonder in an agentic harness.

In the case of a customer-support agent, for instance, you might see a heavier model establishing rules for how to handle a particular issue, then sending a lighter-weight model to apply the rules across tens of thousands of cases.
As Meta puts it in the announcement, “Muse Wonder plans, Muse Ember handles the volume.”
The flagship consumer AI product, the Muse Agent, was released in September to unexpected success , with new features like Spaces and video chat rolling out earlier this month.
With volume-heavy use cases in mind, Meta also trained Ember to work well across different types of media, including text, images, and audio.
The result makes the model surprisingly flexible in what kind of inputs it can handle.

Meta particularly emphasized Ember’s cost-per-task, using Artificial Analysis’s composite benchmark score to show Ember as cheaper and smarter than competitors like Anthropic’s Haiku and OpenAI’s Luna.
Meta acquires AI coding startup Conductor Lucas Ropek
Source : Meta releases Muse Ember, a new lightweight model for agent execution | TechCrunch , by Russell Brandom , TechCrunch , Nov 9, 2026
The company built it to sit behind a larger model in an agentic harness: the larger model sets the rules for a task, and Ember applies them across thousands of cases.
"Muse Wonder plans, Muse Ember handles the volume," Meta said.

Meta Superintelligence Lab released Muse Ember on Monday, its lightest and most cost-efficient model, priced at 10 cents per million input tokens and built for the tool calls and parsing agents run all day.
Ember is the fourth model under Meta's Muse brand.
Spark arrived in April as a mid-weight option.
Glimmer followed in August as Spark's open source twin.
Wonder launched in October as the frontier model.
The Muse Agent, Meta's flagship consumer AI product, shipped in September to unexpected success, and Meta rolled out features such as Spaces and video chat earlier this month.
That figure undercuts Anthropic's Haiku and OpenAI's Luna, and it matches open source options such as DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GLM 5.3 Flash.
Meta pointed to Artificial Analysis's composite benchmark score to argue Ember delivers more capability per dollar than those rivals.
Engineers building agents already split planning from execution.
9, 2026, and TechCrunch reported it as a new lightweight model built for agent execution.
It carries a 1 million token context window and a 512,000 token output ceiling.
