Fable 5.2 is available across the company's platforms today. Mythos 5.2 is limited to organizations that are a part of Anthropic's Life Sciences and Cyber verification programs.

The company says Fable 5.2 will also be less expensive to run than Fable 5.1. Fable 5.2 will now cost $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. Fable 5.1 cost $10 per million inputs and $50 per million outputs.
Tokens are a unit of measurement in AI that represent pieces of words or phrases you type or speak to a model and its responses.
AI companies are engaged in a pricing war as models become more efficient and customers look for ways to save on AI services.

Industry experts say that over time, enterprises will likely rely on a mix of closed-weight models like Anthropic's and open-weight AI models to meet their needs. The idea is to avoid being locked into a single model vendor, while also being able to reduce overall costs.
Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 come ahead of Anthropic's anticipated initial public offering later this month.
But recent market turmoil around the AI trade could derail that.
While Wall Street was initially targeting upward of a $2 trillion valuation for Anthropic's debut, that could now end up between $1 trillion and $1.5 trillion.
There are also concerns that the company could end up pushing out its debut to a later date in hopes that market conditions will improve.

extraction.body: Anthropic released new versions of its most advanced models on Monday, with the launch of Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2. The company says the new models “show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision” and communicate more clearly with users. Notably, Anthropic is lowering the cost of Fable from $10 to $8 per million input tokens. As a result, Fable 5.2 is now cheaper than its primary competitor GPT-6 Astra. Anthropic says that the new version of Fable will return responses 30% faster across effort levels. Faster inference serving is available for double the price. Fable 5.2 is also compatible with zero data retention (ZDR) policies through the Enterprise Frontier Safeguards system , long a sticking point for many enterprise clients. It’s Anthropic’s first model release since the arrival of a third-party report from the assessment group METR , which suggested the lab might be approaching recursive self-improvement (RSI) — or the ability for AI models to carry on model training independently. The METR report found internal models were speeding up Anthropic’s AI progress by roughly 2x, although many uncertainties remain. Still, Anthropic’s release notes significant ongoing challenges in accurately testing model capabilities. “Claude Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 each voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any of our recent models, which challenges our ability to assess how they will act in real-world settings. As these settings expand and capabilities increase with future models, we expect this challenge to grow.” Anthropic maintains that the new version of Mythos does not have the ability to act covertly against its user, a verdict that’s detailed further in Mythos 5.2’s system card . “Claude Mythos 5.2 shows stronger covert capabilities than prior Claude models on several of our evaluations, particularly when its reasoning is hidden from the monitor,” the system card reads. “That said, we believe that low levels of absolute performance on our new covert evaluations support claims that rely on detection of harmful actions in high-stakes situations.” Fable 5.2 has been available to select parties in pre-release for some time, and Anthropic says the model has already “solved two open problems in theoretical physics, formalized Fermat’s Last Theorem, and supported numerous other research projects.” Also on Monday, AI startup Physical Superintelligence announced a new proof of the Aaronson‑Ambainis conjecture, a pivotal step in setting theoretical limits for quantum computing. Notably, the lab said the result was achieved by running “a non-public Anthropic model” within PSI’s own system. Anthropic did not confirm or deny whether Fable 5.2 was the model in question. sources.title: Anthropic Ships Mythos and Fable Models Days Before IPO
passages: The company announced Mythos and Fable on Monday, claiming improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision capabilities just weeks after filing its IPO paperwork.
Anthropic's IPO filing revealed a staggering $542B data center spending plan, raising eyebrows across Wall Street about whether the company can sustain that level of infrastructure investment.
Anthropic is playing a high-stakes game, dropping new AI models while sprinting toward an IPO and burning billions on infrastructure.
What's clear is that Anthropic is trying to build momentum heading into its IPO roadshow.

What's clear is that Anthropic is trying to build momentum heading into its IPO roadshow.

extraction.body: Anthropic just dropped two new AI models into the wild. The company announced Mythos and Fable on Monday, claiming improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision capabilities just weeks after filing its IPO paperwork. The timing isn't subtle - Anthropic is racing to prove its technical chops while investors scrutinize its S-1 filing and its massive infrastructure spending plans come under the microscope. The AI startup behind Claude just released Mythos and Fable, two new models that the company says deliver sharper performance in coding, reasoning, vision tasks, and user communication. The announcement lands at a critical moment - just weeks after Anthropic filed to go public and started the clock on one of the year's most anticipated tech IPOs. The company says the new models "show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision," while also communicating more clearly with users. But Anthropic isn't just fighting on features - it's fighting to prove it can execute at scale while burning through unprecedented amounts of capital. Anthropic's IPO filing revealed a staggering $542B data center spending plan, raising eyebrows across Wall Street about whether the company can sustain that level of infrastructure investment. The new model releases give the company something tangible to point to when investors ask what all that money is buying. Just last week, Anthropic dropped $3.4B on gas turbines to power its AI infrastructure, a massive bet on securing energy supplies as data center backlash intensifies. Despite the scale Anthropic is building, the company's compute margins are actually worsening, defying the economies of scale that usually come with growth. That's a red flag for potential investors trying to model when - or if - Anthropic reaches profitability. The company updated its IPO paperwork earlier this month with Q3 financials in an amended S-1 filing, accelerating the timeline toward a public debut. Those numbers will get intense scrutiny, especially as analysts try to figure out whether Anthropic's massive infrastructure bets will pay off or become an anchor. Mythos and Fable represent Anthropic's answer to the fundamental question facing every AI startup right now: can you build a sustainable business, or are you just renting compute at a loss? The models need to be good enough to command premium pricing in an increasingly crowded market where Claude competes head-to-head with ChatGPT for enterprise customers. OpenAI recently launched Dots, transforming its developer tools into an always-on AI companion that directly targets the coding use case Anthropic is now emphasizing with Mythos and Fable. Every capability Anthropic adds, rivals are matching or exceeding within weeks. Anthropic's IPO filing warned investors they're essentially betting on miracles, with the 335-page S-1 prospectus outlining existential risks alongside promises of transformative upside. The new models are part of the proof that the upside is real, not just PowerPoint slides and projections. The company hasn't disclosed pricing for Mythos and Fable yet, or whether they'll slot into Claude's existing tier structure or command premium rates. That pricing decision will signal how confident Anthropic is that the improvements justify higher costs - and whether the company is prioritizing market share or margin expansion as it heads into public markets. What's clear is that Anthropic is trying to build momentum heading into its IPO roadshow. New model releases generate buzz, demonstrate technical progress, and give the sales team fresh ammunition for enterprise deals. Anthropic is playing a high-stakes game, dropping new AI models while sprinting toward an IPO and burning billions on infrastructure. Mythos and Fable need to prove the company can turn massive capital investments into defensible technical advantages, not just keep pace with rivals. The next few weeks will reveal whether investors buy the vision or balk at the burn rate. For now, Anthropic is betting that shipping beats talking - and that these models are good enough to justify the hype and the spending.

sources.title: Anthropic Launches New Fable, Mythos Models Ahead of IPO: Up to 30% Speed Boost Poised to Support Offering Valuation - TradingKey
passages: TradingKey - Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 on November 9, upgrading their coding, reasoning, and vision capabilities while lowering usage prices.

The company stated that output generation speeds for both models are up to 30% faster than the previous generation, with a focus on complex software development, scientific research, and engineering tasks.
Amid upcoming IPO valuation pressures—exacerbated by regulatory concerns over data centers and cooling investor expectations—Anthropic aims to leverage these upgrades to drive enterprise adoption.
Whether these performance gains and cost efficiencies can sufficiently stimulate long-term commercial demand remains a critical factor for investor cash flow evaluations.

According to a Bloomberg report on November 6, the valuation range discussed by potential buyers for Anthropic's IPO has dropped from an earlier $1.4 trillion to $1.5 trillion to between $1.2 trillion and $1.3 trillion.
This reflects a shift in investors' bidding willingness, while the final offering valuation has yet to be determined.
Fable is aimed at a broader user base and retains safeguards in cybersecurity and biological domains, while Mythos is tailored to vetted institutions to support specialized research.
From an IPO pricing perspective, launching a new model at this juncture provides Anthropic with an opportunity to showcase its R&D achievements.

Upgraded capabilities can bolster market confidence in its technological competitiveness, while declining task costs provide justification for expanding practical applications, making revenue growth expectations easier to link to specific business demand.

TradingKey - Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 on November 9, upgrading their coding, reasoning, and vision capabilities while lowering usage prices. The company stated that output generation speeds for both models are up to 30% faster than the previous generation, with a focus on complex software development, scientific research, and engineering tasks. The launch comes as the company prepares for an IPO. Earlier, regulatory concerns regarding data centers triggered a decline in AI stocks, leading prospective investors to lower their valuation expectations for Anthropic. Therefore, whether the new models can expand enterprise adoption and improve return on investment has emerged as another key focal point beyond the product upgrades. Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 share the same underlying model, with the primary differences lying in safety restrictions and eligible users. Fable is aimed at a broader user base and retains safeguards in cybersecurity and biological domains, while Mythos is tailored to vetted institutions to support specialized research. Both models share identical specifications and pricing. Coding is a major focus of this upgrade. According to tests released by Anthropic, Fable 5.2's score on FrontierCode 2.0 increased to 49.1% from 32.4% in the previous generation. The benchmark evaluates whether code modifications submitted by the model are accepted by open-source project maintainers, bringing it closer to real-world development delivery requirements. The company also stated that in this test, Fable 5.2 achieved performance close to Opus 5.5 at maximum reasoning effort while operating at High reasoning effort, with per-task costs roughly half that of the latter. This suggests that for specific tasks, more capable models may reduce the total cost of completing work by cutting processing volume and the number of attempts. Standard pricing for both models is $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. Fable 5.2 is accessible via Claude and major cloud platforms, whereas Mythos requires institutions to undergo vetting. Lower pricing and broader access channels help enterprises integrate the models into existing workflows. The key to commercialization therefore hinges on task efficiency. If complex tasks can be completed with less human intervention, enterprises will have greater incentive to expand paid adoption. For Anthropic, incremental call volume and specialized customer demand are expected to offset the impact of declining unit pricing. Following the U.S. midterm elections, in which Democrats won both houses of Congress and several key governorships, market concerns mounted that data center approvals and construction restrictions would tighten, impacting AI computing power expansion and revenue realization. On November 5, the Nasdaq 100 Index fell 6.4%, with related risks also spilling over to unlisted AI companies. This reflects a shift in investors' bidding willingness, while the final offering valuation has yet to be determined. A decline in valuation expectations means investors are beginning to scrutinize future growth more rigorously: amid massive computing power investments and uncertainty surrounding infrastructure expansion, how much are customers willing to pay for AI, and how much profit can the company retain from it? coreStoryFacts.text: Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) introduced Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 AI models on Monday.
Fable 5.1 cost $10 per million inputs and $50 per million outputs.
While Wall Street was initially targeting upward of a $2 trillion valuation for Anthropic's debut, that could now end up between $1 trillion and $1.5 trillion.
Industry experts say that over time, enterprises will likely rely on a mix of closed-weight models like Anthropic's and open-weight AI models to meet their needs.
The idea is to avoid being locked into a single model vendor, while also being able to reduce overall costs.

Still, Anthropic’s release notes significant ongoing challenges in accurately testing model capabilities. “Claude Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 each voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any of our recent models, which challenges our ability to assess how they will act in real-world settings.
As these settings expand and capabilities increase with future models, we expect this challenge to grow.”
The company says the new models “show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision” and communicate more clearly with users.
Notably, Anthropic is lowering the cost of Fable from $10 to $8 per million input tokens.
Anthropic says that the new version of Fable will return responses 30% faster across effort levels.
Faster inference serving is available for double the price.

It’s Anthropic’s first model release since the arrival of a third-party report from the assessment group METR , which suggested the lab might be approaching recursive self-improvement (RSI) — or the ability for AI models to carry on model training independently.
Also on Monday, AI startup Physical Superintelligence announced a new proof of the Aaronson‑Ambainis conjecture, a pivotal step in setting theoretical limits for quantum computing.
The company announced Mythos and Fable on Monday, claiming improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision capabilities just weeks after filing its IPO paperwork.
Anthropic's IPO filing revealed a staggering $542B data center spending plan, raising eyebrows across Wall Street about whether the company can sustain that level of infrastructure investment.
Anthropic is playing a high-stakes game, dropping new AI models while sprinting toward an IPO and burning billions on infrastructure.
What's clear is that Anthropic is trying to build momentum heading into its IPO roadshow.

The company says the new models “show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision” and communicate more clearly with users. Fable 5.2 is also compatible with zero data retention (ZDR) policies through the Enterprise Frontier Safeguards system , long a sticking point for many enterprise clients. It’s Anthropic’s first model release since the arrival of a third-party report from the assessment group METR , which suggested the lab might be approaching recursive self-improvement (RSI) — or the ability for AI models to carry on model training independently. Still, Anthropic’s release notes significant ongoing challenges in accurately testing model capabilities. “Claude Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 each voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any of our recent models, which challenges our ability to assess how they will act in real-world settings. As these settings expand and capabilities increase with future models, we expect this challenge to grow.” Anthropic maintains that the new version of Mythos does not have the ability to act covertly against its user, a verdict that’s detailed further in Mythos 5.2’s system card . “Claude Mythos 5.2 shows stronger covert capabilities than prior Claude models on several of our evaluations, particularly when its reasoning is hidden from the monitor,” the system card reads. “That said, we believe that low levels of absolute performance on our new covert evaluations support claims that rely on detection of harmful actions in high-stakes situations.” Fable 5.2 has been available to select parties in pre-release for some time, and Anthropic says the model has already “solved two open problems in theoretical physics, formalized Fermat’s Last Theorem, and supported numerous other research projects.” Also on Monday, AI startup Physical Superintelligence announced a new proof of the Aaronson‑Ambainis conjecture, a pivotal step in setting theoretical limits for quantum computing. Notably, the lab said the result was achieved by running “a non-public Anthropic model” within PSI’s own system. Anthropic did not confirm or deny whether Fable 5.2 was the model in question. sources.title: Anthropic Ships Mythos and Fable Models Days Before IPO
passages: The company announced Mythos and Fable on Monday, claiming improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision capabilities just weeks after filing its IPO paperwork.
Anthropic's IPO filing revealed a staggering $542B data center spending plan, raising eyebrows across Wall Street about whether the company can sustain that level of infrastructure investment.
Anthropic is playing a high-stakes game, dropping new AI models while sprinting toward an IPO and burning billions on infrastructure.
What's clear is that Anthropic is trying to build momentum heading into its IPO roadshow.

extraction.body: Anthropic just dropped two new AI models into the wild. The company announced Mythos and Fable on Monday, claiming improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision capabilities just weeks after filing its IPO paperwork. The timing isn't subtle - Anthropic is racing to prove its technical chops while investors scrutinize its S-1 filing and its massive infrastructure spending plans come under the microscope. The AI startup behind Claude just released Mythos and Fable, two new models that the company says deliver sharper performance in coding, reasoning, vision tasks, and user communication. The announcement lands at a critical moment - just weeks after Anthropic filed to go public and started the clock on one of the year's most anticipated tech IPOs. The company says the new models "show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision," while also communicating more clearly with users. But Anthropic isn't just fighting on features - it's fighting to prove it can execute at scale while burning through unprecedented amounts of capital. Anthropic's IPO filing revealed a staggering $542B data center spending plan, raising eyebrows across Wall Street about whether the company can sustain that level of infrastructure investment. The new model releases give the company something tangible to point to when investors ask what all that money is buying. Just last week, Anthropic dropped $3.4B on gas turbines to power its AI infrastructure, a massive bet on securing energy supplies as data center backlash intensifies. Despite the scale Anthropic is building, the company's compute margins are actually worsening, defying the economies of scale that usually come with growth. That's a red flag for potential investors trying to model when - or if - Anthropic reaches profitability. The company updated its IPO paperwork earlier this month with Q3 financials in an amended S-1 filing, accelerating the timeline toward a public debut. Those numbers will get intense scrutiny, especially as analysts try to figure out whether Anthropic's massive infrastructure bets will pay off or become an anchor. Mythos and Fable represent Anthropic's answer to the fundamental question facing every AI startup right now: can you build a sustainable business, or are you just renting compute at a loss? The models need to be good enough to command premium pricing in an increasingly crowded market where Claude competes head-to-head with ChatGPT for enterprise customers. OpenAI recently launched Dots, transforming its developer tools into an always-on AI companion that directly targets the coding use case Anthropic is now emphasizing with Mythos and Fable. Every capability Anthropic adds, rivals are matching or exceeding within weeks. Anthropic's IPO filing warned investors they're essentially betting on miracles, with the 335-page S-1 prospectus outlining existential risks alongside promises of transformative upside. The new models are part of the proof that the upside is real, not just PowerPoint slides and projections. The company hasn't disclosed pricing for Mythos and Fable yet, or whether they'll slot into Claude's existing tier structure or command premium rates. That pricing decision will signal how confident Anthropic is that the improvements justify higher costs - and whether the company is prioritizing market share or margin expansion as it heads into public markets. What's clear is that Anthropic is trying to build momentum heading into its IPO roadshow. New model releases generate buzz, demonstrate technical progress, and give the sales team fresh ammunition for enterprise deals. Anthropic is playing a high-stakes game, dropping new AI models while sprinting toward an IPO and burning billions on infrastructure. Mythos and Fable need to prove the company can turn massive capital investments into defensible technical advantages, not just keep pace with rivals. The next few weeks will reveal whether investors buy the vision or balk at the burn rate. For now, Anthropic is betting that shipping beats talking - and that these models are good enough to justify the hype and the spending.

Amid upcoming IPO valuation pressures—exacerbated by regulatory concerns over data centers and cooling investor expectations—Anthropic aims to leverage these upgrades to drive enterprise adoption.
Whether these performance gains and cost efficiencies can sufficiently stimulate long-term commercial demand remains a critical factor for investor cash flow evaluations.

story.title: Anthropic releases new Mythos and Fable models amid RSI concerns

facts.text: Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) introduced Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 AI models on Monday.
Fable 5.1 cost $10 per million inputs and $50 per million outputs.
While Wall Street was initially targeting upward of a $2 trillion valuation for Anthropic's debut, that could now end up between $1 trillion and $1.5 trillion.
Industry experts say that over time, enterprises will likely rely on a mix of closed-weight models like Anthropic's and open-weight AI models to meet their needs.
The idea is to avoid being locked into a single model vendor, while also being able to reduce overall costs.

Still, Anthropic’s release notes significant ongoing challenges in accurately testing model capabilities. “Claude Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 each voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any of our recent models, which challenges our ability to assess how they will act in real-world settings.
As these settings expand and capabilities increase with future models, we expect this challenge to grow.”
The company says the new models “show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision” and communicate more clearly with users.
Notably, Anthropic is lowering the cost of Fable from $10 to $8 per million input tokens.
Anthropic says that the new version of Fable will return responses 30% faster across effort levels.
Faster inference serving is available for double the price.
Also on Monday, AI startup Physical Superintelligence announced a new proof of the Aaronson‑Ambainis conjecture, a pivotal step in setting theoretical limits for quantum computing.
The company announced Mythos and Fable on Monday, claiming improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision capabilities just weeks after filing its IPO paperwork.
Anthropic's IPO filing revealed a staggering $542B data center spending plan, raising eyebrows across Wall Street about whether the company can sustain that level of infrastructure investment.
Anthropic is playing a high-stakes game, dropping new AI models while sprinting toward an IPO and burning billions on infrastructure.
What's clear is that Anthropic is trying to build momentum heading into its IPO roadshow.

extraction.body: Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation? One of the Artificial Intelligence (AI) industry's most important figures has been accused of having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, prompting an investigation. US intelligence officials believed that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who had a close relationship with Nvidia CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang, was a spy for Beijing , according to a New York Times report. On Sunday, Huang admitted , external to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. US tech giant Nvidia, one of the most valuable companies in the world, has opened an independent investigation into the reports. The firm said it does not believe US national security had been compromised - and added that Huang was committed to continuing to lead the company. President Donald Trump said on Monday that the FBI is also investigating the affair . The FBI declined to comment further when contacted by the BBC. Trump said he spoke with Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign. "I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters. Here is what we know about the affair and why it matters. Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond US officials believed that Alice Huang had been recruited to spy by China's top intelligence agency, the New York Times reported , external . Her current whereabouts are unknown. Alice Huang, who is of no relation to Jensen Huang, was a top executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed between March and November 2023. The firm had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia maintains was investigated and debunked. However, the BBC understands Megaspeed is under investigation by the Singapore government regarding previous allegations that the company was circumventing US sanctions on the export of Nvidia's high-end chips. The BBC has contacted Megaspeed for comment. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters on Monday at a regular daily press briefing: "We have already responded to this. The allegations about Chinese spies are entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China." The New York Times reported in late October that Trump had been briefed last year on intelligence alleging Alice Huang was spying on China's behalf. Asked by reporters on Sunday whether he wished he had "acted on the intelligence", Trump responded: "No, I don't think so. I think he's an honourable guy." US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, refused to comment when asked about Huang. Last spring, the secretary of state reportedly oversaw the drafting of a memo that warned the Trump administration about Huang's relationship with the Chinese businesswoman, according to the New York Times. Nvidia shares slide as US tech giant investigates CEO's affair with suspected Chinese spy Why Trump is all-in on AI despite the warnings Nvidia is at the heart of US and China's AI race , which is why the billionaire's affair has sparked national security fears among American lawmakers. Trump has said "whoever wins AI wins", and the fear is that if China gains the upper hand in AI, it will supercharge the country's military and surveillance capabilities. The US advantage is in large part because of US companies like Nvidia, working with producers like the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which makes more than 90% of the world's most advanced chips. Since 2022, the US has used various export controls to keep the top tech out of China, which it says helps retain America's competitive edge and protects its national security. This means companies like Nvidia have been largely locked out of the world's most lucrative market, with Huang once saying that Nvidia's share of the Chinese market had gone from around 95% to effectively zero. Huang has engaged in shuttle diplomacy between Washington and Beijing, hoping to find a US-approved way back in, and shaping US policy on China along the way. Sunday's revelations may explain why Huang has failed to bring home the biggest prize of all to Nvidia: the Trump administration's blessing to sell all but its most advanced chips to China . Huang has soared to international importance with his company Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang was nine years old when his family moved to the West Coast of the US. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a master's degree in the same field from Stanford University. His children, Spencer and Madison, and son-in-law Nico Caprez work at Nvidia in senior roles. Lori Huang accompanied her husband at the state dinner held by President Donald Trump for his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping in September Huang met his future wife Lori Mills at Oregon State University while studying electrical engineering in the early 1980s. passages: Here are Trump’s responses to questions about Jensen Huang from his press briefing today.

In October, The New York Times reported that Trump had been briefed “roughly a year ago” on intelligence that Huang and the alleged spy, Alice Huang, had developed a close relationship, but he didn’t do anything with the information.
I think that he’ll be in good shape. > … > Are you going to bring up the case of Jensen Huang with President Xi when you visit with him next week? > No, I don’t think so.
And I really believe him. > … > I want to put a finer point on when exactly you were made aware of the intelligence around Jensen Huang. > Oh, I’d have to check.
But Trump said Huang told him today that he had “no idea” the person was a spy.
Yesterday, the NYT reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio helped draft a memo to Trump officials about the relationship before Trump visited China in May.
In the press conference, Trump wasn’t specific about when he learned of the affair.

extraction.body: President Trump held a White House press briefing earlier today and responded to several questions about his knowledge of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Huang said this weekend that he had been “​​unfaithful” to his wife, and the company has opened an investigation into Huang. Recent articles from The New York Times indicated that Trump had been aware of a relationship between Huang and Alice Huang, the suspected spy, before information about it became public. In October, The New York Times reported that Trump had been briefed “roughly a year ago” on intelligence that Huang and the alleged spy, Alice Huang, had developed a close relationship, but he didn’t do anything with the information. Yesterday, the NYT reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio helped draft a memo to Trump officials about the relationship before Trump visited China in May. In the press conference, Trump wasn’t specific about when he learned of the affair. But Trump said Huang told him today that he had “no idea” the person was a spy. Here are Trump’s responses to questions about Jensen Huang from his press briefing today. You can watch a replay of the press conference on MS Now’s YouTube channel. > When were you first informed that there was an issue with Jensen Huang and the affair? What was presented to you at the time? > I would say that when I heard about it, first of all, I was amazed because I view him as a very high-quality person. When you think about it, you’ve got a chip that’s 10 years advanced, can’t be… the Blackwell can’t even be copied. If there is a problem, we’ll let you know about it. But he is definitely suffering. > Just to follow up on the, “When were you first told of these potential issues with Mr. Huang?” You didn’t answer that question. > Well I’ve been hearing about it, and I’ve been reading a little bit about it over a period of time. I think that he’ll be in good shape. > … > Are you going to bring up the case of Jensen Huang with President Xi when you visit with him next week? > No, I don’t think so. Maybe, I’m sure, President Xi will ask me about it. I feel very confident that he’ll be in good shape. > Sticking with Jensen Huang, when you went to China earlier this year in May, did you know about these alleged ties to the spy then? > No, I didn’t hear about it then. I asked him today, because I did speak to him today just to see if he’s feeling alright, how are you doing… and I asked him about that. He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy. And I really believe him. > … > I want to put a finer point on when exactly you were made aware of the intelligence around Jensen Huang. > Oh, I’d have to check. Did you read that memo? > I’d certainly check with the intelligence people.

extraction.body: Nvidia’s board of directors said Sunday that it is opening an independent investigation after CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. The announcement followed recent reporting by The New York Times and the Financial Times about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who the newspapers reported had been recruited to spy for China. A person familiar with the matter told NBC News late Sunday that U.S. intelligence agencies had determined that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy and had a relationship with Nvidia’s Jensen Huang. “The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort,” the company said in a statement. “A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation. The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders.” The company added that while it “has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information.” In a memo to Nvidia employees that the company shared with NBC News, Huang said: “I was unfaithful to my wife. There is no excuse for what I did.” The New York Times and the Financial Times reported that Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen whose Singapore-based company was buying Nvidia’s advanced chips, had been under surveillance by U.S. intelligence agencies. Those agencies, the reports said, found that she had been recruited to spy by China’s top intelligence agency. Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Monday that “the so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China.” Jensen Huang and Nvidia, for years, have been at the forefront of the artificial intelligence boom. Nvidia’s products are the most highly sought-after chips in the world; however its top-tier products are mostly restricted from being sold to customers in China because of national security fears. Huang, 63, essentially serves as an ambassador for the industry, regularly appearing alongside the likes of President Donald Trump and King Charles III of Great Britain and at conferences to tout his company and what he says will be immense payoff in the future from AI. In October, Trump awarded Huang the National Medal of Science, one of the nation’s highest honors for achievement in science and technology. Nvidia is the world’s second-largest publicly traded company as of Friday, worth nearly $4.5 trillion. Nvidia shares fell more than 4% , erasing almost $200 billion in value. But the drop did not immediately spill over into other major tech stocks or to Nvidia’s peers, all of which appeared largely unaffected. The broader stock market, as tracked by the S&P 500 and Nasdaq, were sharply higher for the day. “Given Huang’s central role in Nvidia’s success and the wider AI investment narrative, even speculation about leadership uncertainty could unsettle investors,” wrote Capital.com senior market analyst Daniela Hathorn in a note. Huang’s wealth has also ballooned as he has led the company. His net worth has soared from around $25 billion at the start of 2022 to almost $160 billion, making him the world’s 10th-richest person, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. In the latest series of reports, published Sunday afternoon, The New York Times reported that concerns inside the U.S. government about Alice Huang and Jensen Huang rose as high as Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Speaking Sunday to reporters in Florida shortly after Nvidia’s announcement, Rubio said, “I just can’t comment because of the nature of it, and I also can’t comment on an internal corporate matter that’s going on with Nvidia.” A short time later, Trump gave Huang his complete support, telling reporters that he thinks Huang is a “fine person” who should remain CEO of Nvidia. “I think he’s an honorable guy,” the president said. “He’s done an amazing job for our country,” Trump added, while touting recent stock market gains. The president also said he would support bringing Huang on his upcoming trip through Asia. Asked by reporters if Trump wished that he had acted on intelligence about Alice Huang, he said, “no, I don’t think so.” On Friday, the FT reported that the U.S. government believed Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang. In response to the article, the FT reported that Nvidia declined to comment and said Jensen Huang meets “thousands of customer executives every year,” as any CEO normally does. Huang previously defended his interactions with Alice Huang, describing them as business-related in a recent statement: “Our relationship, our interactions, have been related to Megaspeed, and it was all completely normal and not unusual.” In Sunday’s memo, Huang wrote: “To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust.” The email to employees continued: “To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence.” A spokesperson for Nvidia told NBC News that “today’s news will not slow” the company and that Huang is “committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption.” Before Sunday’s announcement, Nvidia and Huang were already facing congressional scrutiny over the reports about Megaspeed and its executive. On Thursday, top House Republicans requested a briefing from Huang about the reports. “Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC’s access to sensitive U.S. technology and information,” said Rep. “It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk,” a letter to Nvidia read.

History says the board’s verdict matters more than the first day: in three cases where a board reviewed a chief executive’s personal conduct and the executive left, the shares fell the next trading day every time, by 2.4% to 10.1%, and sat below their starting price six months later; the one time a board looked at its founder and kept him, the stock rose 4.9% that day. Nvidia’s board said Sunday at 2:59 PM ET that it is opening an independent investigation into reports that Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. The same statement says the board has confidence in Huang and that he is cooperating. An independent investigation of the founder who runs a company reads as a warning about key-person risk, the one risk Nvidia’s rise never asked you to price; the limit is that the board says it has confidence in Huang, he is cooperating, and the precedent where the board kept its founder is the one where the stock went up. The board’s statement, released through GlobeNewswire, says it “is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.” A committee of independent directors with outside counsel will oversee it. The board “has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised,” that “Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it,” and that it “has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team.” It sets no date. In a letter to employees obtained by Axios and published in full by Bloomberg, Huang wrote: “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did.” He wrote that he takes full responsibility and will cooperate fully. Bloomberg and Axios reported that the relationship was with a woman U.S. intelligence officials suspected of working for a Chinese spy agency. Nothing in the record says what the committee will find. Intel, June 2018. Intel said before the open on June 21, 2018 that Brian Krzanich had resigned after an investigation by internal and external counsel confirmed a past consensual relationship with an employee violated its non-fraternization policy. From the prior close of $53.46, Intel fell 2.4% on day 1, 8.8% after a week, 2.9% after a month and 14.8% after six months. The S&P 500, measured by the SPY fund, did -0.6%, -2.4%, +1.3% and -10.4% over the same windows, so Intel trailed it by 4.4 points at six months. McDonald’s, November 2019. extraction.body: Nvidia’s board of directors said Sunday that it is opening an independent investigation after CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. The announcement followed recent reporting by The New York Times and the Financial Times about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who the newspapers reported had been recruited to spy for China. A person familiar with the matter told NBC News late Sunday that U.S. intelligence agencies had determined that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy and had a relationship with Nvidia’s Jensen Huang. “The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort,” the company said in a statement. “A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation. The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders.” The company added that while it “has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information.” In a memo to Nvidia employees that the company shared with NBC News, Huang said: “I was unfaithful to my wife. There is no excuse for what I did.” The New York Times and the Financial Times reported that Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen whose Singapore-based company was buying Nvidia’s advanced chips, had been under surveillance by U.S. intelligence agencies. Those agencies, the reports said, found that she had been recruited to spy by China’s top intelligence agency. Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Monday that “the so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China.” Jensen Huang and Nvidia, for years, have been at the forefront of the artificial intelligence boom. Nvidia’s products are the most highly sought-after chips in the world; however its top-tier products are mostly restricted from being sold to customers in China because of national security fears. Huang, 63, essentially serves as an ambassador for the industry, regularly appearing alongside the likes of President Donald Trump and King Charles III of Great Britain and at conferences to tout his company and what he says will be immense payoff in the future from AI. In October, Trump awarded Huang the National Medal of Science, one of the nation’s highest honors for achievement in science and technology. Nvidia is the world’s second-largest publicly traded company as of Friday, worth nearly $4.5 trillion. Nvidia shares fell more than 4% , erasing almost $200 billion in value. But the drop did not immediately spill over into other major tech stocks or to Nvidia’s peers, all of which appeared largely unaffected. The broader stock market, as tracked by the S&P 500 and Nasdaq, were sharply higher for the day. “Given Huang’s central role in Nvidia’s success and the wider AI investment narrative, even speculation about leadership uncertainty could unsettle investors,” wrote Capital.com senior market analyst Daniela Hathorn in a note. Huang’s wealth has also ballooned as he has led the company. His net worth has soared from around $25 billion at the start of 2022 to almost $160 billion, making him the world’s 10th-richest person, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. In the latest series of reports, published Sunday afternoon, The New York Times reported that concerns inside the U.S. government about Alice Huang and Jensen Huang rose as high as Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Speaking Sunday to reporters in Florida shortly after Nvidia’s announcement, Rubio said, “I just can’t comment because of the nature of it, and I also can’t comment on an internal corporate matter that’s going on with Nvidia.” A short time later, Trump gave Huang his complete support, telling reporters that he thinks Huang is a “fine person” who should remain CEO of Nvidia. “I think he’s an honorable guy,” the president said. “He’s done an amazing job for our country,” Trump added, while touting recent stock market gains. The president also said he would support bringing Huang on his upcoming trip through Asia. Asked by reporters if Trump wished that he had acted on intelligence about Alice Huang, he said, “no, I don’t think so.” On Friday, the FT reported that the U.S. government believed Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang. In response to the article, the FT reported that Nvidia declined to comment and said Jensen Huang meets “thousands of customer executives every year,” as any CEO normally does. Huang previously defended his interactions with Alice Huang, describing them as business-related in a recent statement: “Our relationship, our interactions, have been related to Megaspeed, and it was all completely normal and not unusual.” In Sunday’s memo, Huang wrote: “To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust.” The email to employees continued: “To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence.” A spokesperson for Nvidia told NBC News that “today’s news will not slow” the company and that Huang is “committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption.” Before Sunday’s announcement, Nvidia and Huang were already facing congressional scrutiny over the reports about Megaspeed and its executive. On Thursday, top House Republicans requested a briefing from Huang about the reports. “Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC’s access to sensitive U.S. technology and information,” said Rep. “It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk,” a letter to Nvidia read.

History says the board’s verdict matters more than the first day: in three cases where a board reviewed a chief executive’s personal conduct and the executive left, the shares fell the next trading day every time, by 2.4% to 10.1%, and sat below their starting price six months later; the one time a board looked at its founder and kept him, the stock rose 4.9% that day. Nvidia’s board said Sunday at 2:59 PM ET that it is opening an independent investigation into reports that Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. The same statement says the board has confidence in Huang and that he is cooperating. An independent investigation of the founder who runs a company reads as a warning about key-person risk, the one risk Nvidia’s rise never asked you to price; the limit is that the board says it has confidence in Huang, he is cooperating, and the precedent where the board kept its founder is the one where the stock went up. The board’s statement, released through GlobeNewswire, says it “is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.” A committee of independent directors with outside counsel will oversee it. The board “has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised,” that “Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it,” and that it “has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team.” It sets no date. In a letter to employees obtained by Axios and published in full by Bloomberg, Huang wrote: “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did.” He wrote that he takes full responsibility and will cooperate fully. Bloomberg and Axios reported that the relationship was with a woman U.S. intelligence officials suspected of working for a Chinese spy agency. Nothing in the record says what the committee will find. Intel, June 2018. Intel said before the open on June 21, 2018 that Brian Krzanich had resigned after an investigation by internal and external counsel confirmed a past consensual relationship with an employee violated its non-fraternization policy. From the prior close of $53.46, Intel fell 2.4% on day 1, 8.8% after a week, 2.9% after a month and 14.8% after six months. The S&P 500, measured by the SPY fund, did -0.6%, -2.4%, +1.3% and -10.4% over the same windows, so Intel trailed it by 4.4 points at six months. McDonald’s, November 2019. The board voted on Friday, Nov. 1, 2019 and said on Sunday, Nov. 3 that Steve Easterbrook had been separated from the company over a consensual relationship with an employee that violated policy. Anthropic has launched Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, introducing upgrades in software development, reasoning and visual understanding alongside lower API prices and faster response generation. Announced on Monday, November 9, the new models represent the latest versions of Anthropic’s flagship AI systems. According to the company, they can generate output up to 30% faster than the previous Fable 5.1 model and deliver stronger results across several technical benchmarks. The launch also introduces a revised pricing structure that makes the models less expensive to use than their predecessors. Anthropic has reduced the standard API pricing for both models to $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. The previous Fable 5.1 pricing was $10 and $50, respectively. The company has also introduced an optional Fast mode, designed to increase token generation speeds by up to 2.5 times. Fast mode costs $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens. Fable 5.2 is available through the Claude API, Claude Code, Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure. Mythos 5.2, however, has restricted availability. Anthropic is limiting access to organisations participating in its Cyber and Life Sciences verification programmes. Anthropic’s latest AI models, Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, promise faster responses, improved coding capabilities and lower API pricing. With a reported 49.1% score on FrontierCode 2.0, the launch marks a significant update in AI-powered software development. Read the full report for pricing details, benchmark comparisons and new features. Anthropic says Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 share the same underlying model architecture. Their primary difference lies in access restrictions and safety policies. Fable 5.2 includes cybersecurity and biological safety safeguards and is available to regular customers. Mythos 5.2 is intended for organisations working in sensitive dual-use research areas and is accessible only through Anthropic’s verification programmes. The company continues to recommend Claude Opus 5.5 for most everyday coding and knowledge-work requirements. Fable 5.2 is positioned for more demanding, open-ended technical tasks. Both versions support a context window of up to one million tokens and can generate up to 128,000 output tokens. Anthropic reports that Fable 5.2 has achieved its strongest results so far on several internal evaluation benchmarks, particularly those measuring software engineering capabilities. On FrontierCode 2.0, Fable 5.2 recorded a score of 49.1%, compared with 45.5% for Opus 5.5, 42.8% for OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, 41.1% for Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon and 32.4% for Fable 5.1. The model also recorded 69.9% on FrontierSWE v2, 41.3% on the Remote Labor Index and 64.9% on RoboDojo Sim. However, the results do not show Anthropic leading every evaluation. Gemini 4 Carbon scored 53.9% on AutomationBench, ahead of Fable 5.2’s 51.4%. Opus 5.5 also retained a slight advantage on the AA-Briefcase knowledge-work evaluation. Anthropic said Fable 5.2 operating at High effort matched the best FrontierCode performance of Opus 5.5 at approximately half the cost per task. Separately, Cursor reported scores of 56.9% at default effort and 60% at maximum effort on its CursorBench evaluation after adding Fable 5.2 to its platform. The benchmark figures cited here come from company-reported evaluations and should not be treated as independent comparisons. Anthropic has also shared several examples from its internal testing to demonstrate the capabilities of the new models. The company said Fable 5.2 helped engineers complete software migrations that had previously been considered impractical. Its testing also included designing three electronic devices, investigating two open problems involving black-hole physics and formalising a proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem. According to Anthropic, the Fermat’s Last Theorem exercise involved a team of approximately 1,000 AI agents and took 30 hours. The company compared this with an earlier research effort that required 11 days, specialised tooling and human guidance. Anthropic further reported that more than 90% of changes merged into its core codebase are now written by Claude with human guidance. In another engineering exercise, a team of AI agents migrated a critical production service from Python to Rust. Anthropic said the resulting service started approximately 26 times faster. One particularly extensive experiment involved asking Fable 5.2 to build an operating system from an empty directory. The model coordinated more than 1,000 subagents over eight days to produce a system capable of booting on a laptop. The resulting prototype reportedly included its own kernel, drivers, file storage, window management, login screen and installer. Alongside performance upgrades, Anthropic says it has improved the way Fable 5.2 handles cybersecurity and biological safety restrictions. The company claims that the new safeguards maintain the protection levels of Fable 5.1 while reducing unnecessary refusals by approximately 55% during early testing across Claude.ai, Claude Code and Cowork. Developers upgrading from Fable 5.1 will also need to account for four breaking changes outlined in Anthropic’s migration documentation. These include account-level prefix checks, changes to the compatibility of thinking blocks, retirement of the computer_20251124 tool and updated advisor pairing rules. The release of Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 reflects Anthropic’s continued focus on improving the capabilities of AI systems for complex software engineering and technical research. Lower standard pricing could make the models more accessible to developers and organisations that rely on large-scale API usage. Meanwhile, the restricted Mythos programme highlights the company’s approach to managing access to AI systems with advanced capabilities in sensitive research areas. Although Anthropic’s reported benchmark results show substantial improvements in several coding evaluations, independent testing will be important in establishing how the models compare with competing systems in everyday development environments. For developers already using Claude, the combination of faster generation, increased context capacity and revised pricing makes Fable 5.2 a significant update to consider. Anthropic has reduced the standard API pricing for both models to $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. The previous Fable 5.1 pricing was $10 and $50, respectively. The company has also introduced an optional Fast mode, designed to increase token generation speeds by up to 2.5 times. Fast mode costs $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens. Anthropic’s latest AI models, Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, promise faster responses, improved coding capabilities and lower API pricing. With a reported 49.1% score on FrontierCode 2.0, the launch marks a significant update in AI-powered software development. Read the full report for pricing details, benchmark comparisons and new features. Anthropic says Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 share the same underlying model architecture. Their primary difference lies in access restrictions and safety policies. Fable 5.2 includes cybersecurity and biological safety safeguards and is available to regular customers. Mythos 5.2 is intended for organisations working in sensitive dual-use research areas and is accessible only through Anthropic’s verification programmes. The company continues to recommend Claude Opus 5.5 for most everyday coding and knowledge-work requirements. Fable 5.2 is positioned for more demanding, open-ended technical tasks. Both versions support a context window of up to one million tokens and can generate up to 128,000 output tokens. Anthropic reports that Fable 5.2 has achieved its strongest results so far on several internal evaluation benchmarks, particularly those measuring software engineering capabilities. On FrontierCode 2.0, Fable 5.2 recorded a score of 49.1%, compared with 45.5% for Opus 5.5, 42.8% for OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, 41.1% for Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon and 32.4% for Fable 5.1. The model also recorded 69.9% on FrontierSWE v2, 41.3% on the Remote Labor Index and 64.9% on RoboDojo Sim. However, the results do not show Anthropic leading every evaluation. Gemini 4 Carbon scored 53.9% on AutomationBench, ahead of Fable 5.2’s 51.4%. Opus 5.5 also retained a slight advantage on the AA-Briefcase knowledge-work evaluation. Anthropic said Fable 5.2 operating at High effort matched the best FrontierCode performance of Opus 5.5 at approximately half the cost per task. Separately, Cursor reported scores of 56.9% at default effort and 60% at maximum effort on its CursorBench evaluation after adding Fable 5.2 to its platform. The benchmark figures cited here come from company-reported evaluations and should not be treated as independent comparisons. Anthropic has also shared several examples from its internal testing to demonstrate the capabilities of the new models. The company said Fable 5.2 helped engineers complete software migrations that had previously been considered impractical. Its testing also included designing three electronic devices, investigating two open problems involving black-hole physics and formalising a proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem. According to Anthropic, the Fermat’s Last Theorem exercise involved a team of approximately 1,000 AI agents and took 30 hours. The company compared this with an earlier research effort that required 11 days, specialised tooling and human guidance. Anthropic further reported that more than 90% of changes merged into its core codebase are now written by Claude with human guidance. In another engineering exercise, a team of AI agents migrated a critical production service from Python to Rust. Anthropic said the resulting service started approximately 26 times faster. One particularly extensive experiment involved asking Fable 5.2 to build an operating system from an empty directory. The model coordinated more than 1,000 subagents over eight days to produce a system capable of booting on a laptop. The resulting prototype reportedly included its own kernel, drivers, file storage, window management, login screen and installer. Alongside performance upgrades, Anthropic says it has improved the way Fable 5.2 handles cybersecurity and biological safety restrictions. The company claims that the new safeguards maintain the protection levels of Fable 5.1 while reducing unnecessary refusals by approximately 55% during early testing across Claude.ai, Claude Code and Cowork. Developers upgrading from Fable 5.1 will also need to account for four breaking changes outlined in Anthropic’s migration documentation. These include account-level prefix checks, changes to the compatibility of thinking blocks, retirement of the computer_20251124 tool and updated advisor pairing rules. The release of Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 reflects Anthropic’s continued focus on improving the capabilities of AI systems for complex software engineering and technical research. Lower standard pricing could make the models more accessible to developers and organisations that rely on large-scale API usage. Meanwhile, the restricted Mythos programme highlights the company’s approach to managing access to AI systems with advanced capabilities in sensitive research areas. Although Anthropic’s reported benchmark results show substantial improvements in several coding evaluations, independent testing will be important in establishing how the models compare with competing systems in everyday development environments. The announcement followed recent reporting by The New York Times and the Financial Times about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who the newspapers reported had been recruited to spy for China. A person familiar with the matter told NBC News late Sunday that U.S. intelligence agencies had determined that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy and had a relationship with Nvidia’s Jensen Huang. “The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort,” the company said in a statement. “A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation. The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders.” The company added that while it “has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information.” In a memo to Nvidia employees that the company shared with NBC News, Huang said: “I was unfaithful to my wife. There is no excuse for what I did.” The New York Times and the Financial Times reported that Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen whose Singapore-based company was buying Nvidia’s advanced chips, had been under surveillance by U.S. intelligence agencies. Those agencies, the reports said, found that she had been recruited to spy by China’s top intelligence agency. Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Monday that “the so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China.” Jensen Huang and Nvidia, for years, have been at the forefront of the artificial intelligence boom. Nvidia’s products are the most highly sought-after chips in the world; however its top-tier products are mostly restricted from being sold to customers in China because of national security fears. Huang, 63, essentially serves as an ambassador for the industry, regularly appearing alongside the likes of President Donald Trump and King Charles III of Great Britain and at conferences to tout his company and what he says will be immense payoff in the future from AI. In October, Trump awarded Huang the National Medal of Science, one of the nation’s highest honors for achievement in science and technology. Nvidia is the world’s second-largest publicly traded company as of Friday, worth nearly $4.5 trillion. Nvidia shares fell more than 4% , erasing almost $200 billion in value. But the drop did not immediately spill over into other major tech stocks or to Nvidia’s peers, all of which appeared largely unaffected. The broader stock market, as tracked by the S&P 500 and Nasdaq, were sharply higher for the day. “Given Huang’s central role in Nvidia’s success and the wider AI investment narrative, even speculation about leadership uncertainty could unsettle investors,” wrote Capital.com senior market analyst Daniela Hathorn in a note. Huang’s wealth has also ballooned as he has led the company. His net worth has soared from around $25 billion at the start of 2022 to almost $160 billion, making him the world’s 10th-richest person, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. In the latest series of reports, published Sunday afternoon, The New York Times reported that concerns inside the U.S. government about Alice Huang and Jensen Huang rose as high as Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Speaking Sunday to reporters in Florida shortly after Nvidia’s announcement, Rubio said, “I just can’t comment because of the nature of it, and I also can’t comment on an internal corporate matter that’s going on with Nvidia.” A short time later, Trump gave Huang his complete support, telling reporters that he thinks Huang is a “fine person” who should remain CEO of Nvidia. “I think he’s an honorable guy,” the president said. “He’s done an amazing job for our country,” Trump added, while touting recent stock market gains. The president also said he would support bringing Huang on his upcoming trip through Asia. Asked by reporters if Trump wished that he had acted on intelligence about Alice Huang, he said, “no, I don’t think so.” On Friday, the FT reported that the U.S. government believed Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang. In response to the article, the FT reported that Nvidia declined to comment and said Jensen Huang meets “thousands of customer executives every year,” as any CEO normally does. Huang previously defended his interactions with Alice Huang, describing them as business-related in a recent statement: “Our relationship, our interactions, have been related to Megaspeed, and it was all completely normal and not unusual.” In Sunday’s memo, Huang wrote: “To my wife and family: I love you. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust.” The email to employees continued: “To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence.” A spokesperson for Nvidia told NBC News that “today’s news will not slow” the company and that Huang is “committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption.” Before Sunday’s announcement, Nvidia and Huang were already facing congressional scrutiny over the reports about Megaspeed and its executive. On Thursday, top House Republicans requested a briefing from Huang about the reports. “Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC’s access to sensitive U.S. technology and information,” said Rep. “It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk,” a letter to Nvidia read.

"There is clearly risk that Jensen could be removed as CEO depending on the Board investigation, and this will add risk to the stock as he is so important to the Nvidia story and strategy globally.

Nvidia's ( NVDA ) board is launching an independent investigation into reports that a woman CEO Jensen Huang was having an affair with was allegedly spying on him for the Chinese government. Nvidia stock fell 5% before the bell on Monday. In an email to employees Sunday, Huang admitted to having an extramarital affair. "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," Huang wrote. "To my colleagues at Nvidia, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me. Leading Nvidia is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to Nvidia and will work to earn back your confidence," the CEO added. In a statement Sunday, the board said it "a committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation" into the matter. "While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," the board said in a statement. The revelations come after reports of ties between Huang and a woman believed to be passing information to the Chinese government. Last month, the New York Times reported the US intelligence service believed a Chinese national named Alice Huang, a former leader at Megaspeed, an Nvidia chip customer, and someone with a well-documented relationship with Huang himself, may have acted as an intelligence asset , sharing information with the ruling party in Beijing. Yorkville Ives partner and senior managing director Dan Ives wrote in a note to investors on Sunday that the investigation is a "black eye" for Huang and will likely spark multiple congressional investigations. "The key question investors will be asking is: Will Jensen remain CEO of Nvidia?…. The investigation will be key, and we would expect Jensen to continue in his role as CEO with no interruption in the near-term," Ives wrote. "There is clearly risk that Jensen could be removed as CEO depending on the Board investigation, and this will add risk to the stock as he is so important to the Nvidia story and strategy globally. This will also increase major scrutiny regarding selling chips to China, which remains a key battleground issue in DC," he added. The US government banned the sale of Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China, though the company has lobbied to continue offering the hardware, arguing that it is better for the world to use processors from a US company. extraction.body: Nvidia has opened an investigation into co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a businesswoman who intelligence agencies say is a Chinese spy. U.S. intelligence agencies have expressed concerns that the woman, Alice Huang, who is affiliated with a cloud company and an Nvidia customer called Megaspeed, has been passing information to Beijing, according to reports in The New York Times and the Financial Times. Huang told Nvidia staff in an email on Sunday that he had an affair with the woman and that Nvidia's board of directors had opened an independent investigation into the spying allegations. "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did," Huang wrote in the message. "I am deeply sorry." An Nvidia spokesperson said that Huang was committed to continuing as CEO of Nvidia without interruption. In a statement, the Nvidia board said it would investigate the allegations that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. "While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," Nvidia's board said in a statement. Read Huang's email to Nvidia employees and the company board of directors' statement here . The allegations come as Nvidia has become the center of a trade dispute between China and the U.S. as AI is seen as increasingly critical to national security. The U.S. restricts exports of Nvidia's most advanced AI chips to China, though it has approved exports of certain older, slower models. Megaspeed, which Ms. Huang is affiliated with, has been accused of helping restricted Chinese companies acquire Nvidia AI chips. Nvidia representatives previously said that Megaspeed had already been investigated for evading export controls. Nvidia's Huang has pushed for broader AI chip exports to China, saying it is better for the U.S. if the world uses and builds on American technology. He has also aligned with President Donald Trump on American artificial intelligence policy and its infrastructure buildout. In his note to staff, Huang said he was "proud and grateful" to be an American. Three House Republican committee chairs sent a letter to Huang on Wednesday asking him to sit for a closed-door briefing with lawmakers on Nov. 18.
