passages: When Laura Beth moved to Coweta County, Ga., in 2023, she was drawn to her new home’s rural location––it was far from any major roads or highways and had sprawling open land behind it.

“Our last home, the surrounding area was becoming very overdeveloped. We had a distribution center less than a mile from our house, and it was just kind of this urban encroachment,” she says. “We knew about the land behind us, and [thought] the worst thing it could be was a subdivision, because who in their right mind would want to build anything out here?”

Then, at the start of 2025, she saw an article announcing that a new data center would be coming to her hometown. As she read it, a realization dawned on her. A hyperscale data center , spanning more than 4.9 million sq. ft., had been proposed—and was expected to run right through her backyard.

“I didn't know who to reach out to, who to talk to, who could give me some more information,” she says. So she decided to start a Facebook group called “Stop Project Sail” to connect with her neighbors and discuss the proposed plan. More than 8,000 people have now joined the group, and have been organizing petition signings, installing yard signs, and mounting a legal fight against Coweta County and Atlas Development, the company behind the project.

“The Board’s responsibility is to serve the entire community, thoughtfully considering all feedback as decisions are weighed that affect Coweta County's more than 160,000 residents and its long-term future.The Board values the principles of democracy and recognizes the importance of our citizens speaking up on all issues that affect our County,” Coweta County Administrator Michael Fouts said in a statement to TIME. “The Board ultimately voted in favor, 3-2, of Project Sail, with those who approved stating its long-term financial benefits it will provide to Coweta County.” Atlas Development did not respond to TIME’s request for comment ahead of publication.

The Georgia town is not alone. If there’s one thing most Americans across the country agree on, it’s that they hate data centers. A June Reuters poll found that just a third of Americans approve of the pace of data-center construction, and only 14% are comfortable with a data center being built nearby. On July 18, a national day of protest against data centers saw 142 protests across 42 states.

According to one count by The Information , more than 300 cities, towns, and counties—including Monterey Park, Calif., Dekalb County, Ga., and Jefferson County, Pa.—have placed bans or moratoriums on the construction of hyperscale data centers. In the first three months of 2026, 75 major projects worth more than $130 billion were delayed or canceled in part due to organized local opposition. And on July 14, New York governor Kathy Hochul signed an executive order to create the nation's first moratorium on new hyperscale data centers, while several other states, including Pennsylvania, Michigan, and South Carolina are considering similar pauses.

Data centers have long been used to store and process our digital information—whether that be photos in the cloud or the videos we stream online. But the rise of hyperscale data centers in recent years—which are higher performing and often used to power AI—began to change things.

“We've been aware of data center development as early as 2010, but they were much smaller in scale,” says John Farner, executive director of land and water at the Lincoln Institute of Land Policy, a non-profit which has been researching the land and water use of data centers over the last few years. “What we're seeing now, especially with the advent of hyperscale data centers, is that they're much larger, much more powerful. They're much more resource intensive.”

More than 160 new AI data centers have popped up across the U.S. in the past three years—a 70% increase from the last three year period, according to a Bloomberg News analysis . In many instances, they’ve landed in communities with high competition for scarce water resources. A mid-sized data center consumes as much water as a small town , while larger ones require up to 5 million gallons of water every day—as much as a city of 50,000 people. They also consume massive amounts of electricity. Data centers accounted for 4% of total U.S. electricity use in 2024 , and their energy demand is expected to more than double by 2030. In many cases, the additional electricity costs are passed on to nearby residents; in states with a high concentration of data centers electricity prices have increased by up to 267% over the last five years.

Steve Swope, another Coweta County resident, relies on wellwater, and is concerned that the construction of the data center could damage septic tanks or leak into the groundwater. “Our wells will either run dry or they'll become polluted and caked with sediment and mud,” he says.

Residents in other rural areas around the country have already reported that nearby data centers are making well water undrinkable. When Meta began construction on a $750 million data center in nearby Newton County, Ga. in 2018, the construction damaged local wells, caused municipal water prices to soar, and could cause the county to face a water deficit by 2030, according to reporting from the New York Times . Meta said that according to a study it commissioned, its data center project was unlikely to have impacted the water supply.

Soon after Project Sail was approved, four more data centers were proposed in Coweta County. In May, Coweta County approved a data center moratorium on any future projects, but residents say it’s too little, too late.
“It's kind of like, well, the horses are all out of the barn, let's be sure to close the door now,” says Swope.

The fight has left Beth and her family in limbo. They bought their home intending it to be a fixer-upper—the house is drafty, the windows need replacing. But they're hesitant to invest in a home they’re not sure they’ll stay in. “The unknown drives this cycle of [asking] do we move? I don't really want to move. Where do we move to?” she says. “They're everywhere. We'd want to move somewhere that also has a little bit of land, but all of that is that threat. We feel like there's no safe place to move.”
But, as of now, remaining put comes with its own set of problems. “If we stay here, this is going to be in our backyard.”

story.title: The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity

facts.text: But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes.
I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits.
The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity.
The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way.
The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to.
Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines.
Companies also build diesel generators for backup.
Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company.
Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded.
The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts.
The notion of data center companies’ bringing their own power might seem attractive at first, because they wouldn’t be straining the grid.

But generating electricity at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and when public utilities build infrastructure of this magnitude, communities have traditionally expected a say in where it goes.
Now, private companies are undertaking projects on a similar scale.
Companies might also try their chances abroad; Google, in fact, announced the day after the elections that it will spend $15 billion on data center projects in Malaysia.
The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts.
That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport .
But the real fault line is electricity: drawing it from the grid and generating it onsite provoke different kinds of backlash, neither easily solved by public relations.
The backlash to data centers isn’t really about water or electricity.
Greg Abbott has moved from cutting ribbons for big data center projects to issuing a list of demands about their power usage, location and economic contributions .
Economic analyst James Pethokoukis has calculated that even if water consumption by data centers quadruples in 2030, they’ll still take just 1% of our supply.
Enforce transparency about power and water usage .
Governments are already requiring the industry to generate its own electricity, and policymakers are even pushing data centers to provide a net increase in power.

Research indicates that data centers can actually help cut electricity prices because higher demand means more production.

That would save far more water than shutting down every data center.

The New York Stock Exchange is turning to Avalanche to power the behind-the-scenes plumbing of its forthcoming tokenized securities platform, one of the clearest signs yet that Wall Street's oldest institutions are moving core market infrastructure onto public blockchains.
Ava Labs, the company behind Avalanche, said Monday that the blockchain will serve as the "core ledger technology" for the clearing firm behind an NYSE-affiliated digital trading venue.

The New York Stock Exchange is turning to Avalanche to power the behind-the-scenes plumbing of its forthcoming tokenized securities platform, one of the clearest signs yet that Wall Street's oldest institutions are moving core market infrastructure onto public blockchains. Ava Labs, the company behind Avalanche, said Monday that the blockchain will serve as the "core ledger technology" for the clearing firm behind an NYSE-affiliated digital trading venue. The platform, which the NYSE's parent Intercontinental Exchange previously said it was developing, is designed to allow 24/7 trading, clearing and settlement of tokenized securities, subject to regulatory approval. Running on Avalanche, it aims to bring the clearing of tokenized equities onchain at institutional scale. Tokenization, the practice of issuing traditional assets as blockchain-based tokens, has become one of Wall Street's buzziest pursuits, but most efforts so far have centered on individual products rather than the market machinery itself. The NYSE's move is notable because it puts a blockchain underneath the clearing and settlement layer, the plumbing that finalizes trades, rather than just wrapping a single fund or stock in a token. Dennis Lee, the NYSE's head of digital issuance, said the exchange is "picking the right technology for each job," and that while its planned platform will support equities listed across a range of blockchains, the ledger recording and settling trades needs to be fast, reliable and able to control who participates. Emin Gün Sirer, Ava Labs' CEO and founder, framed the deal as proof that blockchains can support not just products but the infrastructure they trade on, citing Avalanche's "24/7 atomic settlement" and predictable costs. The announcement adds to a frenetic race to put stocks and their underlying infrastructure onchain. The NYSE separately tapped Blockchain.com to reach crypto investors with tokenized stocks and ETFs, while ICE and crypto exchange OKX are planning a 24/7 tokenized stock venue under an SEC exemption, and Morgan Stanley has moved to tokenize securities. Apple Completes the Set: Every Magnificent Seven Stock Opts Out of OKX-ICE Venue That OKX-ICE effort has hit friction, though: Every Magnificent Seven stock, including Apple and Meta , opted out of having its shares tokenized on the venue, with 67 companies in all joining them. Research shows the appetite for tokenized stocks is real but uneven. An IMF study found tokenized stocks show genuine demand yet remain volatile and illiquid, a reminder that the infrastructure may be arriving faster than the markets to fill it.

coreStoryFacts.text: The platform, which the NYSE's parent Intercontinental Exchange previously said it was developing, is designed to allow 24/7 trading, clearing and settlement of tokenized securities, subject to regulatory approval.
Running on Avalanche, it aims to bring the clearing of tokenized equities onchain at institutional scale.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.

The New York Stock Exchange is turning to Avalanche to power the behind-the-scenes plumbing of its forthcoming tokenized securities platform, one of the clearest signs yet that Wall Street's oldest institutions are moving core market infrastructure onto public blockchains.
Ava Labs, the company behind Avalanche, said Monday that the blockchain will serve as the "core ledger technology" for the clearing firm behind an NYSE-affiliated digital trading venue.

Emin Gün Sirer, Ava Labs' CEO and founder, framed the deal as proof that blockchains can support not just products but the infrastructure they trade on, citing Avalanche's "24/7 atomic settlement" and predictable costs.
Avalanche (AVAX) will settle trades on a planned 24/7 tokenized securities platform from the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE), the latter said on Monday.
The Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC) took its own tokenization service live on October 28.
Morgan Stanley tokenized US stocks and Treasuries through DTCC’s new service days later, as CryptoPotato reported.

“The upcoming digital trading platform will support equities listed on a range of blockchains, though the ledger that records and settles trades needs to be fast and reliable, let us control who can take part, keep costs predictable, and have a large community of developers behind it.
NYSE will use no other chain for that job, The Wall Street Journal reported , and its existing technology will match buy and sell orders, with Avalanche settling each trade instantly.

sources.title: Meta releases Muse Ember, a new lightweight model for agent execution
passages: Meta Superintelligence Lab released a new AI model on Monday called Muse Ember, the lab’s lightest and most cost-efficient AI model yet.
In its release, Meta said Ember was “designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing.”
Given the emphasis on low cost and accuracy at scale, Ember is designed to pair with a larger model like Meta’s Muse Wonder in an agentic harness.

In the case of a customer-support agent, for instance, you might see a heavier model establishing rules for how to handle a particular issue, then sending a lighter-weight model to apply the rules across tens of thousands of cases.
As Meta puts it in the announcement, “Muse Wonder plans, Muse Ember handles the volume.”
The flagship consumer AI product, the Muse Agent, was released in September to unexpected success , with new features like Spaces and video chat rolling out earlier this month.
With volume-heavy use cases in mind, Meta also trained Ember to work well across different types of media, including text, images, and audio.
The result makes the model surprisingly flexible in what kind of inputs it can handle.

Meta particularly emphasized Ember’s cost-per-task, using Artificial Analysis’s composite benchmark score to show Ember as cheaper and smarter than competitors like Anthropic’s Haiku and OpenAI’s Luna.
Meta acquires AI coding startup Conductor Lucas Ropek

coreStoryFacts.text: Meta Superintelligence Lab released a new AI model on Monday called Muse Ember, the lab’s lightest and most cost-efficient AI model yet.
In its release, Meta said Ember was “designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing.”
Given the emphasis on low cost and accuracy at scale, Ember is designed to pair with a larger model like Meta’s Muse Wonder in an agentic harness.

In the case of a customer-support agent, for instance, you might see a heavier model establishing rules for how to handle a particular issue, then sending a lighter-weight model to apply the rules across tens of thousands of cases.
As Meta puts it in the announcement, “Muse Wonder plans, Muse Ember handles the volume.”
The flagship consumer AI product, the Muse Agent, was released in September to unexpected success , with new features like Spaces and video chat rolling out earlier this month.
With volume-heavy use cases in mind, Meta also trained Ember to work well across different types of media, including text, images, and audio.
The result makes the model surprisingly flexible in what kind of inputs it can handle.

Meta particularly emphasized Ember’s cost-per-task, using Artificial Analysis’s composite benchmark score to show Ember as cheaper and smarter than competitors like Anthropic’s Haiku and OpenAI’s Luna.

relevantPassages.text: Meta Superintelligence Lab released a new AI model on Monday called Muse Ember, the lab’s lightest and most cost-efficient AI model yet.
In its release, Meta said Ember was “designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing.”
Given the emphasis on low cost and accuracy at scale, Ember is designed to pair with a larger model like Meta’s Muse Wonder in an agentic harness.

In the case of a customer-support agent, for instance, you might see a heavier model establishing rules for how to handle a particular issue, then sending a lighter-weight model to apply the rules across tens of thousands of cases.
As Meta puts it in the announcement, “Muse Wonder plans, Muse Ember handles the volume.”
The flagship consumer AI product, the Muse Agent, was released in September to unexpected success , with new features like Spaces and video chat rolling out earlier this month.
With volume-heavy use cases in mind, Meta also trained Ember to work well across different types of media, including text, images, and audio.
The result makes the model surprisingly flexible in what kind of inputs it can handle.

Meta particularly emphasized Ember’s cost-per-task, using Artificial Analysis’s composite benchmark score to show Ember as cheaper and smarter than competitors like Anthropic’s Haiku and OpenAI’s Luna.

Those are the unglamorous steps that sit between a user’s request and a finished result. They also happen to be the steps that burn the most tokens in a production agent. Meta’s documentation, which it publishes through a Muse Ember cookbook on the developer site, describes the model as an efficient execution model for high-volume, repeated work. The same documentation names sub-agent tasks and the processing of collections of images, files, and records as target uses. Muse Code is Meta’s coding environment, and the Meta Model API is the programmatic route for teams that want to wire the model into their own systems. Meta’s announcement does not, based on the sources we reviewed, list a third-party cloud marketplace for the model on day one. The confirmed spec sheet is short, and that is useful. Every figure below comes from Meta’s announcement or its documentation. Nothing here is an estimate or a leak. Where Meta has not stated something, such as benchmark scores, we leave it out instead of guessing. Agent workloads multiply calls. A single user request can fan out into a planning step, a dozen tool calls, several retrieval passes, a few code edits, and a final check. Meta’s answer is a tiered family. Keep the expensive reasoning for the moments that need it, and hand the repetitive volume to a cheaper model. That is not a new idea in software architecture. There is also a distribution angle. By shipping Muse Ember inside Muse Code and the Meta Model API together, Meta gets usage data on how developers split work between a planner and an executor. Whether Meta uses that data is not something the announcement addresses, so treat it as an incentive rather than a stated plan. It describes a two-model pattern in which a larger model decides what to do and a smaller one carries it out. In this pattern the larger model reads the task, breaks it into steps, and decides which steps can run in parallel. It is called rarely. Each call is expensive, but the count is low. The planner’s output is a set of instructions that a cheaper model can follow without needing to rediscover the whole problem. The executor runs the steps. It calls tools, reformats records, classifies requests, and drafts small code changes. Call volume is high and each call is small. This is where Muse Ember’s pricing does its work. If the planner writes a poor plan, the executor will carry it out faithfully and cheaply. Cheap mistakes at scale are still mistakes. Teams adopting the split need evaluation harnesses that check the final result, not only the per-step success rate. Three prices define Muse Ember. Fresh input costs $0.10 per million tokens. Cached input costs $0.004 per million tokens. Output costs $0.50 per million tokens. Output runs five times the fresh input rate, which is a common shape for model pricing because generating tokens costs more compute than reading them. The cached rate stands out. At $0.004, a cached input token costs 4 percent of a fresh one, or one twenty-fifth of the price. For an agent that resends the same system prompt, tool definitions, and reference material on every call, that gap can matter more than the headline $0.10. Meta’s announcement lists the cached price but, in the sources we reviewed, does not spell out cache write fees or expiry rules, so teams should confirm those details in the documentation before modeling costs. Pricing pressure at the low end of the market is already a theme. Our comparison of DeepSeek API pricing against Mistral showed how much room buyers have to shop on price, and Meta now adds a first-party option that undercuts the per-token cost most teams were used to paying for a mid-tier model. We are not claiming Muse Ember is the cheapest model on the market. Meta’s own sources do not establish that. Price per million tokens is abstract. The table below turns Meta’s published rates into concrete scenarios. These are our own illustrative calculations, not Meta figures, and they assume cached input is billed at the published $0.004 rate with no extra cache write charge. Real invoices will differ if Meta bills cache writes separately. Two takeaways stand out. First, long-context reads are cheap enough to be routine. Reading a full 1 million token window once costs about ten cents. Second, caching changes the extraction scenario from $65.00 to $26.60, a 59 percent cut, purely by reusing a shared prefix. The arithmetic is simple, but it shows why Meta published the cached price next to the headline rates. Most agent frameworks resend a large static block on every turn. That block holds instructions, tool schemas, style rules, and often a reference document. In a long-running agent, the static block can dwarf the new content in each call. When the static part is billed at $0.004 per million tokens, the marginal cost of the next call shrinks toward the cost of its fresh tokens alone. Outlets framed the launch competitively right away. The New Stack headlined its coverage as Meta taking on Claude Haiku and GPT-6 Luna. That is the outlet’s framing. The Meta material we reviewed does not publish a head-to-head benchmark against those models, so we cannot say how Muse Ember performs against them. A second framing came from Artificial Analysis , whose article title calls Muse Ember the cheapest model scoring 36 on its Intelligence Index. That is a third-party claim. Our fact sheet for this story treats benchmark scores and “cheapest” status as unconfirmed, because Meta’s own sources do not establish them. Readers who care about the number should read that analysis directly and check its methodology. For buyers, the honest comparison today rests on published prices and your own tests. Our earlier head-to-head of Claude against Gemini showed how close top models can sit on a single index, and how little a one-point gap says about a specific workload. The same caution applies to small models, where task fit counts for more than a leaderboard position. Tiered model lineups, with a large model for hard problems and a smaller one for volume, have become a common way to sell AI. Open-weight and low-cost players pushed the same direction from below. Our report on an open model scoring 72.8 percent on the Vals hacking test shows how far cheap and open options have climbed on specialized tasks, which is the pressure Meta’s pricing responds to. Meta’s wording ties Muse Ember to agent infrastructure, with sub-agent tasks and tool calls at the center. That reflects a shift from selling answers to selling throughput. Developers do not yet know how it handles tool-calling accuracy compared with the larger model it is meant to serve. Rate limits, regional availability, and service-level terms for the Meta Model API also need checking in the docs before a team commits. Lock-in is a second concern. A planner and executor pair from the same vendor is convenient. It also ties a team’s cost structure and evaluation suite to one provider’s pricing decisions. Teams that want flexibility should keep their orchestration layer model-agnostic and test a second executor alongside Muse Ember. Start by picking one high-volume, easy-to-score task in your own stack. Routing and field extraction work well. Build a labeled set of a few hundred examples, run Muse Ember against your current model, and compare accuracy, latency, and cost per thousand calls. Keep the test honest by including your hardest edge cases. Next, audit your prompts for cache friendliness. Move static instructions and tool definitions to the front, keep them identical between calls, and push anything that changes to the end. Then check Meta’s documentation for cache duration and any write fees, so your cost model matches the invoice. Muse Ember is a new Meta model, with the ID muse-ember-1.0 , that Meta calls its smallest and most efficient. It targets repeated agent work such as tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long-document parsing. When did Muse Ember launch? Coverage from TechCrunch is dated Nov. 9, 2026, the date of this article. It is available through Muse Code and the Meta Model API. How much does Muse Ember cost? Meta lists $0.10 per million input tokens, $0.004 per million cached input tokens, and $0.50 per million output tokens. How big is the context window? The context window is 1 million tokens, and the maximum output is 512,000 tokens, according to Meta’s announcement. Is Muse Ember the cheapest model available? Not established. A third-party article from Artificial Analysis makes that claim in its title, but Meta’s own sources do not confirm it, so we do not state it as fact. How does Muse Ember relate to Muse Wonder? Meta’s own line is “Muse Wonder plans, Muse Ember handles the volume.” In that framing, Muse Wonder handles planning and Muse Ember handles high-volume execution.

Second, caching changes the extraction scenario from $65.00 to $26.60, a 59 percent cut, purely by reusing a shared prefix. The arithmetic is simple, but it shows why Meta published the cached price next to the headline rates.

Most agent frameworks resend a large static block on every turn. That block holds instructions, tool schemas, style rules, and often a reference document. In a long-running agent, the static block can dwarf the new content in each call. When the static part is billed at $0.004 per million tokens, the marginal cost of the next call shrinks toward the cost of its fresh tokens alone.

Outlets framed the launch competitively right away. The New Stack headlined its coverage as Meta taking on Claude Haiku and GPT-6 Luna. That is the outlet’s framing. The Meta material we reviewed does not publish a head-to-head benchmark against those models, so we cannot say how Muse Ember performs against them.

A second framing came from Artificial Analysis , whose article title calls Muse Ember the cheapest model scoring 36 on its Intelligence Index. That is a third-party claim. Our fact sheet for this story treats benchmark scores and “cheapest” status as unconfirmed, because Meta’s own sources do not establish them. Readers who care about the number should read that analysis directly and check its methodology.

For buyers, the honest comparison today rests on published prices and your own tests. Our earlier head-to-head of Claude against Gemini showed how close top models can sit on a single index, and how little a one-point gap says about a specific workload. The same caution applies to small models, where task fit counts for more than a leaderboard position.

Tiered model lineups, with a large model for hard problems and a smaller one for volume, have become a common way to sell AI. Open-weight and low-cost players pushed the same direction from below. Our report on an open model scoring 72.8 percent on the Vals hacking test shows how far cheap and open options have climbed on specialized tasks, which is the pressure Meta’s pricing responds to.

Meta’s version is notable for its framing as an execution model. Small models have often been sold as a cheaper chat option. Meta’s wording ties Muse Ember to agent infrastructure, with sub-agent tasks and tool calls at the center. That reflects a shift from selling answers to selling throughput.

Several questions remain open, and the launch material does not answer them. Meta has not published, in the sources we reviewed, benchmark scores for Muse Ember. Developers do not yet know how it handles tool-calling accuracy compared with the larger model it is meant to serve. Rate limits, regional availability, and service-level terms for the Meta Model API also need checking in the docs before a team commits.

Lock-in is a second concern. A planner and executor pair from the same vendor is convenient. It also ties a team’s cost structure and evaluation suite to one provider’s pricing decisions. Teams that want flexibility should keep their orchestration layer model-agnostic and test a second executor alongside Muse Ember.

Start by picking one high-volume, easy-to-score task in your own stack. Routing and field extraction work well. Build a labeled set of a few hundred examples, run Muse Ember against your current model, and compare accuracy, latency, and cost per thousand calls. Keep the test honest by including your hardest edge cases.

Next, audit your prompts for cache friendliness. Move static instructions and tool definitions to the front, keep them identical between calls, and push anything that changes to the end. Then check Meta’s documentation for cache duration and any write fees, so your cost model matches the invoice. For broader context on where this fits among model news, see our AI and machine learning coverage .

What is Muse Ember? Muse Ember is a new Meta model, with the ID muse-ember-1.0 , that Meta calls its smallest and most efficient. It targets repeated agent work such as tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long-document parsing.
When did Muse Ember launch? Coverage from TechCrunch is dated Nov. 9, 2026, the date of this article. It is available through Muse Code and the Meta Model API.
How much does Muse Ember cost? Meta lists $0.10 per million input tokens, $0.004 per million cached input tokens, and $0.50 per million output tokens.
How big is the context window? The context window is 1 million tokens, and the maximum output is 512,000 tokens, according to Meta’s announcement.

Is Muse Ember the cheapest model available? Not established. A third-party article from Artificial Analysis makes that claim in its title, but Meta’s own sources do not confirm it, so we do not state it as fact.

How does Muse Ember relate to Muse Wonder? Meta’s own line is “Muse Wonder plans, Muse Ember handles the volume.” In that framing, Muse Wonder handles planning and Muse Ember handles high-volume execution.

story.title: Meta releases Muse Ember, a new lightweight model for agent execution

facts.text: Meta Superintelligence Lab released a new AI model on Monday called Muse Ember, the lab’s lightest and most cost-efficient AI model yet.
In its release, Meta said Ember was “designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing.”
Given the emphasis on low cost and accuracy at scale, Ember is designed to pair with a larger model like Meta’s Muse Wonder in an agentic harness.

In the case of a customer-support agent, for instance, you might see a heavier model establishing rules for how to handle a particular issue, then sending a lighter-weight model to apply the rules across tens of thousands of cases.
As Meta puts it in the announcement, “Muse Wonder plans, Muse Ember handles the volume.”
The flagship consumer AI product, the Muse Agent, was released in September to unexpected success , with new features like Spaces and video chat rolling out earlier this month.
With volume-heavy use cases in mind, Meta also trained Ember to work well across different types of media, including text, images, and audio.
The result makes the model surprisingly flexible in what kind of inputs it can handle.

Meta particularly emphasized Ember’s cost-per-task, using Artificial Analysis’s composite benchmark score to show Ember as cheaper and smarter than competitors like Anthropic’s Haiku and OpenAI’s Luna.
Meta acquires AI coding startup Conductor Lucas Ropek
Source : Meta releases Muse Ember, a new lightweight model for agent execution | TechCrunch , by Russell Brandom , TechCrunch , Nov 9, 2026

extraction.body: Missile explosions struck Kyiv and led to electricity outages early Saturday as Ukraine prepared for trilateral talks with Russia and the United States next Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, capital of the United Arab Emirates. Ukraine's European allies backing the peace initiative are seeking to be involved in the negotiations. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Interfax news agency the Russian delegation, headed again by Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky as chief negotiator, will include Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov for the first time and senior General Staff officer Yuri Zhigarlovsky. Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday met with all members of the delegation at a Security Council meeting. During the televised portion of the meeting, Putin thanked the UAE for its consistent help in finding a solution to the Ukrainian crisis and said he wanted to discuss preparations with the Russian team for the upcoming talks. Meanwhile, Russian guided aerial bombs that struck a former school and shelter in the village of Komyshuvakha near the front line in the Zaporizhzhia region on Monday have claimed at least 53 lives to date, according to Ukrainian authorities. Rescuers continued to dismantle the shattered structures and clear the rubble in search of bodies. Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy has appealed to Western allies for more deliveries after Russians forceshammered energy infrastructure around Kyiv with missiles and drones overnight. He stated the challenges of widespread power outages and water cuts are "very serious" for the capital's residents and industry. Zelenskyy announced in his daily briefing new agreements on energy supplies from Germany, Spain and Slovakia and other nations are in place for equipment needed for repairs and reserves. He also issued warning of fresh attacks being prepared against Ukraine's energy sector, bridges across the Dnipro River and civilian infrastructure. Speaking at the Ukrainian Embassy in the US, the Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets commended the US efforts in brokering a six-day ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Oleshky region and highlighted a major evacuation operation that enabled residents to be transferred to Ukrainian-held territory. The ombudsman said he hoped to expand such humanitarian efforts with the help of Washington. US President Donald Trump said he had meetings with people on Russia and other issues in his Florida resort. "Mar-a-Lago with a lot of different people having to do with Russia and having to do with other things...We just had a very good meeting and we have a lot of good calls made and we're doing very well, so we're working well with Russia, Ukraine. We're making a lot of progress," he said. In Warsaw, the European Union High Representative Kaja Kallas and Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski both stressed it would be impossible to reach a deal to stop the war in Ukraine without the participation of Europe. Sikorski further contended a ceasefire must come first before any kind of negotiation.

sources.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admits affair as company launches investigation into foreign spy claims
passages: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to having an extramarital affair as his company announced it will investigate reports he was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.” The separate statements come amid growing concern over Huang’s close relationship with an executive from Singapore-based tech company Megaspeed, Alice Huang.
“I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it,” Huang, 63, said, adding that he supports Nvidia’s investigation.

But, the board “has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.” In a note, Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at merchant bank Yorkville & Ives Co., called the news “a black eye moment for Jensen” that will increase scrutiny of chip sales to China, which Huang has previously lobbied for.

Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.” It added that any concerns about illegal chip diversion were “debunked last year.” Huang joked in a previous interview that he wooed his wife, Lori Huang, whom he met in college when he was 17 and she was 19, by offering to help with her homework and vowing to become a CEO by age 30.

“The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress.” China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Monday that the allegation that Alice Huang was gathering information for Beijing was “purely groundless speculation and an attempt to smear and malign China.” State-run tabloid The Global Times accused US media outlets of making up stories that could derail a detente between the two nations.
The investigation will also cast a shadow over Nvidia’s share price, Ives added, as investors question whether Huang will remain at the helm of the company he helped found.

“I don’t think it will serve the best interests of Nvidia shareholders and industry partners either if Jensen suddenly quits tomorrow.” The US government cleared 10 Chinese firms to buy Nvidia’s second-most powerful AI chips, Reuters reported earlier this year, though it’s unclear how many chips have actually been sold following the approval.

I think he probably has an excuse for it.” On Thursday, Republican chairmen of three influential House panels — the committees on Foreign Affairs, the Chinese Communist Party and Intelligence — said in a news release that they sent a letter to Huang requesting his appearance before their committees to answer questions about his relationship with Megaspeed and the company’s security protocols against foreign espionage.
Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption,” a spokesperson for Nvidia told CNN.

The China connection Huang’s connections to Alice Huang and Megaspeed, which buys chips from Nvidia, have come under intense scrutiny as a potential channel for US semiconductors to reach Chinese buyers, despite export controls on advanced technologies.

extraction.body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to having an extramarital affair as his company announced it will investigate reports he was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.” The separate statements come amid growing concern over Huang’s close relationship with an executive from Singapore-based tech company Megaspeed, Alice Huang. Several US outlets have reported that American officials suspect Alice Huang, no relation, has fed intelligence to China and helped smuggle advanced artificial intelligence chips into the country. The controversy could undermine faith in the world’s second-largest company and a poster child for the AI boom, at a time when the US and China are racing to surpass the other in technological supremacy. In a note to Nvidia staff, Huang said that he was “unfaithful” and hurt his wife and children. He did not name the other person in the affair. “I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it,” Huang, 63, said, adding that he supports Nvidia’s investigation. “I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security.” Meanwhile, the company said in a Sunday press release that a committee of independent directors and outside counsel will oversee its investigation. “The Board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” the statement said. But, the board “has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.” In a note, Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at merchant bank Yorkville & Ives Co., called the news “a black eye moment for Jensen” that will increase scrutiny of chip sales to China, which Huang has previously lobbied for. The investigation will also cast a shadow over Nvidia’s share price, Ives added, as investors question whether Huang will remain at the helm of the company he helped found. Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption,” a spokesperson for Nvidia told CNN. Jacob Ward, a tech journalist and CNN contributor, said corporate boards historically tend to oust chief executives caught having extramarital affairs within days. For Nvidia, which holds an outsized role in AI development, global growth and the US stock market, any existential questions about its future will have even greater economic and geopolitical implications. Another unusual factor is that the company has no clear successor for Huang, he added. And this guy who is famously a very, very central commander of all of this stuff, suddenly being caught in this way and especially being caught perhaps being dishonest about it, it’s an incredibly big deal,” Ward said. The China connection Huang’s connections to Alice Huang and Megaspeed, which buys chips from Nvidia, have come under intense scrutiny as a potential channel for US semiconductors to reach Chinese buyers, despite export controls on advanced technologies. The Financial Times previously reported that US intelligence believed that the two were in a romantic relationship. Nvidia said in a past statement that Jensen Huang’s meetings were “not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.” It added that any concerns about illegal chip diversion were “debunked last year.” Huang joked in a previous interview that he wooed his wife, Lori Huang, whom he met in college when he was 17 and she was 19, by offering to help with her homework and vowing to become a CEO by age 30. In 1993, he co-founded Nvidia, which has seen its market capitalization swell to more than $4 trillion as the rise of AI has turbocharged demand for the computer chips it designs. He has since become the face of the company and a prominent figure in the booming business of AI. Huang joined President Donald Trump with a host of other high-profile CEOs in Beijing earlier this year to meet with Chinese leader Xi Jinping. Many people will say Nvidia without Jensen won’t be the same,” George Chen, partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group, wrote in a Monday note. “I don’t think it will serve the best interests of Nvidia shareholders and industry partners either if Jensen suddenly quits tomorrow.” The US government cleared 10 Chinese firms to buy Nvidia’s second-most powerful AI chips, Reuters reported earlier this year, though it’s unclear how many chips have actually been sold following the approval. On Sunday, Trump told reporters that he has not spoken to Huang since Nvidia announced the investigation, but said that he was a “fine person” and praised his contribution to the country. When asked if he wished he had taken action when briefed on the intelligence about alleged spying last year, Trump said, “No I don’t think so. I think he probably has an excuse for it.” On Thursday, Republican chairmen of three influential House panels — the committees on Foreign Affairs, the Chinese Communist Party and Intelligence — said in a news release that they sent a letter to Huang requesting his appearance before their committees to answer questions about his relationship with Megaspeed and the company’s security protocols against foreign espionage. “Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC’s access to sensitive US technology and information,” the chairmen wrote. “The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress.” China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Monday that the allegation that Alice Huang was gathering information for Beijing was “purely groundless speculation and an attempt to smear and malign China.” State-run tabloid The Global Times accused US media outlets of making up stories that could derail a detente between the two nations. On Chinese social media, Huang’s admission of infidelity became one of the top trending topics with more than 40 million views on the X-like platform Weibo. However, the allegation that Alice Huang was working as a Chinese spy was largely absent from tightly-controlled online discussions.

sources.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admits affair as company launches investigation into foreign spy claims
passages: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to having an extramarital affair as his company announced it will investigate reports he was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.” The separate statements come amid growing concern over Huang’s close relationship with an executive from Singapore-based tech company Megaspeed, Alice Huang.
“I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it,” Huang, 63, said, adding that he supports Nvidia’s investigation.

But, the board “has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.” In a note, Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at merchant bank Yorkville & Ives Co., called the news “a black eye moment for Jensen” that will increase scrutiny of chip sales to China, which Huang has previously lobbied for.

Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.” It added that any concerns about illegal chip diversion were “debunked last year.” Huang joked in a previous interview that he wooed his wife, Lori Huang, whom he met in college when he was 17 and she was 19, by offering to help with her homework and vowing to become a CEO by age 30.

“The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress.” China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Monday that the allegation that Alice Huang was gathering information for Beijing was “purely groundless speculation and an attempt to smear and malign China.” State-run tabloid The Global Times accused US media outlets of making up stories that could derail a detente between the two nations.
The investigation will also cast a shadow over Nvidia’s share price, Ives added, as investors question whether Huang will remain at the helm of the company he helped found.

“I don’t think it will serve the best interests of Nvidia shareholders and industry partners either if Jensen suddenly quits tomorrow.” The US government cleared 10 Chinese firms to buy Nvidia’s second-most powerful AI chips, Reuters reported earlier this year, though it’s unclear how many chips have actually been sold following the approval.

I think he probably has an excuse for it.” On Thursday, Republican chairmen of three influential House panels — the committees on Foreign Affairs, the Chinese Communist Party and Intelligence — said in a news release that they sent a letter to Huang requesting his appearance before their committees to answer questions about his relationship with Megaspeed and the company’s security protocols against foreign espionage.
Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption,” a spokesperson for Nvidia told CNN.

The China connection Huang’s connections to Alice Huang and Megaspeed, which buys chips from Nvidia, have come under intense scrutiny as a potential channel for US semiconductors to reach Chinese buyers, despite export controls on advanced technologies.

extraction.body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to having an extramarital affair as his company announced it will investigate reports he was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.” The separate statements come amid growing concern over Huang’s close relationship with an executive from Singapore-based tech company Megaspeed, Alice Huang. Several US outlets have reported that American officials suspect Alice Huang, no relation, has fed intelligence to China and helped smuggle advanced artificial intelligence chips into the country. The controversy could undermine faith in the world’s second-largest company and a poster child for the AI boom, at a time when the US and China are racing to surpass the other in technological supremacy. In a note to Nvidia staff, Huang said that he was “unfaithful” and hurt his wife and children. He did not name the other person in the affair. “I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it,” Huang, 63, said, adding that he supports Nvidia’s investigation. “I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security.” Meanwhile, the company said in a Sunday press release that a committee of independent directors and outside counsel will oversee its investigation. “The Board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” the statement said. But, the board “has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.” In a note, Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at merchant bank Yorkville & Ives Co., called the news “a black eye moment for Jensen” that will increase scrutiny of chip sales to China, which Huang has previously lobbied for. The investigation will also cast a shadow over Nvidia’s share price, Ives added, as investors question whether Huang will remain at the helm of the company he helped found. Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption,” a spokesperson for Nvidia told CNN. Jacob Ward, a tech journalist and CNN contributor, said corporate boards historically tend to oust chief executives caught having extramarital affairs within days. For Nvidia, which holds an outsized role in AI development, global growth and the US stock market, any existential questions about its future will have even greater economic and geopolitical implications. Another unusual factor is that the company has no clear successor for Huang, he added. And this guy who is famously a very, very central commander of all of this stuff, suddenly being caught in this way and especially being caught perhaps being dishonest about it, it’s an incredibly big deal,” Ward said. The China connection Huang’s connections to Alice Huang and Megaspeed, which buys chips from Nvidia, have come under intense scrutiny as a potential channel for US semiconductors to reach Chinese buyers, despite export controls on advanced technologies. The Financial Times previously reported that US intelligence believed that the two were in a romantic relationship. Nvidia said in a past statement that Jensen Huang’s meetings were “not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.” It added that any concerns about illegal chip diversion were “debunked last year.” Huang joked in a previous interview that he wooed his wife, Lori Huang, whom he met in college when he was 17 and she was 19, by offering to help with her homework and vowing to become a CEO by age 30. In 1993, he co-founded Nvidia, which has seen its market capitalization swell to more than $4 trillion as the rise of AI has turbocharged demand for the computer chips it designs. He has since become the face of the company and a prominent figure in the booming business of AI. Huang joined President Donald Trump with a host of other high-profile CEOs in Beijing earlier this year to meet with Chinese leader Xi Jinping. Many people will say Nvidia without Jensen won’t be the same,” George Chen, partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group, wrote in a Monday note. “I don’t think it will serve the best interests of Nvidia shareholders and industry partners either if Jensen suddenly quits tomorrow.” The US government cleared 10 Chinese firms to buy Nvidia’s second-most powerful AI chips, Reuters reported earlier this year, though it’s unclear how many chips have actually been sold following the approval. On Sunday, Trump told reporters that he has not spoken to Huang since Nvidia announced the investigation, but said that he was a “fine person” and praised his contribution to the country. When asked if he wished he had taken action when briefed on the intelligence about alleged spying last year, Trump said, “No I don’t think so. I think he probably has an excuse for it.” On Thursday, Republican chairmen of three influential House panels — the committees on Foreign Affairs, the Chinese Communist Party and Intelligence — said in a news release that they sent a letter to Huang requesting his appearance before their committees to answer questions about his relationship with Megaspeed and the company’s security protocols against foreign espionage. “Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC’s access to sensitive US technology and information,” the chairmen wrote. “The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress.” China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Monday that the allegation that Alice Huang was gathering information for Beijing was “purely groundless speculation and an attempt to smear and malign China.” State-run tabloid The Global Times accused US media outlets of making up stories that could derail a detente between the two nations. On Chinese social media, Huang’s admission of infidelity became one of the top trending topics with more than 40 million views on the X-like platform Weibo. However, the allegation that Alice Huang was working as a Chinese spy was largely absent from tightly-controlled online discussions.

passages: Nominal, a four-year-old, Austin-based startup that offers an AI platform purpose-built for engineering and testing complex hardware, like aircraft, nuclear reactors, and smart factories, has raised another big round of financing that triples its valuation.
On Monday, it announced a $240 million Series C at a $3 billion valuation led by Lightspeed Venture Partners and co-led by Insight Partners.
Nominal says that it has 80 commercial and government organizations as customers.
One of its key customers is Anduril, the defense company co-founded by Stephens.

Nominal also won a government contract in October when the Air Force selected it for a $71.2 million Strategic Funding Increase (STRATFI) investment, which is a program that requires matching funds from outside the Air Force.

For context, OpenAI recently hit a $1.25 trillion valuation on an $11 billion round, while drone delivery startup Zipline soared to $21.5 billion on $1.5 billion in new funding.
But the fact that sophisticated investors are willing to triple Nominal's price in eight months suggests the company is showing strong traction, even if the specifics remain under wraps.
While consumer AI apps struggle to justify their valuations, enterprise-focused platforms like Nominal are commanding premium prices.
The real test will be whether Nominal can convert that sky-high valuation into a sustainable business as more traditional industries wake up to the power of AI tooling.
If Nominal's tools work well enough for Anduril to bet on them, that's a powerful signal to other hardware-heavy industries.
Nominal seems to be riding a similar wave, but in the hardware domain rather than pure software.
The startup, which counts defense tech giant Anduril among its major customers, is riding the wave of AI infrastructure investment that's reshaping how hardware gets built.

extraction.body: AI hardware engineering platform Nominal just closed a funding round that rockets its valuation to $3 billion - a stunning triple from eight months ago. The startup, which counts defense tech giant Anduril among its major customers, is riding the wave of AI infrastructure investment that's reshaping how hardware gets built. The deal marks one of the fastest valuation jumps in the current funding cycle and signals that investors are betting big on AI tools that bridge software and physical engineering. Nominal, a startup building AI-powered tools for hardware engineers, just landed a funding round that tripled its valuation to $3 billion in just eight months - one of the sharpest valuation climbs in today's more cautious venture market. The deal, reported by TechCrunch, puts the young company in rare company among AI infrastructure plays and underscores how desperately the hardware world needs better software tools. While consumer AI apps struggle to justify their valuations, enterprise-focused platforms like Nominal are commanding premium prices. The company's AI platform helps hardware engineers test, validate, and troubleshoot complex systems - the kind of unglamorous but mission-critical work that defense contractors, aerospace companies, and advanced manufacturers desperately need to scale. Anduril, Palmer Luckey's defense tech unicorn, has emerged as a major customer, lending serious credibility to Nominal's approach. That relationship alone likely played a role in the valuation surge, especially as Anduril itself has been partnering with major tech players to build domestic manufacturing capabilities. Nominal's 3x jump in eight months stands out even in a market that's seen wild swings. For context, OpenAI recently hit a $1.25 trillion valuation on an $11 billion round, while drone delivery startup Zipline soared to $21.5 billion on $1.5 billion in new funding. Nominal's rapid ascent suggests investors see it as an early mover in a category that's about to explode - AI for the physical world. The hardware engineering space has long been starved for modern software tools. Nominal's platform uses AI to automate much of that grunt work, spotting anomalies in sensor data, predicting failure modes, and helping teams iterate faster. What makes this deal particularly interesting is the customer profile. If Nominal's tools work well enough for Anduril to bet on them, that's a powerful signal to other hardware-heavy industries. The defense sector alone represents a massive TAM, and Anduril's endorsement could open doors across the industrial base. The funding environment for AI startups remains bifurcated. While some companies struggle to raise at flat or down rounds, others - particularly those with clear enterprise revenue and defensible moats - are seeing valuations climb. Fal recently doubled its valuation to $16 billion on $1.3 billion in new funding, driven by surging demand for AI inference infrastructure. Nominal seems to be riding a similar wave, but in the hardware domain rather than pure software. Just a year ago, most AI investment was flowing to foundation model companies and consumer chatbot plays. Nominal fits squarely in that category, offering specialized AI that solves real pain points for engineers who've been underserved by software innovation. Nominal hasn't disclosed the size of this latest round or which investors led it. The company also hasn't shared revenue figures or customer counts beyond name-dropping Anduril. In a market that's grown skeptical of valuation hype, those details matter. But the fact that sophisticated investors are willing to triple Nominal's price in eight months suggests the company is showing strong traction, even if the specifics remain under wraps. The broader trend is clear: AI is finally coming for hardware. Companies like Nominal are building the connective tissue between AI models and the messy, complex world of atoms and physics. And if this valuation is any indication, investors believe that market is just getting started. Nominal's rocket ride to $3 billion in eight months isn't just a win for one startup - it's a signal that AI's next frontier is the physical world. With Anduril as a marquee customer and investors clearly betting on enterprise AI infrastructure, the company is positioned at the intersection of two massive trends: AI adoption and the modernization of hardware engineering. The real test will be whether Nominal can convert that sky-high valuation into a sustainable business as more traditional industries wake up to the power of AI tooling.

coreStoryFacts.text: Nominal, a four-year-old, Austin-based startup that offers an AI platform purpose-built for engineering and testing complex hardware, like aircraft, nuclear reactors, and smart factories, has raised another big round of financing that triples its valuation.
On Monday, it announced a $240 million Series C at a $3 billion valuation led by Lightspeed Venture Partners and co-led by Insight Partners.
Nominal says that it has 80 commercial and government organizations as customers.
One of its key customers is Anduril, the defense company co-founded by Stephens.

Nominal also won a government contract in October when the Air Force selected it for a $71.2 million Strategic Funding Increase (STRATFI) investment, which is a program that requires matching funds from outside the Air Force.

extraction.body: Nominal, a four-year-old, Austin-based startup that offers an AI platform purpose-built for engineering and testing complex hardware, like aircraft, nuclear reactors, and smart factories, has raised another big round of financing that triples its valuation. On Monday, it announced a $240 million Series C at a $3 billion valuation led by Lightspeed Venture Partners and co-led by Insight Partners. This follows the company’s announcement in March of a $155 million Series B extension at a $1 billion valuation, led by Trae Stephens at Founders Fund. That round was a “preemptive” deal — meaning an offer initiated by the investor, not the startup. Other investors in the company include Sequoia, General Catalyst, and Lux Capital. Nominal says that it has 80 commercial and government organizations as customers. One of its key customers is Anduril, the defense company co-founded by Stephens. Nominal also won a government contract in October when the Air Force selected it for a $71.2 million Strategic Funding Increase (STRATFI) investment, which is a program that requires matching funds from outside the Air Force. Nominal CEO and co-founder Cameron McCord (pictured) is a former U.S. Navy submarine officer and an Anduril alum. For context, OpenAI recently hit a $1.25 trillion valuation on an $11 billion round, while drone delivery startup Zipline soared to $21.5 billion on $1.5 billion in new funding.
Nominal's rapid ascent suggests investors see it as an early mover in a category that's about to explode - AI for the physical world.
The hardware engineering space has long been starved for modern software tools.
Nominal's platform uses AI to automate much of that grunt work, spotting anomalies in sensor data, predicting failure modes, and helping teams iterate faster.
What makes this deal particularly interesting is the customer profile.
If Nominal's tools work well enough for Anduril to bet on them, that's a powerful signal to other hardware-heavy industries.
The defense sector alone represents a massive TAM, and Anduril's endorsement could open doors across the industrial base.
The funding environment for AI startups remains bifurcated.
While some companies struggle to raise at flat or down rounds, others - particularly those with clear enterprise revenue and defensible moats - are seeing valuations climb.
Fal recently doubled its valuation to $16 billion on $1.3 billion in new funding, driven by surging demand for AI inference infrastructure.
Nominal seems to be riding a similar wave, but in the hardware domain rather than pure software.
Just a year ago, most AI investment was flowing to foundation model companies and consumer chatbot plays.
Nominal fits squarely in that category, offering specialized AI that solves real pain points for engineers who've been underserved by software innovation.
Nominal hasn't disclosed the size of this latest round or which investors led it.
The company also hasn't shared revenue figures or customer counts beyond name-dropping Anduril.
In a market that's grown skeptical of valuation hype, those details matter.
But the fact that sophisticated investors are willing to triple Nominal's price in eight months suggests the company is showing strong traction, even if the specifics remain under wraps.
The broader trend is clear: AI is finally coming for hardware.
Companies like Nominal are building the connective tissue between AI models and the messy, complex world of atoms and physics.
And if this valuation is any indication, investors believe that market is just getting started.
Nominal's rocket ride to $3 billion in eight months isn't just a win for one startup - it's a signal that AI's next frontier is the physical world.

With Anduril as a marquee customer and investors clearly betting on enterprise AI infrastructure, the company is positioned at the intersection of two massive trends: AI adoption and the modernization of hardware engineering.
The real test will be whether Nominal can convert that sky-high valuation into a sustainable business as more traditional industries wake up to the power of AI tooling.

facts.text: Nominal, a four-year-old, Austin-based startup that offers an AI platform purpose-built for engineering and testing complex hardware, like aircraft, nuclear reactors, and smart factories, has raised another big round of financing that triples its valuation.

The General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania , United States , has enacted ‘Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act’, after receiving assent from the Pennsylvania Governor, Josh Shapiro, to become an act enforceable under the court of law. The act defines ‘artificial intelligence’ or ‘AI’ as a machine‑based system that, for a given set of human‑defined objectives, can make predictions, recommendations or decisions influencing real or virtual environments, and includes generative artificial intelligence. The Commonwealth of Pennsylvania enacted AI Deceptive Advertising Act, requiring clear and conspicuous disclosure of AI‑generated synthetic content in advertisements.

The General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania , United States , has enacted ‘Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act’, after receiving assent from the Pennsylvania Governor, Josh Shapiro, to become an act enforceable under the court of law. The act defines ‘artificial intelligence’ or ‘AI’ as a machine‑based system that, for a given set of human‑defined objectives, can make predictions, recommendations or decisions influencing real or virtual environments, and includes generative artificial intelligence. Further, the term ‘Generative artificial intelligence’ is defined as the class of models that emulate the structure and characteristics of input data in order to generate synthetic content.

As per the provisions of the act , any advertisement – whether a still image, video, audio or text – that ‘has been significantly modified or generated by artificial intelligence’ include a label in the same format as the ad itself. The requirement applies to advertisements broadcast or displayed in Pennsylvania, regardless of where the ad was created, meaning disclosures may appear in commercials aired in other states if they are also intended for Pennsylvania audiences.

The legislation is among the first in the United States to mandate the labelling of AI-generated advertising content, setting a precedent as to how AI‑derived content may be disclosed to consumers. In a related development, Congresswoman Shontel Brown has also introduced the Securing Elections from AI Deception Act, which seeks to prohibit the use of artificial intelligence to deprive or defraud individuals of their right to vote and require disclaimers on AI-generated campaign content.

extraction.body: Insights on Tech Law, Regulation & Policy, AI, IoT and More On October 22, 2026, the Governor of Pennsylvania signed the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act ( Senate Bill 806 ) (“Act”) into law. The Act joins a growing number of state laws focused on the use of AI in advertising. However, unlike the laws in New York and California, Pennsylvania’s disclosure requirement is not limited to AI-generated advertisements using a synthetic performer. The law takes effect 60 days after enactment, on December 21, 2026. Urgent case for statecraft on green iron and steel to secure Australia's future prosperity

Today, the mounting crisis at Whyalla brings sharply into focus both the risks and opportunities of this pivotal moment in Australia’s energy transition, and the transition of the global steelmaking industry more broadly.
Climate change, energy insecurity, technological transformation and geopolitical competition are reshaping the economic and strategic landscape.
They can no longer be understood – or governed – in isolation.
They demand a more strategic response: one that aligns public institutions and private investment to build the industries that will underpin future prosperity and national resilience.
As a foundation industry , steel underpins Australia’s construction, energy, transport and defence capabilities.
Its successful decarbonisation therefore offers far more than emissions reduction.

It has the potential to unlock billions of dollars in investment, create new employment opportunities across regional Australia, stimulate new renewable energy development, and strengthen Australia’s sovereign industrial capability.
Energy transition is more than an environmental imperative, although this is key as the climate crisis escalates.
If governed strategically, it can become one of Australia’s greatest national security multipliers – strengthening our prosperity, resilience and sovereign capability for decades to come.
The objective is not to shelter industries that cannot compete.
Government’s role is to help overcome the early barriers to commercialisation, not to provide permanent support.

With the right policy architecture, Australia could see renewables-powered electric arc furnaces deployed in low-emissions steelmaking in Collie, Western Australia; Whyalla, South Australia; and greater Brisbane, Queensland, as soon as next year.
Australia is exceptionally well placed to succeed.
Abundant renewable resources, world-class mineral endowments, outstanding research capability and trusted relationships with key Indo-Pacific partners provide a formidable starting position.
Yet these advantages will not translate automatically into industrial leadership or national resilience.

They can no longer be understood – or governed – in isolation. They demand a more strategic response: one that aligns public institutions and private investment to build the industries that will underpin future prosperity and national resilience. Few industries better illustrate both the scale of the challenge – and the opportunity – than iron and steel. As a foundation industry , steel underpins Australia’s construction, energy, transport and defence capabilities. Its successful decarbonisation therefore offers far more than emissions reduction. It has the potential to unlock billions of dollars in investment, create new employment opportunities across regional Australia, stimulate new renewable energy development, and strengthen Australia’s sovereign industrial capability. In short, it calls for a Green Energy Statecraft approach. Green Energy Statecraft starts from a simple proposition: the decarbonisation of strategic industries like iron and steel – and the creation of the green industries that will follow – is not simply a climate imperative. It is an opportunity to strengthen economic, energy, environmental, social and geostrategic security simultaneously. The countries that prosper will not necessarily be those with the greatest natural resources or the deepest fiscal pockets, but those with the governance capabilities to translate comparative advantages into enduring national strength. Australia is exceptionally well placed to succeed. Abundant renewable resources, world-class mineral endowments, outstanding research capability and trusted relationships with key Indo-Pacific partners provide a formidable starting position. Yet these advantages will not translate automatically into industrial leadership or national resilience. The objective is not to shelter industries that cannot compete. It is to use Australia’s structural advantages – particularly its exceptional potential for low-cost renewable energy and its mineral resources – to build industries that can become globally competitive in a decarbonising world. Government’s role is to help overcome the early barriers to commercialisation, not to provide permanent support. Pricing carbon remains an essential part of the policy toolkit. It helps ensure markets better reflect the true costs of emissions and encourages cleaner production and consumption. But no country has ever taxed its way to techno-industrial transformation. This is because the challenge of building entirely new industries is not simply one of price signals. It is one of investment coordination. Green iron and steel projects require billions of dollars in upfront capital while depending simultaneously on renewable energy generation, enabling infrastructure, processing facilities, skilled workforces, long-term customers and supporting supply chains. Each investment depends on the others proceeding, creating a classic coordination problem that private markets alone struggle to resolve. Even where the long-term commercial opportunity is compelling, few investors are willing to move first when so much depends on decisions beyond their control. For these reasons, governments have a key role to play in making strategic projects bankable . In practice, this means coordinating investment, infrastructure, finance, procurement, regulation and skills around a shared long-term national ambition. The central question for policymakers is therefore not simply: Which policy instrument should we use? It is: Which strategic capability are we trying to create – and what combination of public and private action will bring it into being? A new report from think tank Climate Energy Finance, Arc of Ambition , is a timely contribution to that challenge, connecting Australia’s resource and renewable-energy endowments with a practical pathway for industrial renewal in the iron and steel sector. It demonstrates how strategic investment in domestic low-emissions steel production can revitalise regional communities, crowd in private capital, stimulate renewable energy development and strengthen sovereign manufacturing capability. More importantly, it shows how the right governance, financing and institutional arrangements can turn that opportunity into bankable projects. In doing so, it points towards precisely the kind of home-grown recipe that Australia needs if the Future Made in Australia agenda is to move beyond aspiration and deliver globally competitive industries. Energy transition is more than an environmental imperative, although this is key as the climate crisis escalates. extraction.body: Home NSW News Green Energy Statecraft: Turning Australia’s Energy Transition into a National Security Multiplier On Tuesday 3 November, AIIA New South Wales welcomed Elizabeth Thurbon, Professor of International Political Economy in the School of Social Sciences at UNSW Sydney and co-founder and Director of the university’s Green Energy Statecraft Project, to address us on how Australia might view the green energy transition as an opportunity to become a “renewables” superpower. This transition is transforming economies and relationships across the Indo-Pacific. For Australia, it can be a national security multiplier – strengthening economic, energy, environmental, social and geostrategic security. But these gains are not automatic. Drawing on the work of the Green Energy Statecraft Project, Professor Thurbon examined how Australia can use its resources to build clean industries and reduce strategic dependencies. She suggested that cooperation on clean energy and industry can strengthen Australia’s security and reinforce its role as a trusted trade and development partner in the region. Professor Thurbon explained that the energy transition is a techno-economic paradigm shift for governments and economies. To speed the shift, state actors must be both willing and able to invest in green energy creation and in fossil fuel destruction, two outcomes which affect different demographics. In the West, the focus has largely been to start with the latter. But the pattern of the North-East-Asian region has been quite different, starting with billions of dollars of investment in the mid-2000s on ambitious energy generation projects, with pressure on the fossils phase-out only now coming increasingly to the forefront. The other major divergence, Thurbon argued, has been in ways of thinking about the purpose of the energy transition. In Australia, the focus has been on environmental necessity, which has had limited bipartisan appeal. In North East-Asia, pursuing the energy transition quickly has been viewed as a “national security multiplier” – an opportunity to boost environmental security, but also energy security, economic security, social security, and geostrategic security.
