By pursuing green energy transition “at pace”, she argued, Australia can boost its energy security and, by developing new industries, its economic security. In short, it calls for a Green Energy Statecraft approach.

Today, the mounting crisis at Whyalla brings sharply into focus both the risks and opportunities of this pivotal moment in Australia’s energy transition, and the transition of the global steelmaking industry more broadly.
Climate change, energy insecurity, technological transformation and geopolitical competition are reshaping the economic and strategic landscape.
They can no longer be understood – or governed – in isolation.
They demand a more strategic response: one that aligns public institutions and private investment to build the industries that will underpin future prosperity and national resilience.
As a foundation industry , steel underpins Australia’s construction, energy, transport and defence capabilities.
Its successful decarbonisation therefore offers far more than emissions reduction.

It has the potential to unlock billions of dollars in investment, create new employment opportunities across regional Australia, stimulate new renewable energy development, and strengthen Australia’s sovereign industrial capability.
Energy transition is more than an environmental imperative, although this is key as the climate crisis escalates.
If governed strategically, it can become one of Australia’s greatest national security multipliers – strengthening our prosperity, resilience and sovereign capability for decades to come.
The objective is not to shelter industries that cannot compete.
Government’s role is to help overcome the early barriers to commercialisation, not to provide permanent support.

With the right policy architecture, Australia could see renewables-powered electric arc furnaces deployed in low-emissions steelmaking in Collie, Western Australia; Whyalla, South Australia; and greater Brisbane, Queensland, as soon as next year.
Australia is exceptionally well placed to succeed.
Abundant renewable resources, world-class mineral endowments, outstanding research capability and trusted relationships with key Indo-Pacific partners provide a formidable starting position.
Yet these advantages will not translate automatically into industrial leadership or national resilience.

extraction.body: Australia’s iron and steel sector shows why climate policy, industrial strategy and national security now need to be governed together, not treated as separate problems. Australia faces a nation-defining moment. Climate change, energy insecurity, technological transformation and geopolitical competition are reshaping the economic and strategic landscape. They can no longer be understood – or governed – in isolation. They demand a more strategic response: one that aligns public institutions and private investment to build the industries that will underpin future prosperity and national resilience. Few industries better illustrate both the scale of the challenge – and the opportunity – than iron and steel. As a foundation industry , steel underpins Australia’s construction, energy, transport and defence capabilities. Its successful decarbonisation therefore offers far more than emissions reduction. It has the potential to unlock billions of dollars in investment, create new employment opportunities across regional Australia, stimulate new renewable energy development, and strengthen Australia’s sovereign industrial capability. With the right policy architecture, Australia could see renewables-powered electric arc furnaces deployed in low-emissions steelmaking in Collie, Western Australia; Whyalla, South Australia; and greater Brisbane, Queensland, as soon as next year. Realising that opportunity, however, demands more than isolated policy interventions. It requires strategic coordination between the public and private sectors. In short, it calls for a Green Energy Statecraft approach. Green Energy Statecraft starts from a simple proposition: the decarbonisation of strategic industries like iron and steel – and the creation of the green industries that will follow – is not simply a climate imperative. It is an opportunity to strengthen economic, energy, environmental, social and geostrategic security simultaneously. The countries that prosper will not necessarily be those with the greatest natural resources or the deepest fiscal pockets, but those with the governance capabilities to translate comparative advantages into enduring national strength. Australia is exceptionally well placed to succeed. Abundant renewable resources, world-class mineral endowments, outstanding research capability and trusted relationships with key Indo-Pacific partners provide a formidable starting position. Yet these advantages will not translate automatically into industrial leadership or national resilience. The objective is not to shelter industries that cannot compete. It is to use Australia’s structural advantages – particularly its exceptional potential for low-cost renewable energy and its mineral resources – to build industries that can become globally competitive in a decarbonising world. Government’s role is to help overcome the early barriers to commercialisation, not to provide permanent support. Pricing carbon remains an essential part of the policy toolkit. It helps ensure markets better reflect the true costs of emissions and encourages cleaner production and consumption. But no country has ever taxed its way to techno-industrial transformation. This is because the challenge of building entirely new industries is not simply one of price signals. It is one of investment coordination. Green iron and steel projects require billions of dollars in upfront capital while depending simultaneously on renewable energy generation, enabling infrastructure, processing facilities, skilled workforces, long-term customers and supporting supply chains. Each investment depends on the others proceeding, creating a classic coordination problem that private markets alone struggle to resolve. Even where the long-term commercial opportunity is compelling, few investors are willing to move first when so much depends on decisions beyond their control. For these reasons, governments have a key role to play in making strategic projects bankable . In practice, this means coordinating investment, infrastructure, finance, procurement, regulation and skills around a shared long-term national ambition. The central question for policymakers is therefore not simply: Which policy instrument should we use? It is: Which strategic capability are we trying to create – and what combination of public and private action will bring it into being? A new report from think tank Climate Energy Finance, Arc of Ambition , is a timely contribution to that challenge, connecting Australia’s resource and renewable-energy endowments with a practical pathway for industrial renewal in the iron and steel sector. It demonstrates how strategic investment in domestic low-emissions steel production can revitalise regional communities, crowd in private capital, stimulate renewable energy development and strengthen sovereign manufacturing capability. More importantly, it shows how the right governance, financing and institutional arrangements can turn that opportunity into bankable projects. In doing so, it points towards precisely the kind of home-grown recipe that Australia needs if the Future Made in Australia agenda is to move beyond aspiration and deliver globally competitive industries. Australia’s opportunity lies not simply in decarbonising existing industries, but in using the transition to build entirely new sources of national capability, resilience and prosperity. Energy transition is more than an environmental imperative, although this is key as the climate crisis escalates. If governed strategically, it can become one of Australia’s greatest national security multipliers – strengthening our prosperity, resilience and sovereign capability for decades to come. The views expressed in this article may or may not reflect those of Pearls and Irritations. Elizabeth Thurbon is Professor of International Political Economy, Deputy Head of School and Director of Research in the School of Social Sciences at UNSW Sydney. She is also Director of the Green Energy Statecraft Project, a collaborative initiative between UNSW Sydney, the University of Melbourne and the University of Sydney. Urgent case for statecraft on green iron and steel to secure Australia's future prosperity A handful of years ago, South Australia’s Whyalla steelworks, owned by British industrialist Sanjeeev Gupta, was touted as the potential birthplace of an Australian green iron and steel industry. Today, the mounting crisis at Whyalla brings sharply into focus both the risks and opportunities of this pivotal moment in Australia’s energy transition, and the transition of the global steelmaking industry more broadly. A carbon tax will obviously help reduce carbon emissions and achievement of the net zero target, but it will also help raise the revenue needed to fund essential government services and promote Australia’s economic development. The 'Future Made in Australia' plan for solar panels relies on a crucial ingredient: Help from China Twenty-three years ago, a Chinese-Australian solar scientist moved from Sydney to Wuxi to build China's solar panel manufacturing industry from scratch, using technology developed in Australian universities. ‘Too much wind and solar’? Ten years on, South Australia tells a different story Ten years after South Australia’s statewide blackout became a political weapon against renewables, the state now gets more than three-quarters of its electricity from renewable sources. The technology has raced ahead, even if the politics has barely moved.

With the right policy architecture, Australia could see renewables-powered electric arc furnaces deployed in low-emissions steelmaking in Collie, Western Australia; Whyalla, South Australia; and greater Brisbane, Queensland, as soon as next year.

Realising that opportunity, however, demands more than isolated policy interventions. It requires strategic coordination between the public and private sectors. In short, it calls for a Green Energy Statecraft approach.

Green Energy Statecraft starts from a simple proposition: the decarbonisation of strategic industries like iron and steel – and the creation of the green industries that will follow – is not simply a climate imperative. It is an opportunity to strengthen economic, energy, environmental, social and geostrategic security simultaneously. The countries that prosper will not necessarily be those with the greatest natural resources or the deepest fiscal pockets, but those with the governance capabilities to translate comparative advantages into enduring national strength.

Australia is exceptionally well placed to succeed. Abundant renewable resources, world-class mineral endowments, outstanding research capability and trusted relationships with key Indo-Pacific partners provide a formidable starting position. Yet these advantages will not translate automatically into industrial leadership or national resilience.

The objective is not to shelter industries that cannot compete. It is to use Australia’s structural advantages – particularly its exceptional potential for low-cost renewable energy and its mineral resources – to build industries that can become globally competitive in a decarbonising world. Government’s role is to help overcome the early barriers to commercialisation, not to provide permanent support.

Pricing carbon remains an essential part of the policy toolkit. It helps ensure markets better reflect the true costs of emissions and encourages cleaner production and consumption. But no country has ever taxed its way to techno-industrial transformation.

This is because the challenge of building entirely new industries is not simply one of price signals. It is one of investment coordination. Green iron and steel projects require billions of dollars in upfront capital while depending simultaneously on renewable energy generation, enabling infrastructure, processing facilities, skilled workforces, long-term customers and supporting supply chains. Each investment depends on the others proceeding, creating a classic coordination problem that private markets alone struggle to resolve. Even where the long-term commercial opportunity is compelling, few investors are willing to move first when so much depends on decisions beyond their control.

For these reasons, governments have a key role to play in making strategic projects bankable . In practice, this means coordinating investment, infrastructure, finance, procurement, regulation and skills around a shared long-term national ambition. The central question for policymakers is therefore not simply: Which policy instrument should we use? It is: Which strategic capability are we trying to create – and what combination of public and private action will bring it into being?

A new report from think tank Climate Energy Finance, Arc of Ambition , is a timely contribution to that challenge, connecting Australia’s resource and renewable-energy endowments with a practical pathway for industrial renewal in the iron and steel sector. It demonstrates how strategic investment in domestic low-emissions steel production can revitalise regional communities, crowd in private capital, stimulate renewable energy development and strengthen sovereign manufacturing capability.

More importantly, it shows how the right governance, financing and institutional arrangements can turn that opportunity into bankable projects. In doing so, it points towards precisely the kind of home-grown recipe that Australia needs if the Future Made in Australia agenda is to move beyond aspiration and deliver globally competitive industries.

Australia’s opportunity lies not simply in decarbonising existing industries, but in using the transition to build entirely new sources of national capability, resilience and prosperity. Energy transition is more than an environmental imperative, although this is key as the climate crisis escalates. If governed strategically, it can become one of Australia’s greatest national security multipliers – strengthening our prosperity, resilience and sovereign capability for decades to come.
The views expressed in this article may or may not reflect those of Pearls and Irritations.

She is also Director of the Green Energy Statecraft Project, a collaborative initiative between UNSW Sydney, the University of Melbourne and the University of Sydney.

extraction.body: Home NSW News Green Energy Statecraft: Turning Australia’s Energy Transition into a National Security Multiplier On Tuesday 3 November, AIIA New South Wales welcomed Elizabeth Thurbon, Professor of International Political Economy in the School of Social Sciences at UNSW Sydney and co-founder and Director of the university’s Green Energy Statecraft Project, to address us on how Australia might view the green energy transition as an opportunity to become a “renewables” superpower. This transition is transforming economies and relationships across the Indo-Pacific. For Australia, it can be a national security multiplier – strengthening economic, energy, environmental, social and geostrategic security. But these gains are not automatic. Drawing on the work of the Green Energy Statecraft Project, Professor Thurbon examined how Australia can use its resources to build clean industries and reduce strategic dependencies. She suggested that cooperation on clean energy and industry can strengthen Australia’s security and reinforce its role as a trusted trade and development partner in the region. Professor Thurbon explained that the energy transition is a techno-economic paradigm shift for governments and economies. To speed the shift, state actors must be both willing and able to invest in green energy creation and in fossil fuel destruction, two outcomes which affect different demographics. In the West, the focus has largely been to start with the latter. But the pattern of the North-East-Asian region has been quite different, starting with billions of dollars of investment in the mid-2000s on ambitious energy generation projects, with pressure on the fossils phase-out only now coming increasingly to the forefront. The other major divergence, Thurbon argued, has been in ways of thinking about the purpose of the energy transition. In Australia, the focus has been on environmental necessity, which has had limited bipartisan appeal. In North East-Asia, pursuing the energy transition quickly has been viewed as a “national security multiplier” – an opportunity to boost environmental security, but also energy security, economic security, social security, and geostrategic security. This, the Statecraft Project concludes, has prompted a more positive attitude to the energy transition. Thurbon advocated for Australia to view investment in renewables as the cure to our “cascade of converging challenges”. By pursuing green energy transition “at pace”, she argued, Australia can boost its energy security and, by developing new industries, its economic security. It could allow us to grow new export markets, for example, in green ammonia and polysilicon, strengthening our relationships with partners in the Pacific and reducing our dependence on unpredictable global energy prices. Exporting green iron and green steel would offer new, profitable exports. But the government needs to deliver ambitious, strategic policy. Such statecraft can unite voters across the political divide. Professor Thurbon’s presentation invited lots of engagement from the audience. A key question which emerged was why we should be relying on governments, rather than the market, to drive change. Professor Thurbon explained that consultation with industry has revealed that preliminary capital investment costs create a need for demand-side policy; no country has ever taxed its way to a techno-industrial revolution. The Green Energy Project proposes a policy whereby the government contracts to purchase the “green premium” on the first volumes of products like sustainable aviation fuel. The commodity then sells on the market at conventional prices, while the government banks “Clean Commodity Credits” to be traded later. Firm contracts also offer the benefit of being irreversible at the next election, building investor trust. An additional question picked up from the discussion was whether the Project’s research has actually affected real world policy. Lily Manning, one of our Councillors, offered her perspective, shaped by working in government. She agreed with Professor Thurbon that the Project’s focus on demand has impacted the government’s approach to regional engagement.

extraction.body: Promoting best practices for integrated mobility Culver CityBus promotes its official transit app, which provides riders with real-time arrival information and trip planning tools, alongside one of the agency's green New Flyer electric buses. The city of Culver City, Calif., and rabbittransit have partnered with transit technology companies to better the customer experience. The Transit app is now the recommended app for Culver CityBus riders through a Royale sponsorship. With Royale, Culver City notes riders gain access to unlimited departure schedules, additional trip planning options, custom app themes and icons and more. Culver CityBus can also communicate with riders through the app, keeping them informed of important changes and events as they happen. The Transit app helps users navigate public transit in 1000 cities in 28 countries around the world with multi-modal trip planning and nearby departure times. “Reliable public transportation begins with giving riders clear, timely information they can use with confidence,” said Culver City Mayor Freddy Puza. “Our partnership with Transit makes it easier to plan trips, receive real-time service updates and navigate Culver CityBus from one convenient app. This is another important step in our ongoing work to improve the rider experience and make sustainable transportation more accessible to everyone.” Transit and Culver CityBus are also improving the rider experience regarding service disruptions, as planned detours, service changes and disruptions in Culver CityBus’s real-time feed will appear for riders on the map and influence the trip planner results in the Transit app. “Our mission has always been to help people get around without their own car,” said Transit app CEO Sam Vermette. “Every month we help eight million people around the world navigate their cities by bus, train, foot, bike and more, and that wouldn’t be possible without our agency partners. We’re proud to be working hand-in-hand with Culver CityBus to unlock the best app experience for their riders.” Modeshift launched rabbitPAY, a new account-based fare collection platform designed to make paying for mobility services easier, more flexible and more affordable on rabbittransit systems. The rabbitPAY platform introduces mobile ticketing, reloadable smart cards, automatic fare capping and real-time account management tools for riders using Capital Region, Gettysburg, Shippensburg and York fixed-route services, as well as rabbitEXPRESS, Capital Region Commuter Routes and Stop Hopper services. With automatic fare capping capabilities available on fixed urban and fixed rural services, Modeshift notes riders can simply pay as they go. Once they reach the cost of a monthly pass, additional rides during that month are free, ensuring riders automatically receive the best available fare without needing to purchase a pass upfront. "rabbitPAY represents a major step forward in providing a more convenient and modern transit experience for our riders," said rabbittransit Executive Director Richard Farr. "rabbitPAY makes paying for transit as easy as tapping a phone or smart card while ensuring riders automatically receive the best fare available. Our goal is to remove barriers and make public transportation even more convenient, accessible and user-friendly for the communities we serve." Key features of rabbittransit’s new fare collection system include: According to Modeshift, as the rollout continues, rabbittransit will become the first transit agency to deploy Modeshift's new validating fareboxes while continuing to expand the rabbitPAY platform with ticket vending machines and, at a later stage, open payment. Together, the enhancements will unify cash payments, contactless bank cards, mobile wallets, mobile ticketing, smart cards and account-based payments within Modeshift's integrated 360-degree fare collection platform. "rabbittransit is building one of the most modern and flexible fare collection systems in the state," said Modeshift CEO Miroslav Katsarov. "By bringing together digital payment options, farecapping and soon, our validating fareboxes through a single integrated platform, rabbittransit is creating a more seamless rider experience today while laying the foundation for future regional fare integration across Pennsylvania." Modeshift's account-based platform also supports interoperability between transit agencies, creating future opportunities for seamless regional travel and simplified fare payments as additional agencies in the state modernize their systems. With automatic fare capping capabilities available on fixed urban and fixed rural services, Modeshift notes riders can simply pay as they go. Once they reach the cost of a monthly pass, additional rides during that month are free, ensuring riders automatically receive the best available fare without needing to purchase a pass upfront.

"rabbitPAY represents a major step forward in providing a more convenient and modern transit experience for our riders," said rabbittransit Executive Director Richard Farr. "rabbitPAY makes paying for transit as easy as tapping a phone or smart card while ensuring riders automatically receive the best fare available. Our goal is to remove barriers and make public transportation even more convenient, accessible and user-friendly for the communities we serve."
Key features of rabbittransit’s new fare collection system include:

According to Modeshift, as the rollout continues, rabbittransit will become the first transit agency to deploy Modeshift's new validating fareboxes while continuing to expand the rabbitPAY platform with ticket vending machines and, at a later stage, open payment. Together, the enhancements will unify cash payments, contactless bank cards, mobile wallets, mobile ticketing, smart cards and account-based payments within Modeshift's integrated 360-degree fare collection platform.

"rabbittransit is building one of the most modern and flexible fare collection systems in the state," said Modeshift CEO Miroslav Katsarov. "By bringing together digital payment options, farecapping and soon, our validating fareboxes through a single integrated platform, rabbittransit is creating a more seamless rider experience today while laying the foundation for future regional fare integration across Pennsylvania."

Modeshift's account-based platform also supports interoperability between transit agencies, creating future opportunities for seamless regional travel and simplified fare payments as additional agencies in the state modernize their systems.

Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) has dominated the semiconductor market throughout the artificial intelligence (AI) revolutions. Its graphics processing units (GPUs) are essential infrastructure for companies developing generative AI models. Naturally, investors are focusing on competitors like Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD) and Intel (NASDAQ: INTC), both of which make their own GPU and CPU architectures. However, I think Nvidia's biggest competitive threat could come from an entirely different direction. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » AI hyperscalers are developing their own processors, known as application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), to reduce costs and optimize performance for particular workloads. With major customers including Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOGL) (NASDAQ: GOOG), Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META), OpenAI, and Anthropic, Broadcom (NASDAQ: AVGO) is emerging as a formidable competitor for future AI infrastructure spending. Here's why smart investors should pay attention. Nvidia's GPUs are useful because they can handle a wide variety of accelerated computing tasks. However, that flexibility isn't always necessary. Custom ASICs are designed for specific applications, potentially offering better performance per dollar of compute and lower energy consumption for certain workloads. Broadcom is helping design these specialized processors while also supplying networking technology that connects clusters of chips inside data centers. Let's consider its expanding roster of AI chip customers. Alphabet is working with Broadcom on its Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), including the seventh-generation Ironwood processor. These chips support Google Cloud and are being deployed for Anthropic. Broadcom expects Anthropic to deploy 5 gigawatts of eighth-generation TPU v8i capacity in 2027, followed by an additional 10 gigawatts in 2028. Meanwhile, Meta is collaborating with Broadcom on its Meta Training and Inference Accelerator (MTIA) processors. Their partnership extends through 2029, with visibility into 3 gigawatts of deployments through 2028. Last October, Broadcom and OpenAI announced plans to deploy 5 gigawatts of XPUs by the end of 2028. OpenAI's first processor, code-named Jalapeño, is expected to support 1.3 gigawatts of deployments in 2027. These relationships show how Broadcom isn't simply competing for isolated semiconductor contracts. The company is becoming an important partner for world's largest AI developers. Broadcom's financial results suggest demand for custom silicon is accelerating. During the company's fiscal third quarter (period ended Aug. 2), AI semiconductor revenue more than tripled year over year to $16.7 billion. Custom chips accounted for roughly 73% of that total. Management guided for AI semiconductor revenue to reach $21.7 billion in the fourth quarter. The longer-term projections are even more impressive. Broadcom expects AI semiconductor revenue to reach roughly $115 billion in fiscal 2027 and potentially double to $230 billion in fiscal 2028. This is where it gets challenging for Nvidia. As AI adoption accelerates, developers are increasingly focused on inference, the process of using trained models to generate responses and perform tasks. Specialized processors can be attractive for repetitive inference workloads because they are designed around specific requirements. As a result, custom silicon could become a growing market that competes with Nvidia's GPUs in data center budgets. The investment thesis here becomes compelling once you consider Broadcom's valuation. As of this writing (Nov. 6), Broadcom stock trades around $294, representing a 39% decline from its all-time high. Broadcom stock now trades at a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) multiple of 15, its cheapest level since the AI revolution began. I think Broadcom's valuation profile looks reasonable given management's robust expectations for AI semiconductor growth in fiscal 2027 and 2028. Moreover, the company's business extends beyond custom processors. Broadcom also specializes in Ethernet switching, optical connectivity, and other networking technologies that are essential for connecting AI accelerators. On a deeper level, this means Broadcom can actually benefit from expanding AI infrastructure even when customers continue purchasing Nvidia GPUs. This means Nvidia doesn't actually need to lose its dominance for Broadcom to become a winner in the AI chip market. Rather, Broadcom simply needs more hyperscalers to decide that designing their own silicon makes economic sense. Based on its customer relationships and revenue outlook, that transition appears to be gathering momentum. For long-term investors looking for alternatives to Nvidia, Broadcom deserves serious consideration. The 10 stocks that made the cut could produce monster returns in the coming years. Broadcom's financial results suggest demand for custom silicon is accelerating. During the company's fiscal third quarter (period ended Aug. 2), AI semiconductor revenue more than tripled year over year to $16.7 billion. Custom chips accounted for roughly 73% of that total.

Management guided for AI semiconductor revenue to reach $21.7 billion in the fourth quarter. The longer-term projections are even more impressive. Broadcom expects AI semiconductor revenue to reach roughly $115 billion in fiscal 2027 and potentially double to $230 billion in fiscal 2028.

This is where it gets challenging for Nvidia. As AI adoption accelerates, developers are increasingly focused on inference , the process of using trained models to generate responses and perform tasks.

Specialized processors can be attractive for repetitive inference workloads because they are designed around specific requirements. As a result, custom silicon could become a growing market that competes with Nvidia's GPUs in data center budgets.

The investment thesis here becomes compelling once you consider Broadcom's valuation. As of this writing (Nov. 6), Broadcom stock trades around $294, representing a 39% decline from its all-time high. Broadcom stock now trades at a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) multiple of 15, its cheapest level since the AI revolution began.

I think Broadcom's valuation profile looks reasonable given management's robust expectations for AI semiconductor growth in fiscal 2027 and 2028. Moreover, the company's business extends beyond custom processors. Broadcom also specializes in Ethernet switching, optical connectivity, and other networking technologies that are essential for connecting AI accelerators.

On a deeper level, this means Broadcom can actually benefit from expanding AI infrastructure even when customers continue purchasing Nvidia GPUs. This means Nvidia doesn't actually need to lose its dominance for Broadcom to become a winner in the AI chip market. Rather, Broadcom simply needs more hyperscalers to decide that designing their own silicon makes economic sense.

Based on its customer relationships and revenue outlook, that transition appears to be gathering momentum. For long-term investors looking for alternatives to Nvidia, Broadcom deserves serious consideration.

Bloomberg Intelligence expects TPU sales to top $135 billion by 2028, up from an estimated $12 billion this year. Google, the Alphabet Inc. unit, is introducing two new versions of its tensor processing units (TPUs), with an announcement due Monday, November 9, 2026, as Google escalates its Nvidia rivalry in the market for artificial intelligence chips. The market is worth hundreds of billions of dollars. TPUs are custom-made semiconductors that help develop and run AI software. The new variants are called the TPU 8tx and the 8i Max. Google's chip unit is speeding up. It once released a new AI processor every two years. This year it put out two at the same time, and the new variants add to that pair. The four TPU offerings will each serve different needs, Google chip chief Amin Vahdat said in an interview. "The future is going to be about specialization," he said, describing the company's thesis. The two new chips are not entirely new silicon designs. Vahdat said they are reconfigured to take on tasks customers have been requesting. The 8tx targets secure, confidential work for customers such as government agencies and companies in regulated industries. It works with chips from Advanced Micro Devices Inc., as part of a collaboration between the two companies. The 8i Max is built for AI applications that need long-context windows. That term describes the amount of data an AI system can consider in a single request. Vahdat said it matters for drug discovery and math, and for coding applications. The variants will be available next year, he said. TPUs compete in a market dominated by Nvidia Corp.'s graphics processing units, or GPUs. Google began developing the technology more than a decade ago with Broadcom Inc., which helped with design and coordinating production. The aim was to handle the search giant's growing computing needs more efficiently. Google has since begun selling TPUs outside its cloud-computing operation. Bloomberg Intelligence estimates TPU sales, including related software and hardware, will top $135 billion by 2028. That compares with an estimated $12 billion this year and excludes sales to clients using the chips through Google Cloud. Apple Inc., Meta Platforms Inc. and Oracle Corp. are among the customers. Specialized versions should help Google make further progress, Vahdat said. "We could build a single chip that tries to address the whole market, or by building specialized versions of the chips, we actually can deliver much more value," he said. The launch comes at a turbulent time for the industry. Worries about a possible slowdown in infrastructure spending have rattled tech stocks. US midterm elections that swept Democrats into power have raised fresh doubts about data center projects. Demand for Nvidia's AI processors still exceeds what the company can supply. That leaves room for Google and other contenders to build sizable businesses. The English-language global edition of JournalArta.
